n: Caliph al-Mamun (r. 813–833) transformed Baghdad's House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikmah) into a systematic translation and research institution.
Greek philosophical, scientific, and medical works including those of Aristotle, Plato, Galen, and Ptolemy were translated into Arabic under Abbasid patronage.
The Abbasid translation movement employed Christian, Jewish, and Muslim scholars working together.
The Abbasid revolutionary movement originated in Khorasan in eastern Iran and was led by Abu Muslim.
The Abbasids defeated the last Umayyad caliph Marwan II at the Battle of the Zab River in 750.
After taking power the Abbasids moved the capital of the Islamic world from Damascus to the newly founded Baghdad in 762.
Abd al-Rahman III, emir of Córdoba since 912, took the titles of Caliph and Commander of the Faithful in 929.
By declaring the caliphate Abd al-Rahman III asserted parity with the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad and the Fatimid caliph in Cairo.
Abd al-Rahman III built the palace city of Medina Azahara outside Córdoba.
Peter Abelard's Sic et Non ('Yes and No') juxtaposed 158 contradictory patristic opinions on theological questions for the reader to resolve by dialectical reasoning.
Abelard's Sic et Non became a paradigmatic model of the scholastic quaestio method.
Pope Lucius III issued the decretal Ad Abolendam in 1184, jointly with Frederick Barbarossa at Verona, naming Cathars, Patarines, Waldensians, and other heretical movements.
Ad Abolendam obliged secular princes to assist bishops in suppressing heresy.
Henry V's outnumbered English army defeated the French at Agincourt in 1415 through superior use of the longbow against armored knights in muddy conditions.
The French nobility suffered catastrophic losses at Agincourt, with over 6,000 killed against roughly 400 English dead.
Following Agincourt, Henry V negotiated the Treaty of Troyes in 1420, making him heir to the French throne.
Pope Innocent III launched the Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229) against the Cathar heresy in Languedoc in southern France.
The Albigensian Crusade established the Papal Inquisition as a permanent institution in 1233.
The Albigensian Crusade transferred the County of Toulouse to the French crown in 1271.
The Albigensian Crusade was the first crusade directed against fellow Christians.
Charlemagne invited Alcuin of York to head his palace school at Aachen around 782.
Alcuin standardized the Carolingian minuscule script, the ancestor of modern lowercase letters.
Alcuin developed the curriculum of the seven liberal arts that structured medieval education.
Prince Alexander Nevsky of Novgorod led a combined Novgorodian-Suzdal force that defeated the Livonian Order on the frozen surface of Lake Peipus on 5 April 1242.
The Battle on the Ice halted the Teutonic and Livonian Order's eastward expansion.
Alexander Nevsky was later canonized as a national hero by the Russian Orthodox Church.
Alexios I Komnenos seized the Byzantine throne in 1081 with the support of the military aristocracy.
Alexios I replaced the Byzantine thematic system with pronoia grants (military fiefs).
Alexios I wrote to Pope Urban II in 1095 requesting mercenaries, helping trigger the First Crusade.
After his victory at Edington in 878, Alfred the Great reorganized Wessex's defense around a network of fortified towns (burhs).
Approximately 33 burhs were established in Wessex, spaced so no point was more than 20 miles from a fortification.
The Wessex burh system was recorded in the Burghal Hidage, a document of around 919.
Alfred the Great of Wessex established a court school and commissioned translations of Latin texts into Old English, including Boethius, Gregory's Pastoral Care, and Bede's Ecclesiastical History.
Alfred the Great initiated the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.
After Alfred the Great's victory at Edington, the Danish leader Guthrum accepted baptism and the Treaty of Wedmore divided England between Wessex and the Danelaw.
Ferdinand and Isabella issued the Alhambra Decree on 31 March 1492, ordering all Jews in Spain who refused baptism to leave within four months.
Between roughly 40,000 and 100,000 Jews chose exile rather than conversion following the Alhambra Decree, dispersing to Portugal, the Ottoman Empire, North Africa, and the Netherlands.
The combined Christian armies of Castile, Aragon, and Navarre defeated the Almohad caliph Muhammad al-Nasir at Las Navas de Tolosa in July 1212.
Almohad power in Iberia collapsed after the defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.
Within three decades of Las Navas de Tolosa, Castile took Córdoba (1236), Valencia (1238), and Seville (1248).
Under Abd al-Rahman III and al-Hakam II, Córdoba became the largest city in Western Europe with roughly 250,000 inhabitants.
The library of al-Hakam II in Córdoba reportedly held 400,000 volumes.
The muwaššaḥ strophic poetic form was invented in Iberia under the Córdoban caliphate.
Abu Hamid al-Ghazali abandoned his teaching position at the Nizamiyya in Baghdad around 1095 for a decade of Sufi wandering.
Al-Ghazali wrote Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din ('The Revival of the Religious Sciences'), reconciling Sunni orthodoxy with Sufi mysticism.
Caliph al-Mansur founded the circular planned 'City of Peace' (Madinat al-Salam) at Baghdad in 762, with four gates aligned to the cardinal directions.
Within a generation of its founding, Baghdad became the world's largest city, with population estimates ranging from 500,000 to 1,000,000.
The polymath ʿAlī al-Masʿūdī completed Murūj al-Dhahab ('The Meadows of Gold and Mines of Gems'), an encyclopedic universal history and geography in 30 books, around 947.
Al-Masʿūdī's work followed three decades of travel from the Caspian to the Indus and down the East African coast.
Henry II of England died on 6 July 1189 at Chinon Castle.
At Henry II's death the Angevin domains spanning England, Normandy, Brittany, Anjou, Maine, Touraine, and Aquitaine formed the largest personal lordship in Western Europe.
Henry II's reign transformed English law through Common Law reforms including the Assize of Clarendon in 1166.
Henry II of England's three eldest sons rebelled simultaneously in 1173–1174 with the backing of Louis VII of France and William I of Scotland.
Henry II captured King William of Scotland in 1174, after which the rebellion against him collapsed.
Byzantine Emperor Basil II completed the conquest of the First Bulgarian Empire in a campaign culminating in 1018.
After Basil II's conquest, Bulgaria became a Byzantine province for the next 167 years.
An earthquake on 20 May 526 destroyed most of Antioch on the Orontes.
Justin I and Justinian funded extensive reconstruction of Antioch after the 526 earthquake, but the city never recovered its late-antique demographic peak.
Thomas Aquinas began his Summa Theologica around 1265, the most comprehensive medieval synthesis of Aristotelian philosophy and Christian theology.
Left unfinished at Aquinas's death in 1274, the Summa Theologica became the standard text of Catholic philosophy.
Arab Muslim forces under Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated the Byzantine army at Yarmouk in 636 and proceeded to conquer Syria.
Jerusalem surrendered to Caliph Umar in 638 during the Arab conquest of Syria.
The Arab general Amr ibn al-As led a force into Egypt in 639, exploiting Byzantine exhaustion after the Persian wars.
Alexandria surrendered to the Arabs in 641, ending seven centuries of Greco-Roman rule in Egypt.
Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the Strait of Gibraltar in 711 and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic at the Battle of Guadalete.
The Muslim-Berber conquest swept through most of Iberia within three years, with only the mountainous north resisting.
Arab Muslim forces under Saad ibn Abi Waqqas defeated the main Sassanid army at al-Qadisiyyah around 636.
The Sassanid capital Ctesiphon fell shortly after al-Qadisiyyah, and the Sassanid Empire was absorbed into the Rashidun Caliphate within twenty years.
The Umayyad caliph Suleiman dispatched a large fleet and army against Constantinople in 717.
Emperor Leo III defended Constantinople using Greek fire, which destroyed the Arab fleet, and the siege was abandoned in 718.
Alfonso I of Aragon captured Zaragoza, the largest Taifa city, in 1118 after a prolonged siege.
The capture of Zaragoza doubled the size of the kingdom of Aragon and opened the Ebro valley.
Ramiro I inherited Aragon as a kingdom in 1035 after the death of Sancho III of Navarre divided his realms among his sons.
Peter III of Aragon claimed Sicily in 1282 following the Sicilian Vespers uprising against Charles of Anjou.
The War of the Sicilian Vespers established Aragonese dominance in the western Mediterranean.
The marriage of Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona to Petronilla of Aragon in 1137 created the Crown of Aragon, uniting the kingdom of Aragon with the County of Barcelona.

Twelfth-century translators in Toledo, Palermo, and other Islamic-Christian contact zones produced Latin translations of Aristotle's complete works alongside Arabic commentaries by Avicenna and Averroës.
The recovery of Aristotle's works gave European thought a secular rational framework that challenged purely theological approaches.
Attila the Hun's invasion of Gaul was halted at the Battle of the Catalaunian Fields in 451 by a Roman-Visigoth coalition under Aetius.
Attila died in 453 and the Hunnic empire collapsed within a few years.
Pope Alexander IV's bull Licet Ecclesiae catholicae consolidated several eremitic communities into a single Order of Hermits of Saint Augustine in 1256.
The Treaty of Neuberg in 1379 divided Habsburg Austria between Duke Albert III and Duke Leopold III.
The Albertine-Leopoldine division of Habsburg Austria lasted until Albert V reunified the dynasty in 1424.
Charlemagne launched a decisive campaign against the Avar Khaganate from 788 to 796.
The Frankish army captured the Avar treasure that had accumulated from Byzantine tribute over generations.
Former Avar territory in modern Hungary was incorporated into the Carolingian Empire as the Eastern March, precursor of Austria.
Florence's two largest banking houses, the Bardi and the Peruzzi, failed around 1345 after Edward III of England repudiated loans estimated at 1.5 million florins.
The collapse of the Bardi and Peruzzi banks triggered cascade failures among smaller Florentine houses.
Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, proving the Atlantic and Indian Oceans are connected and that a sea route to India existed.
Dias's rounding of the Cape enabled Vasco da Gama's voyage to India in 1498.
Byzantine Emperor Basil II defeated the First Bulgarian Empire under Tsar Samuel at the Battle of Kleidion on 29 July 1014.
After Kleidion, Basil II blinded the great majority of roughly 15,000 Bulgarian prisoners, leaving one eye to one man in each hundred to lead the rest home.
Tsar Samuel died shortly after seeing his blinded army return from Kleidion.
Basil II assumed the senior Byzantine throne at age 18 on the death of John I Tzimiskes in 976.
Basil II's fifty-year reign restored Byzantine territory to its largest extent since the 7th century.
Emperor Valens led the Eastern Roman army to a catastrophic defeat against the Visigoths at Adrianople on 9 August 378, and was killed in the battle.
Adrianople was the worst Roman military defeat since Cannae and inaugurated the era of barbarian settlement within the Empire.
Timur confronted the Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I near Ankara on 20 July 1402.
Bayezid I was captured at Ankara, the only Ottoman sultan ever taken prisoner in battle, and died in Timurid captivity in 1403.
After Ankara the Ottomans lost most of Anatolia and entered the Ottoman Interregnum of 1402–1413.
Henry V's English army defeated a much larger French army at Agincourt on 25 October 1415.
English longbowmen positioned with forest flanks and sharpened stakes devastated the French men-at-arms struggling through muddy ground at Agincourt.
Robert the Bruce defeated Edward II's much larger invasion force at Bannockburn in 1314 by choosing ground that neutralized English archery and cavalry.
The victory at Bannockburn effectively secured Scottish independence, formalized by the Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton in 1328.
The Grand Duchy of Lithuania under Algirdas defeated three Tatar princes of the Golden Horde at the Battle of Blue Waters around 1362.
The victory at Blue Waters extended Lithuanian sovereignty over former Kievan Rus territories toward the Black Sea.
Philip II Augustus of France defeated a coalition of Otto IV, King John of England, and the counts of Flanders and Boulogne at Bouvines in 1214.
Bouvines consolidated Capetian power and confirmed the French conquest of English-held Normandy.
The defeat at Bouvines contributed to King John's baronial crisis that produced Magna Carta in 1215.
Æthelstan of England defeated a coalition of Dublin Vikings, Scots, and Strathclyde Britons at Brunanburh in 937.
The victory at Brunanburh established Æthelstan as the supreme ruler of the British Isles.
French forces defeated an English relief force under John Talbot at Castillon on 17 July 1453, the last major engagement of the Hundred Years' War.
French artillery under Jean Bureau devastated the English at Castillon, where Talbot was killed.
The English loss at Castillon ended roughly 300 years of Plantagenet rule in Aquitaine, leaving only Calais of England's French territories.
The People's Crusade led by Peter the Hermit reached Constantinople in 1096 and was transported to Asia Minor by Emperor Alexios I.
The People's Crusade was annihilated by Kilij Arslan's Turkish forces at Civetot on 21 October 1096.
Pelayo defeated a Muslim force at Covadonga around 722, the first significant Christian military victory over Muslim Iberia.
Pelayo became the first king of Asturias, and Covadonga was later proclaimed the beginning of the Reconquista.
General Belisarius defeated a larger Sassanid Persian force at the fortress of Dara around 530.
The victory at Dara established Belisarius as Justinian's preeminent military commander.
Caliph al-Mutasim led an Abbasid offensive into Anatolia in 838 and defeated the Byzantine army at Dazimon.
Abbasid forces sacked Amorium in 838, a propaganda disaster for Emperor Theophilus.
The First Crusade's vanguard under Bohemond of Taranto was ambushed by a large Seljuk force at Dorylaeum in July 1097.
The arrival of Godfrey of Bouillon's main army turned Dorylaeum into a Crusader victory that opened the road across Anatolia.
The English army under the Earl of Surrey defeated the Scots at Flodden Field in 1513.
James IV of Scotland was killed at Flodden, the last British monarch to die in battle.
French forces under Arthur de Richemont defeated an English relief force at Formigny in 1450 using effective artillery.
After Formigny, Normandy surrendered within weeks and England lost its last major French territory outside Gascony.
The Swiss Confederacy destroyed Charles the Bold's Burgundian army at Grandson in 1476.
The Burgundians fled Grandson abandoning their camp, treasury, and artillery to the Swiss.
Philip IV of France defeated the Flemish infantry at the Battle of Mons-en-Pévèle on 18 August 1304, avenging the French defeat at Courtrai.
The Treaty of Athis-sur-Orge in 1305 imposed heavy reparations on Flanders.
Tariq ibn Ziyad defeated the Visigothic king Roderic near the Guadalete River in July 711, after which Roderic was killed and the Visigothic army disintegrated.
Within three years of Guadalete, Umayyad forces under Musa ibn Nusayr had overrun virtually all of Iberia except the northern mountains.
William the Conqueror defeated and killed King Harold II at Hastings in 1066 as the Saxon shield wall broke under Norman cavalry charges and feigned retreats.
The Norman Conquest transformed England's language, aristocracy, legal system, and architecture, with Norman nobles replacing the Anglo-Saxon thegnhood within a generation.
Dmitri Donskoi of Moscow defeated the Golden Horde general Mamai at Kulikovo Field in 1380, the first major Russian military victory over the Mongols.
Despite the victory at Kulikovo, the Mongols sacked Moscow two years later in 1382.
A coalition of Christian Iberian kings under Alfonso VIII of Castile defeated the Almohad caliph al-Nasir at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.
The Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa was declared a crusade by Pope Innocent III.
Otto I defeated the invading Magyar army near Augsburg at the Battle of Lechfeld in 955, ending half a century of Magyar raids into Western and Central Europe.
A Mongol detachment defeated a combined Polish, German, and Teutonic Knight force under Henry II of Silesia at Legnica on 9 April 1241, where Henry was killed.
After Legnica the Mongols declined to press further west, turning south and later withdrawing east following the death of Great Khan Ögedei.
Alp Arslan's Seljuk army defeated and captured Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes at Manzikert in 1071.
The political crisis after Manzikert allowed Turkic nomads to settle across Anatolia, setting the stage for the Sultanate of Rum.
The aftermath of Manzikert saw civil war erupt in Constantinople as rival claimants fought for the throne.
After Manzikert the Byzantine theme system of provincial defense collapsed and Turkish nomads flooded into Anatolia unopposed.
Rudolf I of Habsburg defeated and killed Ottokar II of Bohemia at the Battle on the Marchfeld on 26 August 1278.
After Marchfeld, Rudolf I distributed Austria, Styria, and Carinthia to his sons, founding the Habsburg hereditary domain.
An Arab fleet under Muawiya's admiral destroyed the Byzantine fleet at the Battle of the Masts off the Lycian coast around 655, the first major Arab naval victory.
Emperor Constans II escaped the Battle of the Masts in disguise by swapping clothes with a sailor.
The Genoese fleet defeated the Pisan navy at Meloria in 1284, capturing 72 Pisan galleys.
After Meloria, Pisa never recovered its naval power, ending its commercial competition with Genoa in the western Mediterranean.
Suleiman the Magnificent defeated and killed King Louis II of Hungary at Mohács in 1526.
Within three weeks of Mohács, Ottoman forces took Buda, and the Hungarian kingdom subsequently split into three parts.
Swiss forest canton fighters ambushed and defeated Duke Leopold I of Austria's cavalry at Morgarten on 15 November 1315.
The victory at Morgarten led the Swiss Confederation to renew and strengthen its founding pact at Brunnen.
Seljuk Sultan Kilij Arslan II ambushed and defeated Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Komnenos at Myriokephalon in 1176.
The defeat at Myriokephalon ended any realistic prospect of Byzantine reconquest of Anatolia.
Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, was killed at the Battle of Nancy on 5 January 1477 against a coalition of Swiss and Lorraine forces.
Charles the Bold's death at Nancy ended the Valois Burgundian state, and his daughter Mary's marriage to Maximilian of Habsburg reshaped European politics.
Sultan Bayezid I annihilated a large Western crusading force at Nicopolis on the Danube in 1396.
The disorganized charge of the Western knights at Nicopolis was repulsed before Bayezid's cavalry destroyed the crusaders.
Henry I of England defeated Louis VI of France at Brémule in 1119, securing Normandy against French pressure.
Henry I's loss of his heir in the White Ship disaster of 1120 triggered the succession crisis known as the Anarchy.
Charles Martel's Frankish army defeated the Umayyad governor Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi at the Battle of Tours in 732.
The Battle of Tours legitimized Charles Martel and the Carolingian family as protectors of Christendom.
Holy Roman Emperor Conrad III defeated the supporters of Welf Duke Henry the Proud at the Battle of Weinsberg around 1140.
The Battle of Weinsberg continued the Staufen-Welf (Ghibelline-Guelf) conflict that would define German and Italian politics for the next century.
Edward the Black Prince defeated a much larger French army near Poitiers on 19 September 1356 and captured King John II of France.
The ransom of 3 million gold écus demanded for John II of France was so large that France could not pay it.
The capture of John II at Poitiers triggered the Jacquerie peasant revolt and a political crisis in the Estates General.
Alfonso XI of Castile and Afonso IV of Portugal defeated the Marinid sultan Abu al-Hasan and the Nasrid emir of Granada at Río Salado in 1340.
Río Salado was the last significant North African military intervention in Iberia, after which control of the Strait of Gibraltar passed to Castile.
Charlemagne's rearguard was ambushed and annihilated by Basque warriors in the pass of Roncesvalles in 778 while withdrawing from Spain.
The ambush at Roncesvalles was later transformed into the epic Chanson de Roland around 1100, in which Saracens replace the Basques as the enemy.
Almoravid Sultan Yusuf ibn Tashfin inflicted a catastrophic defeat on Alfonso VI of Castile-León at Sagrajas near Badajoz in 1086.
After Sagrajas the Almoravids absorbed the taifa kingdoms, transforming al-Andalus into an Almoravid province.
William Wallace and Andrew de Moray ambushed and defeated an English army crossing Stirling Bridge on 11 September 1297.
The victory at Stirling Bridge reversed the English occupation of Scotland and made Wallace Guardian of Scotland.
Abbasid forces under Ziyad ibn Salih defeated the Tang Chinese army under Gao Xianzhi at the Talas River in July 751, the only major clash between the Arab world and Tang China.
Paper-makers captured at Talas spread paper manufacturing to Samarkand, Baghdad, and eventually Europe.
Charles Martel intercepted and defeated a major Umayyad raiding army under Abdul Rahman al-Ghafiqi near Tours in 732, killing the Umayyad commander.
Charles Martel's victory at Tours established the Carolingians as Europe's premier military force.
Sultan Murad II destroyed the Polish-Hungarian crusading army and killed King Vladislaus III at Varna in 1444.
The Ottoman victory at Varna ensured Ottoman control of the Balkans and removed the last serious external threat to Constantinople before 1453.
Danish King Valdemar IV invaded the Hanseatic island of Gotland and massacred its militia outside Visby in July 1361.
The sack of Visby led the Hanseatic League to form the Confederation of Cologne against Danish control of the Baltic.
Clovis I of the Franks defeated and killed Alaric II of the Visigoths at Vouillé near Poitiers in 507.
The Frankish victory at Vouillé drove the Visigoths from Gaul into Iberia and made the Franks the dominant power in Western Europe.
Khalid ibn al-Walid's Arab Muslim army defeated the larger Byzantine force under Vahan near the Yarmouk River in 636.
The defeat at Yarmouk ended Byzantine rule over Syria and Palestine, and Jerusalem fell the following year.
Four knights acting on Henry II's outburst murdered Archbishop Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170.
Henry II and Becket had been in conflict over the Constitutions of Clarendon of 1164, which sought to limit Church courts' jurisdiction over clergy.
After Becket's murder Pope Alexander III forced Henry II to do public penance at Becket's tomb, and Canterbury became England's premier pilgrimage site.
Bede, a monk at Jarrow in Northumbria, completed his Ecclesiastical History of the English People in 731.
Bede's use of Anno Domini dating from the Incarnation helped make the system standard throughout Latin Christendom.
The Venerable Bede of Jarrow completed the Ecclesiastical History of the English People, the foundational text of English history, in 731.
Bede's careful use of sources and chronological precision established the conventions of medieval historiography.
Charles of Anjou defeated and killed Manfred, the Hohenstaufen king of Sicily, at the Battle of Benevento on 26 February 1266.
After Benevento, Charles of Anjou became king of Sicily and southern Italy, establishing Angevin dominance of the western Mediterranean.
Benjamin of Tudela returned around 1173 from an eight-year journey through southern France, Italy, Constantinople, Syria, Mesopotamia, Iran, Yemen, and Egypt.
Benjamin of Tudela's Sefer Massaʿot ('Book of Travels') systematically reported on the Jewish communities of every major city he visited.
Bubonic plague arrived in Europe in 1347 via Genoese trading ships from Caffa in the Crimea.
The Black Death killed an estimated 30–60% of Europe's population within five years.
Labor shortages from the Black Death empowered surviving peasants to demand higher wages, weakening serfdom.
By 1353 the Black Death had killed roughly one-third of Europe's population.
The Church's lack of an effective response to the plague caused it a profound loss of prestige.
The flagellant movement of penitential self-scourging brotherhoods spread across Germany and the Low Countries after the Black Death.
Genoese galleys from Caffa carried plague into Constantinople in 1347.
Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos lost his own son to the plague in Constantinople.
Real wages for English agricultural workers roughly doubled in the generation after the Black Death of 1348.
English landlords shifted from labor-intensive grain farming to sheep grazing after the Black Death, expanding wool exports.
Plague was reported at Melcombe Regis in June 1348 and reached London by autumn 1348.
Westminster Abbey lost 27 of its 50 monks to the Black Death.
The plague reached Marseille in autumn 1347 and Avignon by January 1348, killing perhaps half of Avignon's population.
Pope Clement VI's physician Guy de Chauliac documented the bubonic and pneumonic clinical forms of the plague.
Mass pogroms against Jewish communities accused of poisoning wells erupted in Strasbourg, Mainz, and Cologne during the Black Death, often before the disease arrived.
Plague entered Iberia via Mallorca and Barcelona in spring 1348 and spread through Aragon, Castile, Portugal, and Granada.
King Alfonso XI of Castile died of plague at the siege of Gibraltar in 1350, the only reigning European monarch killed by the Black Death.
During the Golden Horde's siege of Caffa, Jani Beg reportedly catapulted plague-infected corpses over the walls, possibly the first recorded instance of biological warfare.
Genoese merchants fleeing Caffa carried the plague to Messina in October 1347.
Twelve Genoese merchant ships carrying plague-stricken crews docked at Messina in October 1347.
Despite Messina's port authorities ordering the plague ships out, the disease spread through Sicily and reached mainland Italy by spring 1348.
Plague arrived at Pskov via the Hanseatic Baltic route in 1352 and spread through Novgorod, Smolensk, Tver, and Moscow over the next two years.
Grand Prince Simeon of Moscow and most of his court died of plague in 1353.
The plague recurrence of 1361, known as the pestis secunda or pestis puerorum, disproportionately killed children who lacked acquired immunity.
The 1369 outbreak was the third pan-European recurrence of plague since 1347, with roughly 10–15% additional mortality in affected regions.
Following the treaty of Nymphaeum in 1261, Genoa established a network of Black Sea colonies including Caffa, Tana, and Trebizond factories.
Genoa's Black Sea colonies handled Central Asian silk, Chinese goods, Persian spices, Crimean grain, and enslaved peoples.
Giovanni Boccaccio wrote the Decameron between 1348 and 1353, a hundred novellas told by ten young people sheltering from the Black Death in a Florentine villa.
The Decameron was the first major work of Italian secular prose narrative and influenced Chaucer and Shakespeare.
Giovanni Boccaccio completed the Decameron around 1353, a collection of one hundred novelle told by ten young Florentines fleeing the Black Death.
The Decameron's frame narrative is a foundational document of plague literature.
Theoderic the Great executed the philosopher-statesman Boethius on charges of treason and sorcery around 524.
Awaiting execution in prison, Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy, one of the most widely read books of the Middle Ages.
Jan Hus was burned at the stake at the Council of Constance on 6 July 1415 despite a guarantee of safe conduct from Emperor Sigismund.
The execution of Jan Hus triggered the Hussite Revolution in Bohemia, provoking five crusades and fifteen years of religious warfare.
Henry Tudor defeated and killed King Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth Field on 22 August 1485 after Lord Stanley's forces switched sides.
Richard III was the last English king to die in battle, and Henry Tudor became Henry VII, founding the Tudor dynasty.
The Battle of Bosworth ended the Wars of the Roses of 1455–1485.
The Navigatio Sancti Brendani Abbatis, elaborating the Irish abbot Brendan's legendary Atlantic voyage, became one of the most-copied Latin texts of the central Middle Ages.
Alan II Barbetorte returned from exile in England around 942 and drove out the Vikings who had occupied Brittany since 919.
Anne of Brittany, twice queen of France, died in 1514.
The Edict of Union of 1532 incorporated Brittany into the French crown, ending Breton sovereignty.
Nominoe of Brittany defeated the Frankish army of Charles the Bald at the Battle of Ballon in 845, establishing Breton de facto independence.
Bulgarian Khan Boris I adopted Eastern Christianity under Byzantine auspices around 864, taking the baptismal name Michael.
After flirting with Rome, the Bulgarian church was incorporated under Constantinople, and disciples of Cyril and Methodius brought a Slavonic-language clergy to Preslav.
Philip the Bold received Burgundy as an appanage in 1363, founding the Valois Duchy of Burgundy.
The assassination of Duke John the Fearless of Burgundy at Montereau in 1419 drove his successor Philip the Good into alliance with England.
The Burgundian-English alliance enabled Henry V's conquest of northern France and the Treaty of Troyes.
Charles the Bold's death at Nancy in 1477 ended independent Burgundian ambitions, after which Louis XI seized the duchy.
Charles the Bold's daughter Mary married Maximilian of Habsburg, transferring the Low Countries to the Habsburg dynasty.
Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy from 1467, sought to transform Burgundy from a French duchy into an independent kingdom.
Charles the Bold conquered Lorraine in 1475 to connect his northern and southern Burgundian territories.
The Buyid amir Muizz al-Dawla entered Baghdad in 945 and effectively deposed the Abbasid caliph, taking the title Amir al-Umara.
The Shia Buyids kept the Sunni Abbasid caliphate as a source of symbolic legitimacy while exercising real political power until the Seljuk conquest of Baghdad in 1055.
Byzantine Emperor Nicephorus II Phocas retook Aleppo and much of Cilicia around 962, reversing centuries of Arab expansion.
The campaigns of Nicephorus II, John Tzimiskes, and Basil II temporarily extended Byzantine borders to Syria and parts of the Holy Land.
By 1018 Basil II had fully incorporated Bulgaria into the Byzantine Empire for the first time since 681.
Basil II eased the Bulgarian transition by retaining Bulgarian nobles' estates as Byzantine pronoiai and preserving the Bulgarian Patriarchate.
Michael V's attempt to exile Empress Zoe in 1042 provoked a popular uprising in Constantinople.
The death of the last Macedonian empress Theodora in 1056 opened a power struggle that ended with Isaac I Komnenos seizing the throne in 1057.
Byzantine general Alexios Strategopoulos captured Constantinople without a siege on 25 July 1261 while the Latin garrison was absent.
The recapture of Constantinople in 1261 ended the Latin Empire after 57 years and restored the Byzantine Empire under Michael VIII Palaiologos.
Papal legate Cardinal Humbert excommunicated Patriarch Michael Cerularius in Hagia Sophia on 16 July 1054, and Cerularius excommunicated the legates in return.
The 1054 schism arose from disputes over the filioque clause and papal primacy atop centuries-old liturgical and theological differences.
Emperor Heraclius and his successors reorganized Byzantine provincial administration into themes, military districts commanded by strategoi who combined civil and military authority.
Under the theme system Byzantine soldiers received hereditary land grants in exchange for military service.
According to Procopius, monks smuggled silkworm eggs from Central Asia to Constantinople, enabling Justinian I to establish a Byzantine silk industry.
The Byzantine imperial silk workshops produced luxury garments used in diplomacy as gifts, tribute, and symbols of imperial majesty.
Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV stood barefoot in the snow outside Canossa for three days in 1077 to seek absolution from Pope Gregory VII.
Pope Gregory VII lifted the excommunication of Henry IV at Canossa, which had been levied during the Investiture Controversy.
French nobles elected Hugh Capet king of France in June 987 following the death of the last Carolingian king Louis V without an heir.
Hugh Capet associated his son Robert as co-king, establishing the Capetian practice that ensured peaceful succession for centuries.
The Fourth Crusade stormed Constantinople on 12–13 April 1204, the first fall of the city in 874 years.
The Crusaders established the Latin Empire of Constantinople after the sack, and the Byzantine Empire splintered into the successor states of Nicaea, Trebizond, and Epirus.
Pope Innocent IV's bull Quae honorem Conditoris of 1247 mitigated the Carmelite eremitic rule, permitting the friars to settle in towns and beg for alms.
Carolingian minuscule, a standardized legible script, spread across Frankish scriptoria during the cultural program of Charlemagne and Alcuin.
Carolingian minuscule made spaces between words and consistent letter forms the new norm.
Alcuin of York directed Charlemagne's palace school at Aachen and oversaw a systematic recovery of classical Latin learning.
Carolingian copying programmes preserved most surviving Latin classical texts.
A Christian coalition of Castile, Aragon, Navarre, and Portugal defeated the Almohad Caliphate at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.
Las Navas de Tolosa effectively ended Almohad military power in Iberia and opened Andalusia to Christian reconquest within a generation.
Alfonso VI of Castile captured Toledo, the ancient Visigothic capital, from its Taifa ruler in 1085.
The fall of Toledo alarmed the other Taifa rulers into inviting the Almoravids from North Africa.
The Chagatai Khanate governed Central Asia's heartland including the Silk Road cities of Samarkand, Bukhara, and Khotan.
The Chagatai khans converted to Islam relatively late, under Kebek Khan around 1318.
The Champagne Fairs, six annual trade fairs across four towns, became the commercial center of western Europe in the 12th century.
The counts of Champagne guaranteed merchants' safety and enforced contracts at the fairs, whose courts developed commercial law.
The Champagne Fairs declined in the early 14th century as Genoese galley services and Philip IV's fiscal policies diverted traffic to sea routes and Paris.
Around 1200 six fairs across four Champagne towns sustained a year-round trade cycle linking Flemish cloth, English wool, Italian silk, German silver, and Levantine spices.
Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne 'Emperor of the Romans' in St Peter's Basilica on Christmas Day 800.
Charlemagne's coronation revived an imperial title in the Latin West vacant since 476, challenging the Byzantine emperor.
Charlemagne besieged Pavia and deposed the Lombard king Desiderius in 774.
Charlemagne took the title 'King of the Franks and Lombards' and incorporated the Lombard kingdom into the Carolingian Empire.
Charles IV was crowned emperor at St Peter's by a papal legate in 1355.
Charles IV promulgated the Golden Bull of 1356, codifying imperial election procedure.
Charles Martel served as Mayor of the Palace, effectively ruling Frankland, from 714 to 741.
Charles Martel distributed church lands to his military followers, creating a class of armed horsemen bound to him by personal loyalty.
Charles V inherited Spain in 1516 and the Holy Roman Empire in 1519, creating the most extensive European empire since Rome.
Charles V abdicated in 1556, dividing his empire between his son Philip II and his brother Ferdinand I.
The cathedral school at Chartres became the leading centre of 12th-century Latin Platonist philosophy under masters such as Bernard and Thierry of Chartres.
The alumni and texts of the school of Chartres shaped the early universities of Paris and Oxford.
Geoffrey Chaucer began the Canterbury Tales around 1387, a frame narrative of pilgrims from all social classes telling stories on the road to Canterbury.
By writing the Canterbury Tales in Middle English, Chaucer established English as a literary language worthy of French or Italian.
Two mass popular movements led by Stephen of Cloyes and Nicholas of Cologne, later mythologized as the Children's Crusade, attracted tens of thousands of followers in 1212.
Neither group of the Children's Crusade reached the Holy Land; Stephen's followers dispersed at Marseille and Nicholas's struggled back over the Alps.
The wool-workers (ciompi) of Florence revolted against the guild oligarchy in July 1378 and briefly established a worker-led government.
The oligarchic guilds suppressed the Ciompi revolt within three months and dissolved the new worker guilds.
Robert of Molesme founded the Abbey of Cîteaux in Burgundy in 1098 as a return to strict Benedictine observance.
Under Bernard of Clairvaux from 1115 the Cistercian order expanded to roughly 340 houses across Europe by 1200.
Stephen Harding drafted the Carta Caritatis, approved in 1119, binding all Cistercian houses into a single legal order with annual general chapters and mutual visitation.
In the 1280s and 1290s the Florentine commune built its third circuit of city walls, enclosing about 630 hectares to accommodate anticipated growth.
Florence's third circuit of walls was nearly 9 kilometers in circumference with 73 towers and 15 gates.
Pope Urban II preached at the Council of Clermont in 1095, calling on Western Christians to liberate Jerusalem and aid the Byzantine emperor.
Urban II's call at Clermont launched the First Crusade and established the papacy's claim to direct wars of religious conquest.
Brian Boru, High King of Ireland, defeated a coalition of Leinster Irish and Dublin Norse at the Battle of Clontarf on 23 April 1014.
Brian Boru was killed after the Battle of Clontarf, and his death without a strong successor ended the brief period of unified Irish kingship.
Clovis I, king of the Franks, converted to Nicene Catholic Christianity, unlike the Arian Germanic kings, and was baptized by Bishop Remigius of Reims.
Clovis's conversion to Catholicism gave him the support of the Gallo-Roman clergy and population.
Clovis I was baptized a Catholic Christian by Bishop Remigius of Reims around 498.
Clovis's conversion was reportedly influenced by his Burgundian wife Clotilde and a battlefield vow at Tolbiac.
Clovis I defeated the Alamanni at the Battle of Tolbiac near Cologne, reportedly vowing to convert to Christianity if he won.
The victory at Tolbiac halted Alamannic expansion into the Rhine valley and established Frankish dominance over the central Rhineland.
Duke William I of Aquitaine founded the Abbey of Cluny in Burgundy in 910, placing it directly under papal authority and exempting it from local bishops and lords.
The Cluniac congregation grew to over 1,000 dependent houses across Europe by the 11th century.
Archbishop Konrad von Hochstaden laid the foundation stone of the new Cologne Cathedral in 1248, designed in French High Gothic style.
The nave and west towers of Cologne Cathedral remained unfinished for nearly 600 years.
The Concordat of Worms of 1122 resolved the Investiture Controversy between Emperor Henry V and Pope Calixtus II.
Under the Concordat of Worms the emperor renounced investing bishops with ring and staff but retained investiture with the scepter for temporal lands.

Kingdom of Poland (Piast) — campaigns and battles spanned 1000–1375, from Pomeranian Tribes Resist Polish Expansion to Hungarian–Ottoman War.
Kingdom of Portugal — campaigns and battles spanned 733–1510, from Reconquista to Portuguese Conquest of Goa.
Kingdom of Scotland — campaigns and battles spanned 937–1513, from Battle of Brunanburh to Battle of Flodden — Scotland Loses a King.

Lombard Kingdom — campaigns and battles spanned 568–1176, from Lombard invasion of Italy to Battle of Legnano.

Mongol Empire — campaigns and battles spanned 1209–1307, from Irghiz River skirmish to Genoese–Mongol Wars.

Ostrogothic Kingdom — campaigns and battles spanned 507–553, from Franco-Gothic War to Siege of Urviventus.

Ottoman Empire — campaigns and battles spanned 1302–1526, from Battle of Bapheus to Battle of Mohács — Ottoman Conquest of Hungary.

Principality of Antioch — campaigns and battles spanned 1000–1268, from Armenian-Byzantine wars to Siege of Antioch.
Principality of Moldavia — campaigns and battles spanned 1352–1498, from Moldavian–Horde Wars to Moldavian campaign in Poland.

Principality of Wallachia — campaigns and battles spanned 1330–1479, from Battle of Posada to Battle of Breadfield.
Principality of Zeta — campaigns and battles spanned 1463–1478, from First Ottoman–Venetian War to Siege of Shkodra.

Republic of Genoa — campaigns and battles spanned 1014–1495, from Mujahid's invasion of Sardinia to Battle of Rapallo (1495).
Republic of Pisa — campaigns and battles spanned 1014–1325, from Mujahid's invasion of Sardinia to Naval Battle of Cagliari.
Republic of Ragusa — campaigns and battles spanned 1403–1463, from Bosnian–Ragusan War to Battle of Kljuc.
Republic of Siena — campaigns and battles spanned 1260–1479, from Siena Defeats Florence at Montaperti to Battle of Poggio Imperiale.
Republic of Venice — campaigns and battles spanned 700–1500, from Croatian-Venetian Wars to Siege of the Castle of Saint George.
Second Bulgarian Empire — campaigns and battles spanned 680–1389, from Byzantine–Bulgarian Wars to Hungarian–Ottoman War.

Serbian Despotate — campaigns and battles spanned 1415–1459, from Hungarian–Ottoman War to Ottoman Conquest of Serbia.
Serbian Empire — campaigns and battles spanned 1350–1389, from Bosnian–Serbian War to Battle of Kosovo Polje.

Swiss Confederation — campaigns and battles spanned 1315–1499, from Battle of Morgarten to Swabian War.
State of the Teutonic Order — campaigns and battles spanned 1233–1485, from Teutonic Order Begins Prussian Crusade to Polish-Ottoman War of 1485–1503.
Timurid Empire — campaigns and battles spanned 1370–1469, from Timur Establishes His Empire to Battle of Qarabagh.
Umayyad Caliphate — campaigns and battles spanned 627–800, from Khazar campaigns in Georgia to Campaign of the mud.
Emirate of Córdoba — campaigns and battles spanned 711–1340, from Battle of Guadalete to Battle of Río Salado — Last Moroccan Invasion of Spain.
Visigothic Kingdom — campaigns and battles spanned 410–713, from Sack of Rome by the Visigoths to Battle of Orihuela.
West Francia — campaigns and battles spanned 845–978, from Siege of Paris to Franco-German War of 978–980.
Emperor Constans II visited Rome in 663, the last Byzantine emperor to do so for centuries, and stripped bronze from the city's monuments.
Constans II moved his court to Syracuse in Sicily but was assassinated there in 668.
Henry II issued the Constitutions of Clarendon in 1164, asserting royal authority over ecclesiastical courts and clergy accused of crimes.
Archbishop Thomas Becket's refusal to seal the Constitutions of Clarendon led to a conflict culminating in his murder in 1170.
Frederick II promulgated the Liber Augustalis at Melfi in 1231, a comprehensive legal code for the Kingdom of Sicily.
The Liber Augustalis established a centralized bureaucratic state with professional judges, regulated taxation, and free internal trade.
Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania accepted Catholic baptism around 1387 and converted his domains to Christianity, making Lithuania the last pagan state in Europe to convert.
Lithuania's conversion deprived the Teutonic Order of its crusading justification.
Visigothic King Reccared I converted from Arianism to Catholic Christianity at the Third Council of Toledo in 589.
Reccared's conversion ended the religious divide between the Arian Germanic ruling class and the Catholic Hispano-Roman majority.
Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne 'Emperor of the Romans' in St Peter's Basilica on Christmas Day 800, reportedly without Charlemagne's prior agreement.
Charlemagne's coronation created the claim that a Western Roman Emperor existed alongside the Eastern emperor in Constantinople.
The jurist Tribonian completed the Corpus Iuris Civilis under Emperor Justinian I around 534, comprising the Codex, Digest, Institutes, and Novellae.
The Corpus Iuris Civilis became the foundation of modern European civil law and, rediscovered at Bologna in the 11th century, the basis for the revival of legal education.
An Alexandrian Greek merchant-turned-monk completed the Christian Topography around 547, recounting commercial voyages to the Red Sea, Persian Gulf, Aksum, and the Indian coast.
The Christian Topography argued for a flat-earth cosmology but preserved uniquely valuable first-hand reports on Aksumite Christianity and Indian Ocean trade.
After the death of Ludwig the Child in 911, the East Frankish nobles elected Conrad I of Franconia as king at Forchheim, choosing a non-Carolingian for the first time.
Conrad I's election established the elective principle that would define the Holy Roman Empire.
A council convoked by Basil I in 869 deposed Patriarch Photius and restored communion with Rome.
The 869 council is recognized as the Eighth Ecumenical Council in the Latin West but not in the Greek East.
The Second Council of Nicaea in 787, convened by Empress Irene, resolved the First Iconoclast Controversy by defining the veneration of icons as legitimate.
The Second Council of Nicaea was the last ecumenical council recognized by both Eastern and Western Christianity.
The Council of Basel, convoked in 1431, asserted the supremacy of general councils over popes.
The Council of Basel conducted negotiations with the Hussites and the Byzantine Church.
The Council of Chalcedon in 451 defined Christ as having two natures, divine and human, united in one person.
Egypt, Syria, Armenia, and Ethiopia rejected the Chalcedonian formula, establishing Monophysite churches that created lasting divisions in the Byzantine east.
The Council of Pisa in 1409 deposed both rival popes and elected Alexander V, but neither rival accepted the deposition.
After the Council of Pisa the Western Schism had three rival papal claimants until the Council of Constance.
The accession of Henry Plantagenet to the English throne in 1154 brought the County of Anjou into the Angevin Empire.
Philip II Augustus of France captured Anjou from King John of England in 1204 during his dismantling of the Angevin Empire.
The loss of Anjou and Normandy transformed the Plantagenet kings from continental lords into primarily English monarchs.
The marriage of Petronilla of Aragon and Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona in 1137 created the dynastic union that became the Crown of Aragon.
Wilfred the Hairy received the County of Barcelona as a hereditary possession in 878, breaking the tradition of Frankish royal appointment.
Wilfred the Hairy's dynasty ruled Barcelona continuously for five centuries, making it the nucleus of Catalan culture.
The County of Holland consolidated in the 11th century, named for the hollow peat-bog lowlands.
Hollanders' engineering to reclaim land from the sea through dykes and drainage created the distinctive Dutch landscape and agricultural wealth.
Count Siegfried of the Ardennes received the castle of Lucilinburhuc in 963, founding the County of Luxembourg.
Humbert I established the House of Savoy around 1003, receiving territories controlling the western Alpine passes.
Savoy's position commanding routes between France, Italy, and Germany let the small county exert influence exceeding its size.
At the Battle of Courtrai in 1302, a Flemish infantry militia defeated a French army under Robert of Artois.
Courtrai, the 'Battle of the Golden Spurs', demonstrated that disciplined infantry could defeat heavy cavalry on prepared ground.
Edward III's English army defeated a much larger French force under Philip VI at Crécy on 26 August 1346.
English longbowmen at Crécy annihilated successive charges of French knights and Genoese crossbowmen.
A submarine earthquake near Crete on 8 August 1303 triggered a tsunami across the southern Aegean and the Egyptian coast.
The 1303 earthquake severely damaged the Pharos lighthouse of Alexandria, which was subsequently abandoned.
The Crimean Khanate, a Golden Horde successor under Ottoman suzerainty, organized systematic slave raids into Poland, Lithuania, and Muscovy.
Slaves taken by the Crimean Khanate were sold through the port of Kaffa to Ottoman buyers.
Italian city-states received quarters of Crusader cities and trade privileges amounting to extraterritorial rights.
Sugar plantation agriculture developed in the Crusader states was later transferred to Cyprus, Madeira, and the Americas.
The excommunicated Emperor Frederick II negotiated the Treaty of Jaffa in 1229, returning Jerusalem to Christian control for ten years without fighting.
Under the Treaty of Jaffa, Muslims retained control of the Temple Mount including the al-Aqsa Mosque and Dome of the Rock.
Three large armies following the First Crusade were destroyed in Anatolia by Seljuk forces in 1101.
The defeats of 1101 showed the route through Anatolia was no longer safe without Byzantine support, isolating the Crusader states.
Guy of Lusignan established the Kingdom of Cyprus as a feudal Latin Christian state in 1192.
Cyprus became a major logistics hub and sugar producer for the Crusader states.
A Mamluk fleet sacked Limassol and defeated the Cypriot army at Khirokitia in 1426, capturing King Janus.
After the 1426 Mamluk raid, Cyprus was forced to pay annual tribute to Egypt.
Richard I of England conquered Cyprus from the Byzantine governor Isaac Komnenos during the Third Crusade in 1191.
Richard I sold Cyprus to the Knights Templar and then to Guy of Lusignan, beginning three centuries of Latin rule.
Emperor Michael III sent the brothers Cyril and Methodius to Moravia around 863 at the request of Prince Rastislav.
Cyril created the Glagolitic alphabet, the first Slavic writing system, to transcribe a Slavic liturgy.
The Black Death reached Scandinavia via Bergen and Malmö in 1349, killing 40-60% of Norway's population.
The demographic collapse from the Black Death contributed to the conditions that made the Kalmar Union attractive in 1397.
Sweyn Forkbeard of Denmark conquered England in 1013, compelling the submission of Northumbria, the Danelaw, and the southern kingdoms.
Sweyn's son Canute completed the conquest of England by 1016, ruling England, Denmark, and Norway as the North Sea Empire.
King Christian II of Denmark executed around 90 Swedish aristocrats and clergy in the Stockholm Bloodbath of November 1520.
The Stockholm Bloodbath provoked Gustav Vasa's successful Swedish independence revolt, permanently ending the Kalmar Union.
Dante Alighieri completed the Divine Comedy around 1315-1321, the first major literary work in Italian rather than Latin.
Dante wrote the Divine Comedy in exile after the Guelphs expelled him from Florence in 1302.
Dante Alighieri completed the Paradiso, the third canticle of the Commedia, during his exile in Ravenna around 1320, shortly before his death in 1321.
The Commedia is a 100-canto vernacular epic written in Tuscan terza rima.
The Commedia established Italian as a literary language and provided medieval Christendom with an ambitious literary synthesis of theology, philosophy, and politics.
Dante Alighieri, exiled from Florence, wrote the Commedia (later called the 'Divine Comedy') between approximately 1308 and 1321.
The Commedia synthesizes medieval theology, classical learning, contemporary politics, and vernacular Italian, creating the Italian literary language.
The Commedia places contemporary popes in hell and imagines a universe ordered by Thomistic theology and Aristotelian cosmology.
The Second Crusade, led by Louis VII of France and Conrad III of Germany, attacked Damascus in 1148 and failed after only four days of siege.
Damascus was an ally of the crusader states at the time of the 1148 attack.
The failure of the 1148 siege of Damascus strengthened Nur ad-Din of Aleppo.
Charlemagne died on January 28, 814, at Aachen, aged approximately 72, after a reign of 46 years.
Charlemagne was succeeded solely by his surviving son, Louis the Pious, avoiding the Frankish custom of partible inheritance.
At Charlemagne's death in 814, the Carolingian Empire stretched from the Ebro to the Elbe and from the North Sea to central Italy.
Charlemagne's court at Aachen was a center of Latin learning and Christian culture known as the Carolingian Renaissance, systematizing literacy, scripture, and law across Western Europe.
Ali ibn Abi Talib, fourth Rightly Guided Caliph, was assassinated by a Kharijite extremist at Kufa in January 661.
Following Ali's death and his son Hasan's abdication, Muawiya I founded the Umayyad Caliphate, making the caliphate hereditary rather than elected.
The dispute over caliphal succession after 661 produced the division between Shia, who held that succession should remain with the Prophet's family, and Sunnis, who accepted Umayyad legitimacy.
Louis IX of France led his second crusade against Tunis in 1270, where his army was devastated by dysentery.
Louis IX died of plague during the 1270 crusade and became the only French king canonized as a saint.
The death of Louis IX in 1270 effectively ended the era of large royal-led crusades.
King Olaf II of Norway was killed at Stiklestad in 1030 fighting Danish-backed Norwegian rebels.
Olaf II's death in 1030 was followed by rapid Christianisation of Norway and his canonisation as Saint Olaf, patron saint of Norway.
Cnut the Great conquered England in 1016 and subsequently inherited Denmark and Norway, creating the North Sea Empire.
At its peak the North Sea Empire united England, Denmark, Norway, and parts of Sweden under a single king.
Valdemar I captured the pagan stronghold of Arkona on Rügen island in 1169, completing the Danish conquest of the Baltic coast.
Under Valdemar I and II, Denmark dominated the Baltic Sea and controlled lucrative herring fisheries.
The Despotate of Dobruja emerged around 1346 CE as a successor state in the Black Sea coastal region between the declining Bulgarian Empire and the Byzantine sphere.
Under the despot Dobrotitsa, the Despotate of Dobruja controlled strategic Danube delta ports and maintained a small but effective navy.
The Ottoman Empire absorbed the Despotate of Dobruja around 1388 CE, eliminating one of the last independent successor states in the Black Sea region.
The Ottoman conquest of Dobruja gave the Ottomans control of the Danube delta and prepared the ground for later campaigns against Bulgaria, Wallachia, and Constantinople.
Michael Komnenos Doukas founded the Despotate of Epirus in 1205 as one of three Byzantine successor states following the Fourth Crusade's capture of Constantinople.
The Despotate of Epirus preserved Greek Orthodox culture and Byzantine administrative traditions against Latin domination.
Theodore Doukas of Epirus captured Thessaloniki from the Latin Kingdom in 1224 and proclaimed himself Emperor of the Romans.
Theodore Doukas's defeat at Klokotnitsa in 1230 by Bulgaria ended the Epirote bid for Byzantine restoration.
John VI Kantakouzenos established the Despotate of the Morea in 1349, creating a semi-autonomous Byzantine province in the Peloponnese.
Under the Palaiologos family, the Despotate of the Morea became a centre of late Byzantine cultural flourishing in art, philosophy, and scholarship.
The Ottoman conquest of the Morea in 1460, seven years after the fall of Constantinople, extinguished the last Byzantine political entity.
Following the Ottoman conquest of the Morea, many Greek scholars and artists fled to Italy, contributing to the Renaissance.
The Peloponnese remained under Ottoman rule from 1460 until the Greek War of Independence in the 19th century.
Frederick I Barbarossa convened the Diet of Roncaglia in 1158, where imperial jurists from Bologna enumerated the regalia, the emperor's rights over Italian territories.
The Bolognese lawyers at Roncaglia justified the imperial regalia claims through Justinianic Roman law.
The Italian communes' resistance to the regalia asserted at Roncaglia provoked the conflict leading to the Lombard League in 1167 and Barbarossa's defeat at Legnano in 1176.
On October 13, 1307, Philip IV of France ordered the simultaneous arrest of all Templars in France, including Grand Master Jacques de Molay.
Under torture, many arrested Templars confessed to heresy, sodomy, and denial of Christ.
Pope Clement V ordered the arrest of Templars across Europe, and the Council of Vienne formally dissolved the Order in 1312.
Jacques de Molay and Geoffrey de Charney were burned at the stake in 1314.
Dante Alighieri, exiled from Florence, completed the Paradiso shortly before his death in Ravenna in 1321.
The Divine Comedy is a vernacular Tuscan poem encompassing scholastic theology, contemporary Florentine politics, and the moral cosmology of medieval Christendom.
Enrico Dandolo, aged about 80 and nearly blind, led Venice into the Fourth Crusade in 1202 as the dominant partner.
After diverting the Fourth Crusade to sack Zara and Constantinople, Venice received three-eighths of the Byzantine Empire under the Partitio Romaniae, including Crete and a quarter of Constantinople.
Enrico Dandolo died in 1205, having secured Venice's commercial empire.
William I ordered a comprehensive administrative survey of England, completed in a single year in 1086.
Royal commissioners interrogated local juries about landholders, tenants, livestock, and taxable value at the time of Edward the Confessor, at William's accession, and in 1086.
The resulting Great Survey, called 'Domesday' by contemporaries, recorded roughly 13,000 English place-names and the landholdings of over 1,400 tenants-in-chief.
William I commissioned the Domesday survey in 1086 as a comprehensive census of English landholding to determine taxes owed.
Royal commissioners travelled through every English shire, recording who held land in 1086 and before the Conquest of 1066.
The two Domesday volumes assessed virtually every English village, listing landowners, tenants, livestock, mills, and fisheries.
Following his victory over the Lombard king Aistulf, the Frankish king Pepin the Short conveyed the formerly Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna and adjacent territories to Pope Stephen II in 756.
The deed of 756 formally constituted the territorial holding of the bishop of Rome known as the Papal States.
Pippin III made two military expeditions into Italy in 754 and 756 at Pope Stephen II's request to expel the Lombards from territories seized from the Exarchate of Ravenna.
Rather than returning the territories to Byzantium, Pippin donated them to the papacy in the Donation of Pippin, creating the temporal basis of the Papal States.
In exchange for the donation, Stephen II anointed Pippin and his sons as 'Patricians of the Romans'.
Otto de la Roche established the Duchy of Athens following the Fourth Crusade's partition of the Byzantine Empire in 1205.
The Frankish Duchy of Athens occupied the Acropolis and introduced Western feudalism to Greece.
The Catalan Company massacred the Frankish knights at the Battle of Halmyros in 1311 and seized Athens.
Catalan rule brought Athens relative stability but also isolation until Florentine and later Venetian rule.
Emperor Henry IV granted King Vratislaus II of Bohemia the royal title in 1085 as reward for support during the Investiture Controversy.
The royal title granted to Vratislaus II in 1085 was initially personal rather than hereditary.
Emperor Charles IV's Golden Bull of 1356 formalised Bohemia's status as an electoral principality, exempting it from normal imperial jurisdiction.
Charles IV, simultaneously King of Bohemia, made Prague a major European cultural and administrative centre.
The Přemyslid duke of Bohemia accepted Frankish overlordship at Regensburg in 895 CE, integrating Bohemia into the Carolingian world.
The 895 acceptance of Frankish overlordship began the Christianisation of Bohemia and established the duchy as a component of the emerging Holy Roman Empire.
The Duchy of Brabant was formally established in 1183 when Godfrey III received the ducal title.

At the crossroads of trade routes connecting the Rhine to the sea, Brabant became one of the wealthiest territories in Europe, with cities like Brussels, Louvain, and Antwerp growing into major commercial centres.
The Joyeuse Entrée of 1356 established a constitutional charter for Brabant, requiring each new duke to confirm the rights and privileges of the nobility, clergy, and towns before entering the duchy.
The Joyeuse Entrée of 1356 prefigured later parliamentary developments in the Low Countries.
The War of the Breton Succession (1341–1364) pitted two rival claimants to the Duchy of Brittany, supported respectively by England and France.
The War of the Breton Succession became a theatre of the Hundred Years War and devastated the Duchy of Brittany.
John IV of Montfort's victory in the War of the Breton Succession established his line as the ruling house of an autonomous Brittany.
Nominoë, the first Duke of Brittany, defeated a Frankish army at the Battle of Ballon in 845 CE.
Nominoë's victory at Ballon in 845 CE established Breton independence from the Carolingian Empire.
Nominoë expelled the Frankish bishops in Brittany and replaced them with Breton clergy, cementing ecclesiastical autonomy.
The Habsburg dynasty inherited Carinthia in 1335, beginning the consolidation of the Austrian Alpine lands under a single ruling house.
Combined with Austria, Styria, and later Tyrol, Carinthia formed the core of Habsburg territorial power in the German-speaking world.
Carinthia was separated from Bavaria as a distinct duchy in 976 CE under Emperor Otto II.
As an Alpine duchy controlling key passes between Germany and Italy, Carinthia held lasting strategic importance in imperial politics.
The Este family consolidated signorial control over Ferrara in 1264, beginning one of the longest-lasting dynastic rules in Italian history.
The Este court at Ferrara became a renowned centre of Renaissance patronage, supporting poets including Ariosto and Tasso.
Ferrara thrived as a cultural and commercial hub of the Po valley.
Emperor Frederick III elevated Ferrara to a duchy in 1452.
The 1452 elevation confirmed the Este family's status among the major Italian powers.
Marco Sanudo of Venice established the Duchy of the Archipelago (Duchy of Naxos) in 1207 following the Fourth Crusade's partition of the Byzantine Empire.
The Duchy of Naxos comprised the Cyclades and ruled much of the Aegean.
The Duchy of Naxos maintained Venetian trade interests and Latin culture in the Greek islands.
The Crispo family inherited the Duchy of Naxos in 1383, continuing Latin rule.
The Duchy of Naxos survived as an Ottoman vassal after 1537, paying tribute while maintaining relative autonomy.
The Duchy of Naxos was finally absorbed into the Ottoman Empire in 1579.
The Lombards established the Duchy of Spoleto around 570 CE, one of their two major southern duchies alongside Benevento.
Spoleto's location in central Italy made it a constant flashpoint between Lombard, Byzantine, Frankish, and Papal interests throughout the early medieval period.
Following Charlemagne's conquest of the Lombard kingdom in 774 CE, the Duchy of Spoleto accepted Frankish suzerainty.
The Duchy of Spoleto remained semi-autonomous under its own dukes while becoming integrated into the Carolingian political structure.
The Duchy of Spoleto served as a buffer zone protecting the Papacy.
Styria was elevated to an independent duchy in 1180 CE, separated from Bavaria.
Rich in iron ore and controlling Alpine trade routes, Styria was a strategically and economically valuable territory that later became one of the core Habsburg hereditary lands.
Rudolf of Habsburg acquired Styria in 1276 after defeating Ottokar II of Bohemia, who had briefly controlled it.
Combined with Austria, Styria gave the Habsburgs a powerful base in the Alpine region.
The death of Conradin, last of the Hohenstaufen, in 1268 ended the Duchy of Swabia as a political unit.
After 1268 the territory of Swabia fragmented among numerous lords, cities, and bishops.
From the fragmentation of Swabia the Swiss Confederation emerged as the Alpine communities sought mutual defence.
The Duchy of Swabia was formally established in 917 CE as one of the five major stem duchies of the emerging Holy Roman Empire.
The Duchy of Swabia's territory covered modern southwest Germany and parts of Switzerland.
The Hohenstaufen dynasty, who later became Holy Roman Emperors, rose from Swabian roots.
The death of Countess Matilda of Tuscany in 1115 ended one of the most powerful independent rulers in Italy.
Matilda of Tuscany's bequest of her lands to the Papacy was disputed by the Holy Roman Emperor.
The dispute over Matilda's bequest fuelled the territorial dimension of the Investiture Controversy and destabilised central Italy for generations.
Frederick Barbarossa's Italian campaigns attempted to reassert imperial authority over Tuscany and northern Italy.
The Tuscan cities resisted imperial control during Barbarossa's campaigns.
The growing commune movement transformed Florence, Siena, and Pisa into self-governing city-states.
At the Battle of Civitate in 1053, Norman adventurers defeated a coalition including Pope Leo IX, marking the decisive turning point for Norman power in southern Italy.
The Duchy of Benevento's political independence effectively ended as the Normans systematically absorbed southern Italian territories.
The Lombard Duchy of Benevento was established in southern Italy around 571 CE, becoming the southernmost and most enduring Lombard political entity.
While the northern Lombard kingdom fell to Charlemagne in 774, Benevento maintained independence until the Norman conquests of the 11th century.
The Treaty of Tarbert in 1098 between Magnus Barefoot of Norway and Edgar of Scotland clarified the boundary between Norwegian and Scottish spheres.
Under the 1098 arrangement Norway retained Orkney, Shetland, and the Hebrides.
Norwegian Norse settlers led by Rognvald Eysteinsson established control over Orkney around 875 CE during Harald Fairhair's unification of Norway.
The Pictish population of Orkney was displaced or absorbed following the Norse settlement.
Orkney became a Norse earldom that served as a base for raids and settlement across the British Isles.
Sassanid Emperor Khosrow II exploited a Byzantine civil war beginning in 602 to launch a major Roman-Persian conflict.
Persian forces captured Antioch, Damascus, Jerusalem (614), and Egypt (619) during the war.
Emperor Heraclius counterattacked and defeated Persia by 628, recovering all lost territory.
Both the Byzantine and Sassanid empires were left financially and militarily exhausted at the time Islam emerged.
Edward I completed the conquest of Wales by 1283, following the death of Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in 1282 and the execution of his brother Dafydd in 1283.
The Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 imposed English law and administration on Wales, dividing it into shires on the English model.
Edward I built massive concentric castles including Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech, and Beaumaris to control conquered Wales.
A large basaltic fissure eruption occurred at Eldgjá in southern Iceland around 939 CE, among the largest effusive eruptions of the past 1,500 years.
Chronicle reports of darkened skies and cold winters across Europe and the Mediterranean coincide with the Eldgjá eruption window.
The Hundred Years' War ended at the Battle of Castillon on 17 July 1453, the last major land battle on French soil.
At Castillon a French army with artillery defeated an English relief force under John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury.
Bordeaux surrendered on 19 October 1453, leaving England with only Calais on the continent.
The loss of the Hundred Years' War helped trigger the Wars of the Roses as English nobles blamed each other for the defeat.
Norse raiders sacked the monastery of Lindisfarne in 793 CE, marking the beginning of the Viking Age in Britain.
The Lindisfarne raid exposed the vulnerability of coastal religious communities and prompted decades of defensive reorganisation.
Alfred of Wessex decisively defeated the Danish Great Army at the Battle of Edington in 878 CE after a guerrilla campaign from the Somerset marshes.
The Treaty of Wedmore that followed Edington established the Danelaw boundary and preserved English Christian culture south of the Thames.
Eric Bloodaxe, the last independent Viking king of York, was killed at the Battle of Stainmore in 954, ending the Viking kingdom of Jorvik.
Eric Bloodaxe's death allowed King Edred of Wessex to reunify England and absorb the Danelaw region.
Norse cultural influence persisted in place names such as by, thorpe, and thwaite across Yorkshire and the East Midlands.
After his banishment from Iceland for manslaughter, Erik Thorvaldsson led a fleet to settle south-west Greenland at Brattahlíð and Garðar around 985 CE.
The Norse Greenland colony reached perhaps 2,500 settlers at its peak.
The Exarchate of Ravenna was established around 584 CE as Byzantium's administrative response to Lombard invasions of Italy.
With Ravenna as its capital, the Exarchate represented the last significant Byzantine territorial presence in Italy, governing a fragmented coastline against constant Lombard pressure.
The Lombard king Aistulf captured Ravenna in 751 CE, ending Byzantine administration of Italy.
The fall of Ravenna led the isolated Pope to appeal to the Frankish kingdom for military support.
The crisis directly led to Pepin the Short's Italian campaigns and the Donation of Pepin, establishing the Papal States.
Edward I of England issued the Edict of Expulsion on July 18, 1290, ordering all Jews out of England by November 1, 1290.
Approximately 2,000 to 3,000 Jews were expelled from England in 1290.
England remained without a recognized Jewish community for 356 years after the 1290 expulsion, until Cromwell's tacit readmission in 1656.
The Mamluk Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil besieged Acre, the last major Crusader stronghold in the Holy Land, beginning in April 1291.
Acre fell to the Mamluks on May 18, 1291, after a six-week siege.
The fall of Acre in 1291 ended the Crusader presence in the Holy Land after 192 years.
Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II's forces breached the walls of Constantinople on May 29, 1453, after a 53-day siege.
The last Byzantine Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos died fighting on the walls of Constantinople in 1453.
After capturing Constantinople in 1453, Mehmed II converted Hagia Sophia into a mosque.
On January 2, 1492, Muhammad XII (Boabdil), the last Nasrid sultan of Granada, surrendered the keys of the Alhambra to Ferdinand and Isabella.
The final campaign against Granada from 1482 to 1492 used superior artillery to reduce Granada's mountain fortresses one by one.
The loss of Málaga in 1487 cut Granada off from Moroccan reinforcement.
In 476, the Germanic chieftain Odoacer deposed the last Western Roman Emperor Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople.
After 476, Odoacer ruled Italy as king, theoretically under Byzantine suzerainty.
Sultan Murad II captured Thessaloniki on March 29, 1430, after a brief siege.
Thessaloniki had been under Venetian administration since 1423, the Venetians having purchased the city from the Byzantine Despot to defend it.
Murad II's forces sacked Thessaloniki for three days in 1430, enslaving many inhabitants and converting the city's churches to mosques.
Mehmed II personally led the Ottoman siege of Trebizond, whose Emperor David surrendered on August 15, 1461, eight years after Constantinople's fall.
After taking Trebizond, Mehmed II deported the Greek population to Constantinople.
Mehmed II executed David Komnenos and his sons two years after the 1461 conquest of Trebizond.
Mehmed II's Ottoman forces besieged Trebizond, the last Byzantine successor state, in August 1461.
Emperor David Komnenos surrendered Trebizond after about a month's siege and was later executed despite promises of safety.
The fall of Trebizond in 1461, eight years after Constantinople, eliminated the last surviving Christian Greek imperial state.
Fatimid commander Jawhar founded the Al-Azhar mosque in Cairo in 970 as both a center of Shia Ismaili learning and a congregational mosque.
After Saladin's conquest of Egypt in 1171 returned the country to Sunni rule, Al-Azhar shifted to Sunni Shafi'i learning.
In 909, Ubayd Allah al-Mahdi Billah led the Kutama Berber army to conquer the Aghlabid emirate of Tunisia, proclaimed himself caliph, and founded the Fatimid dynasty.
Ubayd Allah al-Mahdi Billah claimed descent from the Prophet Muhammad through his daughter Fatima.
From their Tunisian base, the Fatimids subsequently conquered Egypt in 969 and founded Cairo.
In 969, Fatimid general Jawhar al-Siqilli conquered Egypt from the Ikhshidid dynasty, ending Abbasid nominal control over the country.
Jawhar al-Siqilli founded the new city of Cairo as the Fatimid capital.
Within a year of conquering Egypt in 969, Fatimid forces took Jerusalem and much of Syria.
The Fifth Crusade adopted the strategy of capturing Egypt rather than attacking Jerusalem directly, to cut off the Ayyubid heartland.
Crusaders captured the Egyptian port of Damietta in 1219 after a prolonged siege.
Sultan al-Kamil offered to exchange Damietta for Jerusalem, but the papal legate Pelagius refused the offer.
The Fifth Crusade army marched toward Cairo during the Nile flood, became trapped, and negotiated a withdrawal.

The Bulgar Khan Asparuh defeated a Byzantine army and forced Emperor Constantine IV to negotiate, leading to the Treaty of 681 recognizing the First Bulgarian Empire as an independent state south of the Danube.
Under the Treaty of 681, Byzantium agreed to pay annual tribute to the Bulgars.
The First Crusade, launched by Pope Urban II's call in 1095, culminated in the capture of Jerusalem on July 15, 1099.
The capture of Jerusalem in 1099 was followed by a massacre of the city's Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.
The Crusader states established after the First Crusade included the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch, the Kingdom of Jerusalem, and the County of Tripoli.
Filippo Brunelleschi completed the dome of Florence Cathedral, 42 meters in diameter, built without external buttresses or wooden centering using a double-shell herringbone brick technique.
Pope Eugenius IV consecrated Florence Cathedral in 1436.
In 1252 the commune of Florence issued its first gold coin, the fiorino d'oro, containing 3.5 grams of pure gold and bearing the lily of Florence and a standing John the Baptist.
The florin was the first widely circulating gold coinage struck in Western Europe since Carolingian times.
The murder of Buondelmonte dei Buondelmonti at the Ponte Vecchio in 1216 triggered the Guelph-Ghibelline factional conflict in Florence.
In Florence's factional conflict, the Guelphs supported papal authority while the Ghibellines supported imperial authority.
The Guelph victory at Benevento in 1266 established permanent Guelph domination in Florence.
Representatives of the three forest cantons of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden signed a mutual defense pact, the Federal Charter, in August 1291.
The 1291 Federal Charter committed each canton to mutual aid against external aggressors and to resolving disputes by arbitration.
August 1, 1291 is celebrated as Swiss National Day.
A popular uprising in Venice in 976 burned the ducal palace and killed Doge Pietro IV Candiano and his family.
The 976 uprising reflected Venetian opposition to the doge's attempt to build a personal dynastic power base.
The University of Bologna began formal instruction in Roman law around 1088, traditionally under the legal scholar Irnerius.
By 1200, the University of Bologna had over a thousand students from across Europe.
In 910, Duke William I of Aquitaine founded Cluny Abbey in Burgundy and placed it directly under papal authority, exempting it from local episcopal and secular control.
Cluny Abbey eventually controlled over 1,000 dependent monasteries as the center of the 10th–11th century monastic reform movement.
The Fourth Crusade, originally intended for Egypt, was diverted to attack Constantinople, which crusaders sacked for three days in 1204.
After the 1204 sack of Constantinople, the Latin Empire replaced Byzantine rule, while Greek successor states survived at Nicaea, Trebizond, and Epirus.
In 1209, Francis of Assisi obtained an oral approbation of his rule of evangelical poverty from Pope Innocent III, launching the Order of Friars Minor.
The Franciscan and Dominican mendicant orders broke with the older monastic pattern of stable rural cloisters and embedded themselves in the growing towns.
Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor, led the Sixth Crusade while under excommunication.
Frederick II negotiated the Treaty of Jaffa with Ayyubid Sultan al-Kamil, returning Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Nazareth, and a corridor to the sea to Christian control for ten years.
Frederick II crowned himself King of Jerusalem in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre on March 18, 1229.
Charles VIII of France invaded Italy in September 1494 to press his dynastic claim to the Kingdom of Naples.
Charles VIII's army of approximately 25,000 troops, including Swiss pike infantry and a modern artillery train, reached Naples in February 1495.
The Italian states formed the League of Venice in 1495 to expel Charles VIII, who then retreated.
Philip IV of France expelled the Jews in 1306 and confiscated their property.
Philip IV of France arrested the Knights Templar in 1307 and seized their wealth.
Philip IV of France imposed heavy taxation on the French clergy.
In 1206, Temüjin was proclaimed Genghis Khan at a great quriltai on the Mongolian steppe, unifying the Mongol and Turkic tribes under a single authority.
Genghis Khan issued the Yasa, a code of laws, and created a meritocratic military organization based on decimal units.
In 1252 the Genoese mint began striking the genovino d'oro, one of the first stable gold coinages in the Latin West in more than five centuries.
The genovino was rapidly imitated by Venice's ducato in 1284 and used for trans-Mediterranean and Levantine trade.
David IV the Builder defeated a Seljuk-led coalition at the Battle of Didgori in 1121.
After the Battle of Didgori, David IV captured Tbilisi from Muslim control, beginning Georgia's Golden Age.
Shota Rustaveli composed the Georgian epic The Knight in the Panther's Skin at the court of Queen Tamar.
In 1220, the Mongol expedition under Subutai and Jebe swept through Georgia and defeated Georgian armies twice.
Continued Mongol invasions through the 1230s forced Georgia into vassalage.
The Mongol invasions ended the Georgian Golden Age.
Queen Tamar reigned over Georgia from 1184 to 1213.
Under Queen Tamar, Georgia achieved its greatest territorial expansion, controlling much of the Caucasus and Anatolia.
Queen Tamar's Georgia sponsored the founding of the Empire of Trebizond in 1204.
Queen Tamar patronized poets including Shota Rustaveli, author of The Knight in the Panther's Skin.
On July 11, 1302, Flemish infantry drawn primarily from weavers and artisans of Bruges, Ghent, and Ypres defeated the French cavalry at the Battle of Courtrai.
