At Courtrai the French cavalry charged into a drainage ditch and was slaughtered.
After the Battle of Courtrai the Flemish victors collected 500 golden spurs from the dead French knights as trophies.
The Golden Bull of 1356 was issued by Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV and served as the constitutional framework of the Holy Roman Empire for the next 400 years.
The Golden Bull of 1356 confirmed that the emperor was elected by seven princes by majority vote with no papal approval required.
The Golden Bull of 1356 gave Bohemia, Charles IV's hereditary domain, precedence as first among the electors.
Emperor Charles IV issued the Golden Bull in 1356 at the Diet of Nuremberg and Metz, codifying the constitutional framework of the Holy Roman Empire.
The Golden Bull of 1356 specified seven electoral princes: the archbishops of Mainz, Trier, and Cologne, the Count Palatine, the Duke of Saxony, the Margrave of Brandenburg, and the King of Bohemia.
The Golden Bull of 1356 established the electors' near-sovereign rights, the indivisibility of electoral territories, and primogeniture succession.
In 1212, Emperor Frederick II issued the Golden Bull of Sicily confirming Bohemia as a hereditary kingdom and recognizing Přemyslid succession.
The Golden Bull of Sicily exempted Bohemia from obligations to participate in imperial expeditions beyond Bohemia's borders.
The Golden Bull of Sicily formalized Bohemia's special status within the Empire and is regarded as the Bohemian Magna Carta.
Batu Khan's Mongol forces destroyed Vladimir in February 1238 and most of northeastern Rus.
Mongol forces breached the walls of Kiev in December 1240 and destroyed the city.
The conquest of Kiev completed the subjugation of Kievan Rus.
During the Golden Horde's 'Great Troubles' from 1360 to 1380, approximately 20 khans ruled in 20 years.
During the Great Troubles, Mamai, a non-Genghisid controlling the western Golden Horde, faced challenges from Tokhtamysh, backed by Timur.
The Golden Horde's internal chaos enabled Moscow's growing military resistance, culminating in the Battle of Kulikovo in 1380.
Batu Khan established Sarai, near modern Astrakhan, as the capital of the Golden Horde.
Russian princes had to travel to Sarai to receive a yarlyk (patent of rule).
The Golden Horde converted to Islam under Berke Khan, who ruled from 1257 to 1267.
Justinian I's Gothic Wars from 535 to 554 reconquered Italy from the Ostrogothic Kingdom.
General Belisarius captured Sicily in 535 and took Naples and Rome in 536.
The Ostrogoths rallied under Totila, who recaptured Rome twice, in 546 and 550.
Narses defeated and killed Totila at the Battle of Busta Gallorum in 552, with the last Gothic resistance ending in 554.
Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Nasr established the Emirate of Granada as an independent Muslim state in southern Iberia after the Almohad collapse.
The Nasrid dynasty founded by Muhammad I ruled Granada for over 250 years as the last Muslim polity in Iberia.
The Emirate of Granada survived partly by paying tribute to and occasionally allying with Castile.
Muhammad I ibn al-Ahmar founded the Nasrid Emirate of Granada after the Almohad collapse.
Muhammad I accepted Castilian suzerainty, paying tribute and providing military assistance, in exchange for political independence.
Construction of the Alhambra palace complex began under Muhammad I and his successors.
Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile launched the systematic conquest of the Nasrid Emirate of Granada, the last Muslim state in Iberia.
The ten-year campaign against Granada used artillery to reduce one castle at a time, avoiding pitched battles.
Ferdinand and Isabella launched the final campaign against the Nasrid sultanate of Granada from 1482 to 1492 as a systematic artillery-supported siege war.
In the Granada war, Ronda fell in 1485, Loja in 1486, Málaga in 1487, and Baza in 1489.
Granada was invested in 1491, and Boabdil surrendered on January 2, 1492.
Around 1140, the monk Gratian, teaching at Bologna, compiled the Concordia Discordantium Canonum, known as the Decretum, a systematic harmonisation of canon law.
The Decretum became the first part of the Corpus Iuris Canonici, the basis of medieval canon law down to 1917.
Beginning in 1315, seven years of catastrophic harvest failures struck Northern Europe, associated with the start of the Little Ice Age.
The summer of 1315 saw almost uninterrupted rainfall across England, France, the Low Countries, and the Holy Roman Empire, rotting crops in the fields.
Mortality during the Great Famine is estimated at 10 to 25 percent in the worst-affected regions.
In 1054, Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida placed a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia, excommunicating Patriarch Michael I Cerularius.
Patriarch Michael I Cerularius excommunicated the papal legates in return.
The mutual excommunications of 1054 formalized centuries of theological and political divergence over papal supremacy and the Filioque clause.
In 1480, Ivan III of Moscow refused to pay tribute to the Golden Horde and faced down Khan Akhmat's army at the Ugra River without battle.
Khan Akhmat withdrew after his Crimean ally failed to support him, and the Golden Horde dissolved shortly after.
The 'Great Stand' on the Ugra marked the end of the Mongol Yoke that had dominated Russia for 240 years.
A catastrophic North Sea storm surge on 15–16 January 1362, known as the 'Great Drowning of Men', killed about 25,000 people.
The 1362 storm surge permanently submerged the trading port of Rungholt and reshaped the Frisian coastline.
On July 15, 1410, the combined Polish-Lithuanian army under Władysław II Jagiełło and Vytautas confronted the Teutonic Order's army under Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen at Grunwald.
At Grunwald the Teutonic Grand Master and most of his senior officers were killed, permanently breaking the Teutonic Order's military power.
The Battle of Grunwald established Poland-Lithuania as the dominant power in central-eastern Europe.
At the Battle of Crécy in August 1346, the English under Edward III defeated Philip VI's French army.
At Crécy the English deployed small cannon, among the first recorded battlefield uses of artillery.
Around 1455 Johannes Gutenberg completed the printing of approximately 180 copies of his Latin Bible in Mainz, 135 on paper and 45 on vellum.
The Gutenberg Bible used a typeface designed to resemble hand-lettered manuscripts.
Around 1445 Johannes Gutenberg worked in Mainz developing the printing press, combining oil-based ink, a screw press, and moveable metal type.
Gutenberg's partnership with Johann Fust provided the capital for his printing venture.
Gutenberg's breakthrough was the hand mold enabling rapid type casting, whose first major product was the 42-line Bible around 1454-1455.
In 1273 the German princes elected Rudolf of Habsburg as Holy Roman Emperor, ending the Great Interregnum.
Rudolf of Habsburg defeated King Ottokar II of Bohemia at the Battle of Marchfeld in 1278.
Rudolf granted Austria and Styria to his sons, establishing the hereditary territorial base of Habsburg power.
Around 870, Muhammad al-Bukhari completed the Sahih, a critical compilation of some 7,275 hadith reports collected over sixteen years.
Al-Bukhari's Sahih became one of the two most authoritative Sunni hadith collections.
Emperor Justinian I dedicated the rebuilt Hagia Sophia in Constantinople on December 27, 537.
The rebuilt Hagia Sophia was built in five years under the architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidorus of Miletus.
The Hagia Sophia served as the center of Eastern Christianity until the Ottoman conquest of 1453.
Justinian I inaugurated the rebuilt Hagia Sophia on 27 December 537 after a five-year construction supervised by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus.
The Hagia Sophia's 31-metre central dome on pendentives was the largest enclosed interior space in the world for nearly a thousand years.
Muhammad made his final pilgrimage in 632, after which the hajj was institutionalized as one of the Five Pillars of Islam.
The institutionalized hajj created an annual gathering at Mecca that drew Muslims from across the expanding Islamic world.
Valdemar IV's sack of the Hansa-protected port of Visby on Gotland in 1361 triggered a multi-year naval war by the Wendish towns against Denmark.
The Treaty of Stralsund in 1370 ended hostilities on Hanseatic terms, granting the League sweeping commercial privileges and a veto on Danish royal succession.
In 1294, German merchants from Lübeck and other Wendish towns secured formal trading privileges at Bergen.
The Bryggen Kontor at Bergen gave the Hanseatic League a near-monopoly on Norwegian stockfish and grain trade for the next three centuries.
Around 900 CE, Hedeby at the base of the Jutland peninsula was the largest Viking Age trading center in northern Europe.
Around 900 CE, Hedeby drew merchants from England, Germany, Byzantium, and the Arab world.
At its peak around 900 CE, Hedeby used Arabic dirhams as its primary currency and had 1,000-1,500 inhabitants.
Henry V of England died of dysentery at Vincennes on August 31, 1422, at age 36.
At his death in 1422, Henry V left a nine-month-old son, Henry VI, as heir to the English crown and, under the Treaty of Troyes, the French crown.
After Charles VI of France died weeks after Henry V in 1422, Henry VI theoretically became king of both England and France.
By 628, after six years of counteroffensive campaigns into Persian territory, Heraclius forced the assassination of Khosrow II.
In 628, Heraclius secured the return of the True Cross.
By 628 both the Byzantine and Persian empires were exhausted, and within three years Islam emerged to conquer both.
Emperor Heraclius defeated the Sassanid army at Nineveh in December 627 and drove deep into Mesopotamia.
Following the defeat at Nineveh, Khosrow II was overthrown and murdered by his son, and the Sassanid court sued for peace.
Heraclius recovered the True Cross in 628 and entered Jerusalem in triumph.
Councils held in Constantinople in June and August 1341 endorsed Gregory Palamas's defence of hesychasm against the humanist Barlaam.
Further councils in Constantinople in 1347 and 1351 confirmed Palamite theology.
The Benedictine abbess Hildegard of Bingen completed Scivias in 1151 after ten years of composition.
Scivias is a trilogy of twenty-six theological visions accompanied by programmatic illuminations.
Scivias circulated widely after Pope Eugenius III endorsed it at the synod of Trier in 1147.
Otto I was crowned at Aachen in 936 in a ceremony deliberately evoking Charlemagne.
Otto I developed the Reichskirchensystem, using bishops and abbots as royal administrators appointed through royal investiture.
Otto I defeated the Magyars at the Battle of Lechfeld in 955.
Otto I's Roman imperial coronation in 962 created the Holy Roman Empire.
Around 830, Caliph al-Maʾmūn institutionalised the systematic translation of Greek philosophical, mathematical, medical, and astronomical texts into Arabic at Baghdad.
Translators such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq and Thabit ibn Qurra worked from Greek and Syriac sources.
The translation work at Baghdad was followed by original research, including al-Khwārizmī's algebra and astronomical tables.
In 1337, Edward III of England formally asserted his claim to the French throne through his mother Isabella, triggering the Hundred Years' War.
The Hundred Years' War began with an English naval victory at Sluys in 1340 and land victories at Crécy in 1346 and Poitiers in 1356.
The Treaty of Brétigny in 1360 gave England vast French territories in exchange for dropping the royal claim.
The English chevauchée strategy of systematic large-scale raids was designed to devastate the French agricultural economy and show that the French king could not protect his subjects.
The Black Prince's 1355 chevauchée through Languedoc destroyed approximately 500 towns and villages.
In 1337, Edward III of England formally claimed the French throne through his mother Isabella, rejecting Philip VI of Valois's succession.
The immediate trigger of the Hundred Years' War was Philip VI's confiscation of Gascony, English territory held as a French fief.
The Council of Constance burned Czech reformer Jan Hus at the stake in 1415 despite an imperial safe-conduct.
The Hussite Wars from 1419 to 1434 repelled five successive papal crusades and established a tolerated Utraquist Czech church.
In 1420, Jan Žižka led a Hussite force to victory over Emperor Sigismund's crusading army at Vítkov Hill near Prague.
Žižka's Wagenburg tactic combined improvised mobile fortifications with infantry armed with crossbows, flails, and handguns.
The Hussites repelled all five papal crusades against them between 1420 and 1431.
The execution of Jan Hus in 1415 triggered the Hussite revolt in Bohemia, beginning with the First Defenestration of Prague in 1419.
The Hussite commander Jan Žižka, blind after 1420, was reputedly never defeated in battle.
The Council of Basel's Compactata of 1436 granted the Hussites communion in both kinds.
Jan Hus was summoned to the Council of Constance under a safe-conduct promise from Emperor Sigismund.
Jan Hus was tried for heresy based on his advocacy of Wycliffite doctrines including lay communion in both kinds and Bible authority over church tradition.
Jan Hus refused to recant and was burned at the stake on July 6, 1415, in violation of his safe-conduct.
The execution of Jan Hus ignited the Hussite revolt in Bohemia in 1419.
In 1354, Muhammad ibn Battuta ended his 29-year journey across North Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia, India, Southeast Asia, and China, returning to Fez.
Ibn Battuta's travelogue, dictated as the Rihla, is the most extensive eyewitness account of the 14th-century Islamic world.
Aḥmad ibn Faḍlān served as secretary on an Abbasid embassy, dispatched by Caliph al-Muqtadir in 921, to the king of the Volga Bulgars.
Ibn Faḍlān's Risāla contains the earliest detailed first-hand Arabic description of the Rus' on the Volga, including a report of a Rus' ship-burial.
Around 1025, Avicenna (Ibn Sina) completed Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, a five-volume synthesis of Galenic, Aristotelian, and Islamic medical knowledge.
Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb was translated into Latin in the 12th century and remained the standard European medical textbook until the 17th century.
At the Althing in 1000, the lawspeaker Þorgeirr Ljósvetningagoði ruled in favour of formal conversion to Christianity to prevent the island fracturing.
The 1000 conversion ruling permitted private pagan practice to continue for a transitional period.
In 1000 CE, the Althing voted to adopt Christianity as the official religion of Iceland.
The 1000 CE conversion compromise allowed private pagan practice to continue.
After decades of civil conflict during the Sturlung Age, the Icelandic Althing agreed to submit to the Norwegian crown through the Old Covenant of 1262.
The Old Covenant of 1262 ended 330 years of Icelandic independence.
The Althing was established in 930 CE at Þingvellir in Iceland.
The Althing made laws, resolved disputes, and made major decisions without a king.
The Icelandic Althing established in 930 lasted until 1262.
The Eldgjá eruption of 939 was one of the largest basaltic flood-lava eruptions of the past two millennia.
Eldgjá's tephra and sulphate aerosols depressed Northern Hemisphere temperatures for several years.
In 726, Byzantine Emperor Leo III ordered the removal of the image of Christ above the Chalke Gate, beginning the first period of Byzantine Iconoclasm.
The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 restored icon veneration.
A second period of Byzantine Iconoclasm followed from 815 to 843.
In 726, Emperor Leo III ordered the destruction of religious icons, launching a century-long theological dispute.
After Pope Gregory III condemned iconoclasm, Leo III seized papal estates in Italy in retaliation.
The iconoclasm controversy pushed the papacy toward the Franks for military protection and accelerated Italy's drift from Byzantine influence.
In 754, Constantine V convened 338 bishops at the imperial palace of Hieria in the absence of all five patriarchs.
The Council of Hieria formally condemned the veneration of icons as idolatry and ordered their destruction.
In 815, Emperor Leo V summoned a synod at the Hagia Sophia that reversed the decisions of 787 and reinstated iconoclasm.
In the 815 iconoclast revival, the patriarch Nikephoros was deposed and Theodore the Studite led the iconodule resistance.
Following the Mongol destruction of Baghdad in 1258, Western Christian powers attempted to forge an alliance with the Ilkhanate against the Mamluks.
Hulagu Khan's mother and wife were Nestorian Christians, and he was open to diplomatic approaches.
The Mongol defeat at Ain Jalut in 1260 and the Ilkhanate's conversion to Islam under Ghazan Khan in 1295 ended the possibility of a Christian-Mongol alliance.
In February 1076, Pope Gregory VII excommunicated and deposed Emperor Henry IV after Henry attempted to depose Gregory at the Synod of Worms.
The papal excommunication released Henry IV's vassals from their oaths of loyalty and triggered noble defections.
To save his throne, Henry IV undertook a penitential journey to Canossa in January 1077.
In 563, the Irish monk Columba founded a monastery on the island of Iona in the Inner Hebrides.
Iona served as the base from which Celtic Christianity spread across Scotland and northern England.
Iona produced the monk Aidan, who founded Lindisfarne and began the Christianization of Northumbria.
In 563, the Irish monk Columba founded a monastery on the island of Iona off the western coast of Scotland.
The monastery of Iona became the base for the conversion of the Picts and later Northumbria.
Aidan, sent from Iona, founded the monastery of Lindisfarne in 635.
In 1170, Richard de Clare ('Strongbow'), invited by the exiled king of Leinster Diarmait Mac Murchada, landed in Ireland and captured Waterford and Dublin.
Strongbow married Diarmait Mac Murchada's daughter and became King of Leinster on Diarmait's death.
In 1171, Henry II of England led an expedition to Ireland, accepted the submission of Irish kings, and established the Lordship of Ireland.
A massive peasant uprising, the Jacquerie, erupted in northern France in May–June 1358.
During the Jacquerie of 1358, peasants attacked noble castles and manors across the Beauvaisis and Île-de-France.
The nobility under Charles of Navarre massacred the Jacques' leaders, causing the 1358 uprising to collapse within weeks.
Joan of Arc was captured by the Burgundians in 1430 and sold to the English.
Joan of Arc was tried for heresy by an ecclesiastical court at Rouen presided over by Bishop Pierre Cauchon and burned at the stake on 30 May 1431.
A papal retrial in 1456 posthumously rehabilitated Joan of Arc, and she was canonized in 1920.
When Aragonese forces invaded Sardinia in 1323, the Judicate of Arborea initially cooperated with Aragon.
The Judicate of Arborea subsequently led indigenous Sardinian resistance against Aragonese domination for over a century.
Judge Eleonora of Arborea promulgated the Carta de Logu in 1383, an advanced legal code governing criminal and civil law, property rights, and environmental protection.
The Carta de Logu remained in force in Sardinia until 1827.
The Judicate of Cagliari was extinguished in 1258 following dynastic conflicts and Genoese intervention.
After 1258, the territory of the Judicate of Cagliari was absorbed by rival Sardinian powers and Pisan and Genoese commercial interests.
The Judicate of Cagliari in southern Sardinia developed as one of four independent Sardinian giudicati following the Byzantine withdrawal.
The Judicate of Cagliari controlled the most fertile agricultural land of Sardinia and maintained trade relations with Pisa and Genoa.
Emperor Justinian I commissioned the legal scholar Tribonian to compile and codify all Roman law.
The resulting Corpus Juris Civilis (529–534) consisted of the Code, the Digest, the Institutes, and the Novels.
Plague returned to Constantinople in 558, killing thousands daily according to Agathias.
The 558 outbreak was one of approximately eighteen documented plague outbreaks across the Mediterranean between 541 and the early 8th century, known as the First Plague Pandemic.
In 533, Emperor Justinian I launched the reconquest of the western Mediterranean, beginning with Belisarius's campaign against the Vandal Kingdom in North Africa.
The Vandals under King Gelimer were defeated at Ad Decimum and Tricamarum, and the Vandal Kingdom ended in 534.
Justinian I invaded Italy in 535, beginning the Gothic Wars that devastated Italy's economy and population.
In 533, General Belisarius defeated the Vandal king Gelimer at the Battles of Ad Decimum and Tricamarum, destroying the Vandal kingdom in less than a year.
The 533 campaign recovered the western Mediterranean's grain supply for Byzantium and re-established imperial control over North Africa for a century.
At the Battle of the Kalka River on 31 May 1223, a Mongol force under Jebe and Subutai confronted a joint Rus-Cuman army.
At the Kalka River, the Mongols feigned retreat, broke the pursuing Cuman formation, and annihilated the separated Rus-Cuman forces.
The Battle of the Kalka River in 1223 was the first contact between the Mongols and the Rus.
On 10 October 680, Umayyad forces killed Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, with his small party on the plain of Karbala in southern Iraq.
Husayn ibn Ali had refused to acknowledge the caliphate of Yazid I and was journeying toward Kufa when intercepted at Karbala.
Around 740, the Khazar ruling elite converted to Judaism.
The Khazar conversion to Judaism may have been partly a political statement of neutrality between Christian Byzantium and the Islamic Caliphate.
In 965, Prince Sviatoslav I of Kiev destroyed the Khazar capital Atil and the fortresses of Sarkel and Semender.
The Khazar Khaganate disintegrated rapidly after Sviatoslav's attacks of 965.
The Abbasid Revolution of 750 originated in Khorasan, where discontent with Umayyad Arab supremacism was strongest.
The predominantly Iranian and Muslim soldiers of Khorasan formed the military backbone of the Abbasid victory in 750.
Under Duncan I (reigned 1034–1040), the Kingdom of Alba extended its authority to include Strathclyde and parts of Northumbria.
Duncan I was murdered by Macbeth, leading to civil war.
Around 900 CE, the Kingdom of Alba consolidated its hold over mainland Scotland north of the Forth under Kenneth MacAlpin's dynasty.
Gaelic language and culture replaced Pictish as the dominant cultural tradition of the Kingdom of Alba.
Tvrtko I was crowned King of Bosnia in 1377, elevating the territory from a banate to a kingdom.
Tvrtko I briefly incorporated Serbian and Croatian territories and was the most powerful figure in the western Balkans.
The Ottoman conquest of Bosnia in 1463 was swift and decisive, and the last Bosnian king Stjepan Tomašević was captured and executed.
Following the 1463 conquest, Bosnia became an Ottoman province and significant portions of the population eventually converted to Islam.
Connacht forces under Maelseachlainn II fought at the Battle of Clontarf in 1014.
The death of High King Brian Boru at Clontarf in 1014 prevented any single king from dominating Ireland again.
Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair of Connacht became the last High King of Ireland in 1166.
The political difficulties of Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair led the deposed Leinster king Diarmait Mac Murchada to invite Anglo-Norman forces to Ireland.
The Treaty of Windsor in 1175 recognised Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair as High King of Ireland under English overlordship.
The Welsh victory at the Battle of Crug Mawr in 1136 temporarily halted Norman expansion into south Wales.
Deheubarth under Gruffudd ap Rhys experienced a political and cultural resurgence after 1136.
Maredudd ap Owain of Deheubarth briefly united much of Wales under his rule in the late 10th century, repelling Viking raids.
The reign of Maredudd ap Owain represented the high point of Deheubarth's influence before the fragmentation preceding the Norman conquest.
King Edmund of East Anglia was killed by the Danish Great Heathen Army in 869 CE after refusing to renounce Christianity.
Following Edmund's death in 869, East Anglia was conquered by the Vikings and absorbed into the Danelaw.
Edward the Elder of Wessex reconquered East Anglia from Danish control in 917 CE, incorporating the former kingdom into the emerging unified English state.
The union of Castile and León in 1230 under Ferdinand III permanently incorporated Galicia as a province rather than a kingdom.
Although Santiago de Compostela retained its ecclesiastical importance, Galicia's political distinctiveness was subordinated to the Castilian-Leonese state after 1230.
Galicia emerged as a distinct kingdom when Alfonso III of Asturias partitioned his realm among his sons in 910 CE.
As the home of the shrine of Saint James at Santiago de Compostela, Galicia held unique spiritual prestige and attracted pilgrims from across Europe.
David IV (the Builder) completed the unification of the Georgian kingdoms in the early 12th century.
The military campaigns of David IV expelled the Seljuk Turks from Georgian territory, inaugurating the Georgian Golden Age.
Queen Tamar of Georgia reigned from 1184 to 1213, a period regarded as the zenith of medieval Georgia.
Under Queen Tamar's rule, Georgia expanded to its greatest territorial extent.
Queen Tamar of Georgia sponsored the establishment of the Empire of Trebizond as a buffer state.
Llywelyn ap Gruffudd was killed in battle in 1282, ending the last independent Welsh principality.
Edward I completed the conquest of Wales with the Statute of Rhuddlan in 1284.
Edward I created the title Prince of Wales for his heir in 1301.
Rhodri Mawr became King of Gwynedd in 844 CE and briefly united most of Wales under his rule.
Rhodri Mawr defeated a Viking leader in battle and earned a reputation celebrated in Frankish chronicles.
Rhodri Mawr's descendants dominated Welsh politics for two centuries after his reign.
Pope Gregory I's missionary Augustine landed in Kent in 597 CE.
King Æthelberht of Kent received Augustine in 597 CE and converted to Christianity.
The establishment of Canterbury in Kent as the primacy of the English Church made Kent central to English religious history.
Following the Battle of Ellandun in 825 CE, Kent acknowledged West Saxon overlordship under Egbert of Wessex, ending its independence.
After 825 CE, Kent's importance continued through Canterbury's ecclesiastical primacy despite the loss of political independence.
The Kingdom of Majorca was created in 1276 when James I of Aragon divided his territories, giving the Balearic Islands, Montpellier, and Roussillon to his younger son James II.
The Kingdom of Majorca became a prosperous trading crossroads between Iberia, North Africa, and Italy.
Peter IV of Aragon conquered the Kingdom of Majorca in 1343, reabsorbing it into the Crown of Aragon.
Majorcan cartographers produced the Catalan Atlas in 1375, one of the greatest medieval maps of the known world.
Godred Crovan conquered the Isle of Man in 1079, establishing the Norse Kingdom of Mann and the Isles.
The Kingdom of Mann and the Isles served as a conduit for Norse-Gaelic cultural synthesis.
The Treaty of Perth in 1266 transferred the Kingdom of Mann and the Western Isles from Norwegian to Scottish sovereignty.
Under the Treaty of Perth, Norway retained Orkney and Shetland.
The Treaty of Perth ended Scandinavian political dominance in the Scottish islands.
The rise of Brian Boru of Munster in the late 10th century challenged Meath's traditional role as the seat of Irish High Kingship.
The rivalry between Meath and Munster defined Irish politics until the Norman invasion.
Offa seized the Mercian throne in 757 CE, beginning the period of Mercian supremacy in England.
Offa constructed Offa's Dyke, a defensive earthwork along the Welsh border.
Offa was among the first English kings to style himself 'Rex Anglorum' (King of the English).
Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, died in 918 CE, allowing her brother Edward the Elder of Wessex to absorb Mercia directly.
Æthelflæd led Mercian military campaigns against the Danes during her rule.
The death of Æthelflæd in 918 CE ended Mercia's semi-independent status.
Brian Boru of the Dál Cais dynasty became King of Munster in 978 CE, beginning his campaign to become High King of all Ireland.
Brian Boru forged alliances with Norse settlers and used Munster's resources to project power across Ireland.
At the Battle of Carham in 1018, Strathclyde and Scottish forces defeated Northumbria.
The Kingdom of Strathclyde effectively merged with Scotland after 1018 when its last king died without heirs.
Norse and Dublin Viking forces sacked Dumbarton Rock, the capital of Strathclyde, in 870 CE after a four-month siege.
The enslavement of the captured population at Dumbarton in 870 CE severely weakened Strathclyde.
Boniface of Montferrat established the Latin Kingdom of Thessalonica in 1204 following the Fourth Crusade.
The Kingdom of Thessalonica faced constant pressure from the Bulgarian Empire and Greek populations.
The Kingdom of Thessalonica lasted only two decades before falling to the Despotate of Epirus.
The Anglo-Norman adventurer John de Courcy invaded Ulster in 1177.
The Earldom of Ulster was established following the Norman invasion of 1177, creating a permanent English foothold in the province.
The Battle of Moira in 637 CE was one of the largest battles in early medieval Irish history.
At the Battle of Moira, the Uí Néill High King Domnall mac Áedo defeated the Dál Fiatach king of Ulster and his British allies.
The Battle of Moira in 637 CE marked the definitive decline of Ulster as the dominant Irish kingdom.
At the Second Battle of Kosovo (1448), Hungarian regent János Hunyadi led a crusading force against the Ottoman army of Sultan Murad II.
The Ottoman victory at the Second Battle of Kosovo ensured Ottoman control of the Balkans before the fall of Constantinople in 1453.
After the death of Möngke Khan in 1259, Kublai Khan claimed the title of Great Khan despite the opposition of his brother Ariq Böke.
The civil war between Kublai Khan and Ariq Böke (1260–1264) fragmented the unified Mongol Empire irreversibly.
Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in China in 1271 and moved the Mongol capital to Dadu (Beijing).
Dmitry Donskoy, Grand Prince of Moscow, defeated the Golden Horde's army under Mamai at Kulikovo on 8 September 1380.
Moscow was sacked by Khan Tokhtamysh in 1382, two years after the Battle of Kulikovo.
The Battle of Kulikovo established that Russian forces could defeat the Mongols in open battle.
Vladimir I chose Eastern Orthodox Christianity and was baptised at Chersonesus, marrying a Byzantine princess.
The mass baptism of Kievan Rus in the Dnieper River in 988 is the foundational date of Russian Orthodox Christianity.
Yaroslav the Wise codified Russian law in the Russkaya Pravda during his reign beginning in 1019.
Yaroslav the Wise built the Cathedral of Hagia Sophia in Kiev and married his children to royal families across Europe.
At the Battle of Legnano in 1176, the Lombard League defeated Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa's army.
At Legnano the Lombard infantry militia fought from behind the carroccio, halting Barbarossa's cavalry charge.
The Battle of Legnano forced Barbarossa to negotiate the Peace of Constance in 1183.
Around 1001, Leif Erikson sailed west from Greenland and overwintered on the North American coast at the site later excavated as L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland.
The L'Anse aux Meadows excavation confirms a Norse presence in North America around AD 1000–1020.
The permanent union of the crowns of León and Castile in 1230 under Ferdinand III created the largest Christian kingdom in Iberia.
The 1230 consolidation of León and Castile accelerated the Reconquista, leading to the conquest of Córdoba (1236) and Seville (1248).
The Kingdom of León emerged around 910 as the Asturian monarchy relocated its capital southward.
The Kingdom of León became a leading force of the Reconquista, expanding southward against the Emirate of Córdoba.
The Umayyad regent Al-Mansur sacked and burned the city of León in 997 CE.
During Al-Mansur's raid of 997 CE, the cathedral bells of León were carried to Córdoba as trophies.
On 8 June 793, a Viking raiding fleet attacked the monastery of Lindisfarne off the Northumbrian coast.
During the 793 Viking raid on Lindisfarne, the monks were killed or enslaved and the monastery's treasures looted.
The Viking raid on Lindisfarne in 793 is conventionally dated as the beginning of the Viking Age in England.
A major earthquake on 24 August 1356 damaged Lisbon, the Alentejo, and the Algarve.
The 1356 earthquake was among the largest recorded medieval seismic events on the Iberian peninsula.
The Treaty of Montgomery in 1267 recognized Llywelyn ap Gruffudd as Prince of Wales with authority over all other Welsh lords.
Llywelyn ap Gruffudd was killed in a skirmish at Orewin Bridge in December 1282.
Following Llywelyn's death, Edward I completed the conquest of Wales.
John Wycliffe oversaw the first complete English translation of the Bible, completed around 1382-1395.
Wycliffe proposed radical theological reforms including Bible-alone authority, rejection of transubstantiation, and disendowment of the wealthy Church.
Wycliffe's followers, the Lollards, spread his ideas through preaching and manuscript distribution despite persecution.
Wycliffe's ideas directly influenced Jan Hus in Bohemia.
The Lombard Queen Theodelinda, encouraged by Pope Gregory the Great, moved the Lombard kingdom toward Catholic Christianity from Arianism around 603.
The Lombard conversion was gradual, with the nobility remaining largely Arian for another generation.
The Lombard king Alboin led his people from Pannonia into Italy in 568.
Within three years of the Lombard invasion, most of northern Italy fell and the Po Valley became known as 'Lombardy.'
Rome, Naples, Sicily, Ravenna, and coastal cities remained Byzantine after the Lombard invasion, leaving Italy permanently fragmented.
Alboin was assassinated in 572, after which the Lombard kingdom briefly fragmented among regional dukes.
Sixteen northern Italian communes formed the Lombard League at Pontida in 1167 to resist Frederick Barbarossa's reassertion of imperial control.
Frederick I Barbarossa razed Milan in 1162.
The Lombard League rebuilt Milan and constructed the fortress city of Alessandria to block imperial invasion routes.
Henry III's Assize of Arms in 1252 required English and Welsh free men to practice archery regularly.
English longbowmen could shoot 10-12 aimed arrows per minute with bows of 100-180 lb draw weight.
Philip II of France declared King John's French fiefs forfeit, exploiting John's legal difficulties after the murder of his nephew Arthur of Brittany.
Normandy, Anjou, Maine, and Touraine fell to Philip II in a rapid campaign, with Rouen surrendering in June 1204.
England lost the Duchy of Normandy in 1204, 138 years after the Norman Conquest of 1066.
Louis IX of France led the Seventh Crusade, sailing from Aigues-Mortes in 1248 with a strategy targeting Egypt.
Louis IX captured Damietta in 1249 but his advance on Cairo was halted at Mansourah in 1250.
Louis IX was captured in April 1250 and ransomed for 400,000 livres tournois and Damietta.
Emperor Frederick II granted Lübeck the status of Free Imperial City in 1226, confirming its autonomy from territorial princes.
Lübeck became the model and de-facto capital of the developing Hanseatic League.
Basil I, who rose through court intrigue to murder Emperor Michael III, founded the Macedonian dynasty in 867.
The Macedonian dynasty ruled Byzantium for nearly two centuries, from 867 to 1056.
Basil I began the Basilika, a comprehensive Greek revision of Justinian's Latin legal code.
Following King John's death in 1216, the regents of his son Henry III issued a revised version of Magna Carta to win baronial support.
The 1217 revision of Magna Carta added the Forest Charter, and the 1225 version became the definitive form.
On June 15, 1215, King John of England sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede under pressure from a baronial coalition.
Magna Carta contained 63 clauses limiting royal power, including no taxation without consent of the Great Council and no imprisonment without lawful judgment.
King John received papal annulment of Magna Carta, but it was reissued multiple times and became foundational to English constitutional law.
Barons forced King John to seal Magna Carta at Runnymede in 1215, comprising 63 clauses limiting royal prerogative.
Magna Carta's key provisions included no free man imprisoned except by judgment of peers, no taxation without consent of the Great Council, and a committee of 25 barons to enforce compliance.
King John's request for papal annulment of Magna Carta led to the First Barons' War.
Henry III of England reissued Magna Carta in revised form in 1225 in exchange for a grant of taxation.
The 1225 version of Magna Carta was entered into the English statute books and became the permanent foundation of English constitutional law.
Moses Maimonides served as court physician to Saladin's vizier in Cairo.
Maimonides completed the 'Guide for the Perplexed' around 1190, a rationalist synthesis of Aristotelian philosophy and rabbinic Judaism.
Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, made his hajj to Mecca in 1324 with a caravan of 60,000 men and camels laden with gold.
By distributing gold lavishly in Cairo, Mansa Musa depressed gold prices in Egypt for over a decade.
European cartographers depicted Mansa Musa on the Catalan Atlas of 1375.
After the defeat at Manzikert in 1071, the Byzantine Empire entered a decade of civil war between competing claimants, ending with Alexios I Komnenos in 1081.
While Byzantine factions fought each other, the Seljuk Turks colonized virtually all of Anatolia, the empire's tax and recruitment heartland.
Manuel II was crowned in Hagia Sophia in 1391, succeeding his father John V as Byzantine emperor of a state reduced to Constantinople, Thessalonica, and the Morea.
Within months of his coronation, Manuel II was fighting alongside Sultan Bayezid I as a tributary vassal.
Niccolò, Maffeo, and Marco Polo left Venice in 1271 for the court of Kublai Khan.
The Polos returned to Venice 24 years later with the account that became Il Milione.
Marco Polo arrived at Kublai Khan's court at Khanbaliq (Beijing) in 1275.
Marco Polo spent 17 years in Mongol service, traveling extensively across China and Southeast Asia.
Marco Polo's Travels introduced Europeans to Chinese silk, paper money, coal, and the scope of Asian civilization.
Marco Polo and his father and uncle returned to Venice in 1295 after 24 years of travel through the Mongol world.
Captured in a Venetian-Genoese sea battle in 1298, Marco Polo dictated his Travels to fellow prisoner Rustichello of Pisa.
Albert the Bear secured the North March in 1157, founding the Margraviate of Brandenburg.
Albert the Bear colonised Brandenburg with German settlers, making it the spearhead of German eastward expansion.
The Golden Bull of 1356 confirmed Brandenburg's status as one of the seven electoral principalities of the Holy Roman Empire.
Brandenburg's electoral vote gave it disproportionate political influence in German affairs.
Boniface, the English monk who organized the German church and reformed the Frankish church, was martyred in Frisia in 754.
Boniface's founding of monasteries at Fulda and his organizing of the German dioceses created the ecclesiastical framework for Charlemagne's empire.
Richard I of England ordered the execution of approximately 2,700 Muslim prisoners at Acre in 1191 when Saladin delayed the agreed ransom payment.
Saladin retaliated for the Acre massacre by executing his own Christian prisoners.
Maximilian I reorganized the Imperial Diet, with the 1495 Diet of Worms establishing the Eternal Public Peace and an imperial court.
Maximilian I developed the Landsknecht mercenary infantry that became a dominant European military force.
Maximilian I's marriage to Mary of Burgundy and his grandson Charles V's inheritances created the Habsburg global empire.
Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici founded the Banco Medici in Florence on 1 October 1397, opening branches in Rome, Venice, and Geneva.
The Medici bank's holding-company structure became the template for early modern multinational banking.
Cosimo de' Medici returned from exile to Florence in 1434 and established the Medici family's informal dominance over the republic.
Cosimo de' Medici's power rested on his banking fortune, patronage, and control of the electoral bags rather than formal office.
Cosimo de' Medici's patronage supported artists including Brunelleschi, Donatello, and Fra Angelico.
Muhammad's Constitution of Medina around 622 established a political community encompassing Muslim, Jewish, and Arab pagan tribes in Medina.
The Constitution of Medina defined mutual defense obligations, judicial procedures, and the relationship between religious and tribal identity.
Mehmed II issued the Kanunname in 1451, a sultanic legal code existing parallel to Sharia.
The Kanunname covered administrative, fiscal, and criminal law areas not addressed by religious law.
Mehmed II reorganized the palace school, the devshirme system, and the provincial administration.
In 558 CE, Chlothar I, the last surviving son of Clovis I, reunited the entire Frankish realm under his sole rule.
The Merovingian kingdom under Chlothar I absorbed Thuringia, Burgundy, and Provence into a pan-Frankish realm.
Chlothar I's death in 561 led to the partition of the Frankish realm among his four sons, inaugurating civil wars between Austrasia, Neustria, and Burgundy.
The Treaty of Verdun in 843 CE divided the Carolingian Empire among Charlemagne's three grandsons, creating Middle Francia as the central portion.
Middle Francia stretched from the Low Countries to Italy and lacked ethnic or linguistic coherence.
The Treaty of Mersen in 870 divided Lotharingia between East and West Francia, eliminating Middle Francia as a political entity.
The borderlands of former Middle Francia became a contested zone between Germany and France for centuries.
In 1119, Hugues de Payens and eight knights founded the Knights Templar in Jerusalem, taking monastic vows while escorting pilgrims.
Bernard of Clairvaux wrote the Rule of the Knights Templar and argued for their legitimacy in De Laude Novae Militiae.
The Council of Troyes in 1129 granted the Knights Templar formal papal recognition.
The Knights Templar accumulated land donations across Europe that they used to create an international banking network.
Edward I summoned the Model Parliament of 1295, including knights of the shire and burgesses from towns alongside clergy and magnates.
The Model Parliament of 1295 established the precedent of including representatives of the commons in tax-granting assemblies in England.
In 1279, Kublai Khan defeated the last Song dynasty naval forces at the Battle of Yamen, completing the Mongol conquest of China.
The fall of the Southern Song in 1279 ended a civilization that had developed gunpowder weapons, printing, paper money, and large-scale porcelain production.
Kublai Khan established the Yuan dynasty, ruling China from a new capital at Beijing.
In 1219, Genghis Khan launched a campaign against the Khwarazmian Empire after Shah Muhammad II executed Mongol trade envoys.
During the Mongol campaign against Khwarezm, the cities of Samarkand, Bukhara, Merv, Nishapur, and Urgench were systematically destroyed.
Merv, possibly the largest city in the world at the time, was destroyed so thoroughly during the Mongol campaign that it never recovered.
In 1241, Batu Khan and Subutai divided their forces to attack Poland and Hungary simultaneously.
In 1241, the Polish-German coalition was crushed at Legnica and Béla IV's Hungarian army was annihilated at Mohi.
The Mongol advance into Europe halted because the death of Ögedei Khan required Batu's return to Mongolia for the khuriltai.
Genghis Khan's invasion of the Khwarazmian Shah's empire began in 1219 after the Shah massacred a Mongol trade caravan and diplomatic mission.
During the invasion of Persia, the Mongols obliterated cities that resisted while sparing those that submitted.
The Khwarazmian Shah fled to a Caspian island where he died, and his son Jalal ad-Din was defeated at the Indus in 1221.
A Mongol detachment under Baidar and Kadan invaded Poland in late 1240 and sacked Kraków in March 1241.
The Mongols annihilated the combined Polish-German-Teutonic army at Legnica on April 9, 1241.
The Mongol detachment in Poland halted its advance when news arrived of Great Khan Ögedei's death.
Batu Khan's western army invaded the Rus principalities in winter 1237, using frozen rivers as highways for their cavalry.
During the Mongol invasion of Rus, Ryazan fell first and was utterly destroyed, and Vladimir-Suzdal was burned in February 1238.
The Battle of the Sit River in 1238 destroyed the Vladimir army and Grand Prince Yury II was killed.
In 1206, a great kurultai of Mongol tribes on the Onon River proclaimed Temüjin the Genghis Khan, Universal Ruler.
Temüjin spent roughly 20 years unifying the Mongolian steppe tribes.
Genghis Khan created a social order based on merit and a military organized on decimal principles.
Batu Khan's campaigns destroyed Vladimir and Ryazan in 1237-1238 and Kiev in 1240.
Surviving Russian princes submitted to Batu at Sarai, receiving yarlyk patents confirming their rule in exchange for tribute and military service.
Alexander Nevsky of Novgorod chose submission to the Mongols over resistance.
Ivan I of Moscow (Kalita), from 1325, received from the Golden Horde the right to collect tribute from other Russian princes.
Ivan I persuaded Metropolitan Peter to move the Orthodox Church's seat to Moscow in 1326.
Ivan I's policy of submission toward the Golden Horde provided peace that allowed Moscow's growth.
In 661, after the assassination of Ali ibn Abi Talib, Muawiyah I of the Umayyad family became caliph, founding the first hereditary Islamic dynasty.
Muawiyah I moved the capital of the caliphate from Medina to Damascus.
Following the murder of King Sancho IV in 1076, Navarre was temporarily partitioned between Aragon and Castile.
The 1076 partition weakened Navarrese power and began a long period of vulnerability between stronger neighbours.
The extinction of Navarre's native dynasty in 1234 brought the House of Champagne to the throne of Navarre.
The accession of the House of Champagne in 1234 began a long association between Navarre and French dynasties.
The Kingdom of Pamplona (later Navarre) emerged as an independent Basque kingdom around 824 CE.
The Battle of Roncevaux Pass in 778 had demonstrated Basque military capability prior to the emergence of the Kingdom of Pamplona.
Emperor Nicephorus II Phocas led Byzantine campaigns that reconquered Cilicia, Cyprus, and Antioch from the Hamdanid emirate between 963 and 969.
The campaigns of Nicephorus II Phocas represented the greatest Byzantine territorial expansion since Justinian.
Nicephorus II Phocas was assassinated in 969 by his nephew John Tzimiskes.
The Nika Revolt erupted in Constantinople's Hippodrome in 532 when chariot-racing factional violence expanded into political revolt against Justinian I.
During the Nika Revolt, Constantinople burned for five days and Justinian prepared to flee until Empress Theodora urged resistance.
General Belisarius trapped and massacred approximately 30,000 rebels in the Hippodrome to end the Nika Revolt.
In 1066, William of Normandy's victory at the Battle of Hastings killed King Harold II and much of the Anglo-Saxon warrior aristocracy.
William of Normandy was crowned at Westminster on Christmas Day 1066 and distributed English lands to Norman barons.
After the Norman Conquest, French became the language of the English court for three centuries.
Roger I of Hauteville captured Palermo in January 1072 and became Count of Sicily.
Sicily had been under Arab Muslim rule since 827, with a mixed population of Muslims, Greek Christians, and Latin Christians.
The Normans created a multicultural kingdom in Sicily functioning in Arabic, Greek, and Latin.
Norman adventurers carved out a territorial base in southern Italy from the 1030s, initially serving as mercenaries.
Roger de Hauteville and Robert Guiscard expelled the Byzantines from Calabria and Apulia by 1071 and conquered Muslim Sicily from 1061 to 1091.
Roger II unified Sicily and southern Italy into the Kingdom of Sicily in 1130.
In 911, King Charles the Simple granted the Viking leader Rollo territory around Rouen in exchange for baptism and defense of the Seine.
The 911 grant to Rollo created the County (later Duchy) of Normandy.
The Norse settlers of Normandy assimilated into French culture within generations while retaining martial prowess.
In 1163, Bishop Maurice de Sully laid the foundation stone of Notre-Dame on the Île de la Cité.
Construction of Notre-Dame continued nearly two centuries, with the great rose windows completed under Louis IX in the 1250s.
In 1136, the citizens of Novgorod expelled Prince Vsevolod Mstislavich and established a republic governed by the veche.
Novgorod hired princes as military commanders without allowing them to own land or govern, with authority resting with elected officials accountable to the veche.
The Novgorod Republic survived until Ivan III's annexation in 1478.
Franciscan friar Odoric of Pordenone returned around 1330 from a sixteen-year journey via Persia, India, Sumatra, Java, southern China, and Khanbaliq.
Odoric of Pordenone dictated his account of his travels at Padua in 1330 and died the following year.
Joan of Arc arrived at the besieged city of Orléans on April 29, 1429 with a relief army.
Joan of Arc led the assault on the fortress of Les Tourelles and broke the English siege of Orléans on May 8, 1429.
The relief of Orléans reversed the momentum of the Hundred Years' War, and Charles VII was crowned at Reims in July 1429.
In 1369, Murad I captured Adrianople (Edirne) and made it the Ottoman capital.
By establishing its capital at Edirne, the Ottoman Empire centered itself in Europe rather than Anatolia.
Following the Ottoman capture of Adrianople, Constantinople was surrounded on three sides by Ottoman territory.
At the Battle of Nicopolis in 1396, Sultan Bayezid I destroyed a crusading army of Hungarian, French, English, and Burgundian knights.
The Ottoman victory at Nicopolis in 1396 ended serious Western European hopes of reversing Ottoman gains in the Balkans.
On June 20, 1459, Sultan Mehmed II captured Smederevo, the last stronghold of the Serbian Despotate.
The fall of Smederevo in 1459 ended the final organized Serbian resistance to Ottoman rule.
Following the 1459 conquest, Serbia remained under Ottoman rule until 1830.
In 1517, Sultan Selim I defeated the Mamluk Sultan Tumanbay at the Battle of Ridaniyya.
The Ottoman victory in 1517 brought Egypt, Syria, and the Hejaz, including Mecca and Medina, under Ottoman control.
The last Abbasid caliph of Cairo transferred the caliphate to Selim I.
Sultan Murad I transformed the Ottoman beylik into a functioning empire through systematic administrative reforms.
Murad I established the kadi system of Islamic law courts and the provincial sancak administrative units.
Murad I systematized the devshirme levy and built the Janissary corps into a professional standing army.
In March 1354, an earthquake destroyed the walls of Gallipoli, and Ottoman prince Suleyman immediately occupied the fortress.
The occupation of Gallipoli in 1354 gave the Ottomans their first permanent foothold in Europe.
The Ottomans used Gallipoli as a staging point to begin the conquest of Thrace.
Sultan Murad I systematized the devshirme system and created the Janissary corps of elite infantry.
The Janissaries were recruited as children from Christian Balkan families, converted to Islam, and raised in loyalty to the sultan.
The Janissaries' discipline and firearms made them decisive in Ottoman expansion.
Following the conquest of Constantinople in 1453, Mehmed II undertook comprehensive reorganization of the Ottoman state.
Mehmed II established the office of Grand Vizier to coordinate government.
Mehmed II codified Ottoman administrative and criminal law in the Kanunname.
Following the 1453 conquest of Constantinople, Mehmed II formalized the Ottoman millet system, allowing non-Muslim communities to govern themselves under their own religious laws.
Under the millet system, non-Muslim communities paid a special tax in exchange for self-governance.
Mehmed II recognized the Patriarch of Constantinople as the head of the Rum Millet.
On July 28, 1480, an Ottoman fleet under Gedik Ahmed Pasha landed at Otranto in southern Italy and captured the city after a two-week siege.
At Otranto, the garrison and inhabitants were killed or enslaved, and 800 who refused to convert were executed as the 'Martyrs of Otranto'.
The Ottomans were dislodged from Otranto in September 1481, after Mehmed II's death.
In 1456, Sultan Mehmed II besieged Belgrade with a large army and powerful artillery.
John Hunyadi organized the defense of Belgrade with Hungarian soldiers and crusader volunteers raised by John of Capistrano.
In July 1456 a crusader counterattack caused panic in the Ottoman camp, Mehmed II was wounded, and he withdrew from Belgrade.
In 1422, Sultan Murad II besieged Constantinople, the first major Ottoman attempt on the city since 1402.
The 1422 Ottoman siege of Constantinople failed when the Theodosian Walls held and a revolt in Anatolia forced Murad II to withdraw.
In 962, Pope John XII crowned Otto I in St Peter's, reviving the Western imperial title.
The Privilegium Ottonianum redefined the emperor's role as protector of the papacy and confirmed imperial authority over papal elections.
In 962, Pope John XII crowned Otto I of Germany as Holy Roman Emperor in Rome, creating the institutional basis of the Holy Roman Empire.
Otto I defeated the Magyars at the Battle of Lechfeld in 955.
Otto I's coronation inaugurated the Ottonian Renaissance in German learning and church-building.
On February 2, 962, Pope John XII crowned Otto I, King of East Francia, as Holy Roman Emperor in St. Peter's Basilica.
Otto I's coronation in 962 restored the western imperial title, vacant since 924.
In 955, Otto I defeated the Magyars at the Battle of Lechfeld.
Pope John XII, threatened by Berengar II of Italy, appealed to Otto I of Germany for military assistance.
Otto I crossed the Alps and defeated Berengar II of Italy.
On February 2, 962, Otto I was crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope John XII.
Otto I deposed Pope John XII and installed his own pope.
In June 1258, a coalition of English barons led by Simon de Montfort imposed the Provisions of Oxford on Henry III.
The Provisions of Oxford created a permanent Council of Fifteen to govern with the king and required Parliament to meet three times per year.
Henry III later repudiated the Provisions of Oxford, leading to Simon de Montfort's rebellion of 1263-1265.
Oxford University grew rapidly after Henry II's 1167 expulsion of English scholars from Paris.
By the early 13th century, Oxford University had a recognizable institutional structure with master regents and academic halls.
In 1215, Pope Innocent III's legate Robert de Courçon issued a charter for the University of Paris.
The University of Paris had four faculties and governed itself by choosing its own chancellor and setting its own curriculum.
Thomas Aquinas and Albertus Magnus taught at the University of Paris.
At the height of Mongol dominance around 1250, a merchant carrying a paiza could travel from China to Hungary in relative safety.
The Mongol postal relay system, commercial protection, and standardized weights enabled unprecedented long-distance trade.
Friar John of Plano Carpini, William of Rubruck, and Marco Polo made transcontinental journeys during the Pax Mongolica.
On April 26, 1478, the Pazzi family, backed by Pope Sixtus IV, attempted to assassinate the Medici brothers during Mass in Florence Cathedral.
In the Pazzi conspiracy, Giuliano de' Medici was killed while Lorenzo de' Medici escaped wounded.
Florence rallied to the Medici after the Pazzi conspiracy, and the conspirators were hunted down and executed.
The Peace of Constance, signed June 25, 1183, ended the conflict between Frederick Barbarossa and the Lombard League.
The conflict between Barbarossa and the Lombard League had reached its decisive moment at the Battle of Legnano in 1176.
The Peace of Constance granted the Lombard communes self-governing rights in exchange for nominal imperial sovereignty.
The Treaty of Paris of 1229, negotiated between the French crown and Count Raymond VII of Toulouse, ended the Albigensian Crusade.
Under the 1229 Treaty of Paris, Raymond VII surrendered much of his territory to France and agreed to hunt heretics.
Following the 1229 Treaty of Paris, the Languedoc was effectively annexed to the French crown.
Beginning with the Council of Charroux in 989, a series of synods promulgated sacral protections for non-combatants, clergy, and peasants under threat of excommunication.
The Peace of God movement spread across France and into Catalonia and northern Italy over the following half-century.
A synod was convened at Charroux Abbey around 989, traditionally regarded as the inaugural council of the Peace of God movement.
The canons of the Council of Charroux placed unarmed clerics, the poor, and church property under episcopal protection.
In 1454, Milan, Venice, Florence, and Naples agreed at Lodi to a 25-year non-aggression pact, ending the Lombard Wars.
The Peace of Lodi recognized Francesco Sforza as Duke of Milan.
The Peace of Lodi established a quintuple Italian League.
The Treaty of Paris of April 12, 1229 ended the Albigensian Crusade.
Under the 1229 Treaty of Paris, Count Raymond VII of Toulouse surrendered much territory, agreed to persecute heretics, and paid large indemnities.
The 1229 Treaty of Paris integrated the Languedoc into the French royal domain, and the last Cathar stronghold Montségur fell in 1244.
The Second Peace of Thorn, signed October 19, 1466, ended the Thirteen Years' War between Poland and the Teutonic Order.
Under the Second Peace of Thorn, the Teutonic Order ceded Royal Prussia, including Danzig and Toruń, to Poland.
Under the Second Peace of Thorn, the Teutonic Order became a Polish vassal for its remaining territory.
In 1381, the imposition of a poll tax to fund the Hundred Years' War provoked the first mass popular uprising in English history.
The Peasants' Revolt was led by Wat Tyler and encouraged by the priest John Ball, with rebels storming the Tower of London and killing the Archbishop of Canterbury.
Richard II met the rebels at Smithfield, where Wat Tyler was killed, then revoked his promises of reform.
In campaigns of 754 and 756, Pepin III crossed the Alps to defend Pope Stephen II against the Lombards.
Pepin III donated the conquered Exarchate of Ravenna and surrounding territories to the papacy, creating the Papal States.
The Donation of Pepin formed the political basis for papal temporal power until 1870.
Pepin III obtained Pope Zachary's judgment that the holder of power rather than the holder of the title should be king.
In 751, the Merovingian king Childeric III was deposed and Pepin III was anointed king of the Franks.
Pope Stephen II anointed Pepin III as king of the Franks in 754, the first papal coronation of a Frankish king.
Portuguese agent Pero da Covilhã, sent overland by João II in 1487, reached Cairo, Aden, Calicut, and the East African Swahili coast.
Pero da Covilhã reported back to João II via a go-between at Cairo.
Pero da Covilhã continued to Ethiopia, where he was held for the rest of his life at the Solomonic court.
The Peruzzi compagnia of Florence defaulted in 1343 after Edward III of England repudiated his debt.
Edward III of England had borrowed approximately 600,000 florins to finance the early Hundred Years' War.
The Bardi compagnia of Florence followed into bankruptcy in 1345.
Francesco Petrarch was crowned with the laurel wreath on the Capitoline Hill in Rome in 1341.
Petrarch's laurel coronation in 1341 was the first such ceremony since antiquity.
Petrarch's Canzoniere was a collection of vernacular Italian sonnets addressed to Laura.
Petrarch's recovery of classical texts from monastic libraries began the systematic recovery of ancient learning that modeled Renaissance humanism.
Petrarch's Italian sonnets, the Canzoniere, established the Petrarchan sonnet form.
Petrarch's Latin correspondence recreated classical epistolary style.
Petrarch classified medieval history as a 'dark ages' between Rome and the Renaissance, creating a periodization that shaped subsequent European historiography.
Philip II Augustus of France conquered Normandy from King John of England in 1204.
Château Gaillard, built by Richard I to protect Normandy's border, fell to a six-month siege in March 1204.
Philip Augustus took Rouen in June 1204.
Within a year of 1204 Normandy, Anjou, Maine, and Touraine became French, leaving King John only Gascony of his continental possessions.
Patriarch Photius of Constantinople convened a council in 867 that excommunicated Pope Nicholas I.
Photius's council accused the Roman church of doctrinal innovations including the Filioque clause.
The schism with Rome was temporarily healed in 879.
An outbreak of bubonic plague struck the Syrian garrison town of Amwas in 638-639 during the Arab consolidation of the Levant.
Several thousand of the Muslim army perished in the plague of Amwas, including commanders Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah and Shurahbil ibn Hasana.
The plague of Amwas generated foundational hadith-jurisprudential material on contagion and divine decree.
The first pandemic of bubonic plague struck the Byzantine Empire beginning in Egypt in 541.
At its height in Constantinople in 542, contemporary sources describe 5,000 to 10,000 deaths per day.
The population of the Eastern Roman Empire may have fallen by 25 to 50 percent during the plague.
The plague pandemics continued until 750, weakening the Byzantine and Sasanian Empires.
A second major plague epidemic struck Europe in 1360-1363, killing primarily children and young adults born after the first plague.
Subsequent plague waves occurred in 1369, 1374-1375, and 1379-1383, demonstrating that plague was endemic rather than a one-time event.
Total European population did not recover to pre-1348 levels until 1500-1550.
Franciscan friar Giovanni da Pian del Carpine was sent by Pope Innocent IV after the Council of Lyon of 1245.
Giovanni da Pian del Carpine attended the enthronement of Güyük Khan at Karakorum in August 1246.
Giovanni da Pian del Carpine returned via Russia and Kiev in 1247, delivering Güyük's response to the papal embassy.
At Poitiers on 19 September 1356, Edward the Black Prince with about 8,000 English and Gascon troops defeated a French army of about 35,000 under King John II of France.
The English at Poitiers used dismounted knights and longbowmen in prepared positions to repel multiple French charges then counterattack.
King John II of France was captured at Poitiers along with much of the French nobility.
John II's ransom was set at 3 million gold écus and was never fully paid.
At the Battle of Aljubarrota on 14 August 1385, John I of Portugal defeated a substantially larger Castilian army under Juan I of Castile.
The Portuguese at Aljubarrota held a prepared ridge with ditches and were aided by English longbowmen from the Lancaster alliance.
John I of Portugal had married Philippa of Lancaster.
The victory at Aljubarrota ended the Castilian claim to Portugal and secured the Aviz dynasty.
King João I of Portugal captured Ceuta in Morocco on 21 August 1415.
The capture of Ceuta was the first European overseas conquest since the Crusades.
Prince Henry the Navigator participated in the capture of Ceuta and subsequently sponsored Atlantic exploration from 1418 to 1460.
Portuguese exploration reached Madeira in 1419, the Azores in 1427, and Cape Bojador in 1434.
Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate in 1510.
Goa became the capital of the Estado da India, Portugal's maritime commercial empire spanning from West Africa to Japan.
Portuguese control of Indian Ocean ports disrupted the traditional Ottoman-Venetian-Egyptian spice trade.
Afonso Henriques defeated a Moorish force at Ourique in 1139 and was proclaimed King of Portugal by his troops.
In proclaiming himself king, Afonso Henriques rejected the suzerainty of his cousin Alfonso VII of León and Castile.
Pope Alexander III recognized Portugal as an independent kingdom in 1179.
Afonso Henriques captured Lisbon in 1147 with the assistance of Anglo-Norman and Flemish crusaders.
Rudolf of Habsburg defeated and killed Ottokar II of Bohemia at the Battle of Marchfeld in 1278.
Ottokar II had built a central European empire stretching from Silesia to the Adriatic.
After Marchfeld, Rudolf granted Austria, Styria, and Carinthia to his sons, establishing the Habsburg territorial base.
Prince Henry of Portugal patronised systematic Atlantic exploration from his base at Sagres beginning around 1418.
Portuguese exploration reached Madeira in 1419 and the Azores in 1427.
Portuguese explorers rounded Cape Bojador on the African coast in 1434.
Guillaume de Champlitte and Geoffrey de Villehardouin founded the Principality of Achaea in the Peloponnese in 1205 following the Fourth Crusade.
The Principality of Achaea became one of the most stable and culturally vibrant Latin states in Greece, associated with the Chronicle of Morea.
Achaea was defeated at the Battle of Pelagonia in 1259.
After Pelagonia, Prince William of Villehardouin surrendered Peloponnesian fortresses including Mystras to the Empire of Nicaea.
Mystras became a Byzantine cultural centre that eclipsed the Latin principality.
Alexander Nevsky won a victory on the ice of Lake Peipus in 1242.
The Battle on the Ice in 1242 stopped the Teutonic Order's advance into Pskov and Novgorod.
The Treaty of Bolotovo in 1348 recognised Pskov as an independent republic, separating it from Novgorodian overlordship.
Pskov was governed by a veche (popular assembly) and merchant oligarchy.
Tver rebuilt relatively quickly after the Mongol invasion of 1237-1242 due to its location north of the main Mongol routes.
Tver became a major rival to Moscow for leadership of the Russian principalities in the 14th century.
A popular uprising in Tver against Mongol tax collectors occurred in 1327.
Ivan I of Moscow guided a Mongol punitive expedition that brutally suppressed the Tver uprising of 1327.
The suppression of the 1327 uprising ended Tver's chances of leading the Russian recovery and allowed Moscow to emerge as the primary Russian principality.
The Principality of Wallachia traditionally traces its foundation to Radu Negru around 1290.
Wallachia occupied the plain between the Carpathians and the Danube and developed as a Romanian-speaking Orthodox Christian state.
Wallachia was nominally a Hungarian vassal but increasingly independent.
Vlad III the Impaler of Wallachia defied Ottoman overlordship during his second reign from 1456 to 1462.
Vlad III launched raids into Bulgaria and impaled Ottoman envoys.
Zeta received papal recognition as a kingdom in 1077 under Mihailo Vojislavljević.
Zeta was located on the Adriatic coast and navigated between Byzantine, Norman, and Serbian spheres of influence.
Zeta accepted Venetian protection of its coastal territories in 1421 as Ottoman pressure on the Balkans increased.
The Venetian alliance allowed Zeta's coastal towns to survive Ottoman raids while the interior fell under Ottoman influence.
By the 1490s printing presses in Mainz, Venice, Cologne, Paris, and London were producing thousands of political pamphlets, satires, and theological tracts.
Sebastian Brant's Ship of Fools, published in 1494, sold tens of thousands of copies.
Erasmus's In Praise of Folly, published in 1511, was reprinted 36 times in his lifetime.
Johannes Gutenberg perfected moveable-type printing in Mainz around 1450.
The Gutenberg Bible, produced around 1455, was the first book printed in the West with moveable type.
Printing technology spread to Italy by 1465, France by 1470, England by 1476, and across Europe by 1500.
Within 50 years of 1450 over 20 million printed volumes were produced.
Prochoros Kydones translated Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae into Greek around 1355.
Kydones's translation introduced Western Scholastic theology to Byzantine readers for the first time.
The translation sparked controversy between Palamists and Latinophiles in Byzantium.
English barons under Simon de Montfort forced Henry III to accept the Provisions of Oxford in 1258.
The Provisions of Oxford established a permanent council of 15 barons governing with the king's consent and required Parliament to meet three times a year.
The Second Barons' War followed from 1264 to 1267.
Simon de Montfort's parliament of 1265 was the first English parliament to include knights and burgesses.
In 1287 Ilkhan Arghun dispatched a Nestorian Christian monk westward to negotiate a Mongol-Christian alliance against the Mamluks.
The Ilkhanate's envoy travelled to Constantinople, Rome, Genoa, Paris, and Bordeaux during the 1287-1288 embassy to Europe.
In 1288 the Ilkhanate's envoy met King Philip IV in Paris and King Edward I of England at Bordeaux.
Justinian's Gothic War (535-554) destroyed the Ostrogothic kingdom after about twenty years of fighting in Italy.
The general Belisarius captured Rome and Ravenna in the early campaigns of the Gothic War.
The general Narses destroyed the Ostrogothic forces at the Battle of Busta Gallorum in 552.
Ferdinand III of Castile captured Cordoba on 29 June 1236.
Cordoba had been under Muslim rule since 711 before its capture by Castile in 1236.
After the 1236 conquest the Great Mosque of Cordoba was reconsecrated as a Cathedral.
The capture of Cordoba was made possible by the Almohad collapse following the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.
Ferdinand III of Castile captured Seville in 1248 after a sixteen-month siege.
After the fall of Seville in 1248 the emirate of Granada remained the only independent Muslim state in Iberia.
Castilian administration was established in Seville following its conquest in 1248.
Alfonso VI of Castile captured Toledo in 1085.
Toledo had been the old Visigothic capital and a major Islamic city before its capture in 1085.
After 1085 Toledo became a center of the 12th-century translation movement rendering Arabic texts into Latin.

The Fatimid Caliphate claimed the title of rightful caliphs against the Abbasids; the Sunni-Shia divide expressed as a geopolitical rivalry between Cairo and Baghdad, with both powers sponsoring missionaries and proxy rulers across the Islamic world.
Seljuks capture Baghdad (1055) and become protectors of the Abbasid Caliph; the caliph retains religious legitimacy while Seljuk sultans hold all real power.

The Principality of Achaea (the Crusader state in the Peloponnese, established after the Fourth Crusade) was gradually encircled and reduced by the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea. The Treaty of Viterbo (1267) had theoretically restored Byzantine suzerainty over Achaea in exchange for the release of the captured Prince William II of Villehardouin; William later repudiated the terms. Byzantine Emperor Michael VIII established the Despotate of the Morea (1261) as a base for reconquering the Peloponnese; his successors steadily reduced the Latin principality over a century of patient pressure until Achaea was fully absorbed by the Despotate in 1432.

After Kaleb's 525 CE invasion of Himyarite Yemen — undertaken to protect Christian co-religionists — Aksum and Byzantium maintained a Christian commercial alliance against Sasanian Persia. Aksumite ambassadors at Constantinople are attested through the 7th century.

The Kingdom of Alba (the Gaelic-Pictish kingdom that emerged after Kenneth MacAlpin united the Picts and Scots c. 843) gradually became the Kingdom of Scotland through territorial expansion and anglicization under David I (1124–1153). David I introduced Norman feudal institutions, Anglo-Norman settlers, and Benedictine monasteries; his court spoke Latin and French alongside Gaelic. The name 'Scotland' (from 'Scoti,' the Latin for the Irish/Gaelic people) replaced 'Alba' in international usage by the 11th–12th century, reflecting both the Gaelic origin and the subsequent cultural transformation.

The Almohad Caliphate collapsed in al-Andalus following the decisive defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) by a coalition of Castile, Aragon, Navarre, and Portugal. The Almohad governors withdrew or lost authority, creating a third period of Taifa fragmentation (c. 1228–1238). The new Taifa kingdoms were smaller, weaker, and more vulnerable than the first two Taifa periods. Most fell to Castile (Murcia 1243, Seville 1248, Cádiz 1262) within a generation. Only Granada, reorganized under Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Nasr (founder of the Nasrid dynasty, 1232), survived by accepting Castilian vassalage.

The Almohad Caliphate (al-Muwahhidun, 'those who affirm divine unity') arose in the Atlas Mountains of Morocco as a Berber religious reform movement under Ibn Tumart (d. 1130) and his successor Abd al-Mu'min. The Almohads overthrew the Almoravid Empire by capturing Marrakesh (1147), then crossed to al-Andalus and absorbed the Almoravid territories in Iberia (1148–1172). The Almohad regime was more rigidly orthodox than the Almoravids, forcibly converting or expelling Jewish and Christian communities in North Africa and Iberia. The defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) began the Almohad collapse.

Amalfi's commercial golden age (9th–11th centuries) was built on its position as the primary Western intermediary in Byzantine-Islamic trade. The city held Byzantine administrative recognition as a semi-autonomous duchy (the Duke of Amalfi answering nominally to the Byzantine governor of Southern Italy), which gave Amalfi merchants privileged access to Constantinople and Byzantine ports throughout the Mediterranean. Amalfitan merchants established the Hospital of St. John in Jerusalem (c. 1048–1050) — the forerunner of the Knights Hospitaller. The city's dual orientation toward Byzantium and Islam made it uniquely positioned as a commercial and cultural bridge.

Amalfi — one of the four Italian maritime republics (with Venice, Genoa, and Pisa) — was absorbed into the Norman Kingdom of Sicily after Robert Guiscard's conquest of southern Italy. Amalfi had been a nominally Byzantine city-state that built its commercial empire on trade between the Islamic world, Byzantium, and Western Europe; its merchants established trading posts throughout the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. Norman conquest (1073, formalized 1131) ended Amalfi's independent commercial role; Pisa's subsequent sack (1135) destroyed the city as a commercial power. Amalfi's practical contribution — the maritime code Tabula Amalfitana, the compass — outlasted the city-state.
