The County of Anjou — the Plantagenet dynasty's ancestral domain — was held by the Plantagenet kings of England as part of the Angevin Empire until its conquest by Philip II Augustus of France (1204). Geoffrey V of Anjou's marriage to Empress Matilda of England (daughter of Henry I) created the Plantagenet dynasty when their son became Henry II. Anjou provided the dynasty's military culture and administrative traditions; the term 'Angevin' (from Anjou) describes both the French comital and the English royal family. The loss of Anjou in 1204 severed the dynastic-territorial connection that defined the Plantagenet identity.

The County of Anjou — the ancestral domain of the Plantagenet/Angevin dynasty — was conquered by Philip II Augustus of France in 1204 simultaneously with Normandy. John of England's military failures (inability to relieve Château Gaillard, failure at Bouvines in 1214 against a Poitevin rebellion backed by Philip) confirmed French control. Anjou's absorption with its associated counties (Maine, Touraine) gave France the Loire Valley heartland. A restored Angevin dynasty (the House of Valois-Anjou) received Anjou as an appanage in 1360, but it reverted to the crown on René I's death (1480).

The Treaty of Devol (1108) nominally made Bohemund I of Antioch a Byzantine vassal, requiring him to rule Antioch as a fief of the empire. The treaty was imposed after Alexios I Komnenos's successful military pressure on Bohemund's invasion of the Balkans. Emperor John II Komnenos enforced Byzantine suzerainty in 1138–1143 by marching an army to Antioch and receiving homage from Prince Raymond of Poitiers — though he did not attempt to take direct control. Subsequent Byzantine emperors periodically extracted nominal homage from Antiochene princes, but the practical relationship varied with military circumstances.

The Principality of Antioch maintained a fraught relationship with the Byzantine Empire throughout the Crusader period. Antioch had been part of the Byzantine Empire until 1085; Alexios I expected it returned when the First Crusade captured it (1098). Bohemund I refused, arguing he held it by conquest. The Treaty of Devol (1108) theoretically made Antioch a Byzantine vassal, but Bohemund's nephew Tancred refused to honor it. Byzantine emperors (especially John II Komnenos, 1138–1143, and Manuel I) periodically forced Antiochene princes to perform homage, with varying degrees of compliance.

The Principality of Antioch and the Kingdom of Jerusalem were allied but frequently competing Crusader states. The competition centered on precedence (Antioch's prince claimed independence from Jerusalem's king; the king of Jerusalem claimed feudal suzerainty as the senior Crusader monarch) and territorial disputes — particularly over the contested borderlands and the city of Tripoli (technically independent but often aligned with Jerusalem against Antioch). These disputes weakened the capacity for unified defense: the failure of Antioch to relieve Edessa (1144) was partly due to unresolved disputes with the King of Jerusalem about military precedence.
Aquitaine held by English crown after Eleanor's marriage to Henry II until end of Hundred Years' War.

Aquitaine — one of the great fiefs of medieval France, held by the English crown as a remnant of the Angevin Empire — was gradually absorbed into France through the Hundred Years' War. English Gascony (the southern portion of Aquitaine) was the prize that sustained English involvement in France; it provided Bordeaux's wine trade revenues, which funded English military operations. The Battle of Castillon (1453) ended the last English attempt to hold Gascony; Bordeaux surrendered in October 1453. The absorption ended 300 years of English continental presence and transferred France's richest wine-producing region to direct royal control.

The Crown of Aragon was created by the marriage of Petronilla of Aragon to Ramon Berenguer IV, Count of Barcelona (1137), uniting the kingdom of Aragon with the Catalan counties under a single ruler. While technically united, the two components retained separate laws, institutions, and fiscal systems. The Crown's subsequent expansion — Valencia (1238), Sicily (1282), Sardinia (1324), Naples (1443) — was driven primarily by Catalan commercial interests and Mediterranean trade networks rather than Aragonese landlocked interests. The Crown of Aragon became the dominant maritime power in the western Mediterranean.

The marriage of Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile (October 19, 1469) created the personal union that became the basis of the Spanish monarchy. The union preserved the separate institutions of each kingdom — separate Cortes, separate laws, separate currencies — while presenting a united front in foreign policy and the Reconquista. The complementarity was crucial: Castile provided the military manpower and Meseta resources; Aragon the Mediterranean naval experience and Italian connections. Together they conquered Granada (1492), commissioned Columbus's voyages, and established the Spanish overseas empire.

The Kingdom of Majorca was created by James I of Aragon, who divided his realm among his sons at death (1276), with the youngest son James receiving Majorca, Roussillon, and Montpellier. The separate kingdom was a controversial division that created a junior Aragonese kingdom caught between Aragon and France. Peter IV of Aragon invaded and defeated James III of Majorca at the Battle of Llucmajor (1349), killing him and absorbing the kingdom back into the Crown of Aragon. Roussillon remained a Catalan-speaking territory contested between France and Spain.

James I of Aragon ('the Conqueror') divided his realm among his sons in his will (1262, taking effect 1276): his eldest son Peter inherited Aragon, Valencia, and Catalonia; his younger son James received Majorca, Roussillon, and Montpellier, creating the Kingdom of Majorca. The division reflected James's desire to provide for all his sons rather than maintaining unity. The Kingdom of Majorca proved diplomatically unstable — caught between France and Aragon — and was eventually reabsorbed by Peter IV of Aragon after the Battle of Llucmajor (1349). Roussillon remained contested between France and Aragon.

Aragon and Navarre were ruled by the same dynasty for much of the 11th–12th centuries. Alfonso I 'the Battler' of Aragon and Navarre (1104–1134) attempted to unite them permanently; his death without heirs split them: Aragon went to Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona through marriage; Navarre elected García Ramírez as independent king. Subsequent Navarrese dynasties had French affiliations (Champagne, Évreux). The two kingdoms periodically reunited through dynastic accidents — Ferdinand of Aragon became King of Navarre (1512) by conquest — but were never permanently merged.

The Crown of Aragon received Sardinia from Pope Boniface VIII (1297) as a papal fief — in exchange for Aragonese relinquishment of Sicily, which the papacy hoped to recover for the Angevins. Aragon's actual conquest of Sardinia required wars against the indigenous Giudicato of Arborea (1323–1420) and the Genoese colonists. The island was fully pacified only after the defeat of Eleonora d'Arborea's successors in 1420. Sardinia became the Crown of Aragon's poorest but strategically important possession, providing a central Mediterranean base and grain supplies. It remained Spanish then Savoyard until Italian unification.

Peter III of Aragon's acquisition of Sicily through the Sicilian Vespers (1282) transformed the Crown of Aragon from a primarily Iberian power into a Mediterranean empire. Peter claimed Sicily through his wife Constance, daughter of King Manfred of Sicily (Hohenstaufen). His landing in Sicily days after the Vespers massacre of the French gave the revolt legitimate royal leadership. The subsequent Wars of the Sicilian Vespers (1282–1302) forced France to recognize Aragonese Sicily in the Peace of Caltabellotta (1302). Sicily became the first Aragonese possession outside Iberia, establishing the template for the Crown's later Mediterranean expansion.

The Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia (established 1080 by Armenian refugees fleeing Seljuk conquest of Armenia proper) maintained complex relations with Byzantium, oscillating between cooperation (the Armenians provided crucial infantry for crusading armies) and conflict (Byzantine emperors periodically attempted to reassert suzerainty over Cilicia). The Armenian-Byzantine relationship was complicated by theological differences (Armenian Apostolic vs. Greek Orthodox Christianity). Armenian Cilicia aligned with the Crusader states and with the Mongol Ilkhanate against the Mamluks, ultimately being abandoned by both and destroyed by the Mamluks (1375).

The Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia was among the most consistent allies of the Crusader states throughout the 12th–13th centuries. The Armenians provided local geographic knowledge, logistics support, and infantry for Crusader campaigns (notably the First and Third Crusades); Armenian ports (Ayas/Lajazzo) served as the primary entry point for Crusader supplies and reinforcements. Dynastic marriages linked the Armenian Rubenid and Hethumid dynasties to Crusader noble houses. The Armenians' conversion to communion with the Roman Catholic Church (1198) — a controversial decision internally — was driven partly by the desire to maintain Crusader alliance.

The Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia faced sustained Mamluk pressure throughout the 14th century, with major campaigns in 1266 (capturing Sis temporarily), 1275, 1322, and 1337. Armenian Cilicia's alliance with the Mongol Ilkhanate (against the Mamluks) collapsed when the Ilkhanate dissolved (1335). The Crusading powers the Armenians appealed to — the Hospitallers, Cyprus, the papacy — provided inadequate support. The Mamluk Sultan Barquq launched the final campaign (1374–1375) that destroyed the kingdom; King Leo VI escaped to Europe but found no support for a recovery and died in exile (1393).

The Kingdom of Asturias, founded by Pelayo after the Visigothic collapse (718), gradually shifted its political center southward as the Reconquista reclaimed territory from the Umayyads. When Alfonso III reconquered the Leonese plateau (late 9th century), his son Garcia I moved the royal capital from Oviedo to León (910), renaming the kingdom. The shift from Asturias to León reflects both the military southward advance and the symbolic claim to succeed the Visigothic kingdom based at Toledo. León subsequently united with Castile (1230) under Fernando III, completing the largest Reconquista realignment.

The Catalan Company — a mercenary force originally from Aragon and Catalonia — seized the Duchy of Athens (1311) after defeating the French knights at the Battle of the Kephissos. After placing themselves under the nominal sovereignty of the King of Sicily (of the Aragonese line), they created a unique Catalan cultural enclave in Attica and Boeotia. The Catalans maintained Catalan institutions (the General Council of Catalans) and Catalan language in Athens for 77 years (1311–1388). The Acciaiuoli Florentine family then displaced them; the Duchy passed to the Ottomans in 1456.

Saladin's unification of Egypt and Syria put the Kingdom of Jerusalem in an existential strategic bind; Hattin (1187) and the fall of Jerusalem define this rivalry. After Saladin's death, intermittent warfare and diplomacy including the Sixth Crusade's negotiated return of Jerusalem (1229–1244) continued under his successors.

The Mamluk slave-soldiers — the Ayyubid dynasty's own military elite — overthrow and kill Sultan Turanshah immediately after their victory over the Seventh Crusade at Mansura (1250); the Mamluks seize Egypt and gradually eliminate remaining Ayyubid princes from Syria by 1260.

Bavaria was one of the five original stem duchies of the East Frankish/German kingdom, its dukes consistently the most powerful regional rulers in southeastern Germany. Henry 'the Lion' of Bavaria (also Duke of Saxony) was the most powerful prince in Germany until Frederick Barbarossa stripped him of his duchies (1180) for failure to provide military support in Italy. The duchy was divided after Henry's fall: the eastern marches became the Duchy of Austria; the remaining Bavaria was given to the Wittelsbachs (1180), who retained it until 1918 — the longest dynastic continuity in German history.

The Ottoman Empire expanded by absorbing the other Anatolian Turkish beyliks (principalities) — either through conquest or dynastic marriage. Osman I established the beylik in northwestern Anatolia (c. 1300); his successors methodically absorbed neighboring beyliks: Karesi (1345), Germiyan (1390), Hamid (1381), Saruhan (1410). Timur's invasion (1402) temporarily restored some beyliks as Ottoman vassals fled, but Mehmed I reconquered them after the Ottoman civil war (1402–1413). By 1450, the Ottoman state controlled virtually all of Anatolia, with only Karaman holding out until 1468.

The Duchy of Brabant — encompassing modern Belgium and southern Netherlands — emerged as a major imperial duchy in the late 12th century, elevated from county to duchy (1183). Brabant controlled the strategic crossroads between the Rhine, Scheldt, and Meuse river systems, making it the commercial hub of the Low Countries. The duchy attracted textile workers, merchants, and bankers to cities like Brussels, Leuven, and Antwerp. Burgundian acquisition of Brabant (1430) integrated it into the Burgundian state that eventually passed to the Habsburgs, making Antwerp the center of the 16th-century northern European commercial revolution.

Brandenburg emerged as a frontier march (Nordmark) of the Holy Roman Empire in the 10th century, established to defend against Slavic peoples east of the Elbe. Albert the Bear (Albrecht der Bär) of the Ascanian dynasty formalized the Margraviate of Brandenburg in 1157 after acquiring the Hevelli lands. The Golden Bull of 1356 made the Margrave of Brandenburg one of the seven imperial electors, giving this frontier territory extraordinary constitutional significance. The Hohenzollern family inherited Brandenburg in 1415, using their electoral status as the foundation for building the Brandenburg-Prussian state that eventually created Germany.

The Valois Dukes of Burgundy (1363–1477) — a cadet line of the French royal family — built the most powerful principality in 15th-century Europe through a combination of French royal grants, diplomatic marriages, and inheritance: Philip the Bold (1363–1404), John the Fearless (1404–1419), Philip the Good (1419–1467), and Charles the Bold (1467–1477). At its peak, Burgundy controlled the Low Countries, Flanders, Artois, Picardy, and the original duchy — effectively creating an independent state between France and Germany. Charles the Bold's death at Nancy (1477) ended the Burgundian state; Louis XI seized the duchy itself.

The Kingdom of Burgundy (or Kingdom of Arles) was an independent kingdom that passed to the Holy Roman Empire through Conrad II's inheritance in 1033. The kingdom comprised Provence, the Rhône-Saône corridor, Savoy, and parts of modern Switzerland. Imperial suzerainty was nominal in practice — the local counts and bishops governed independently. The French crown gradually absorbed the western portions (Lyonnais, Dauphiné) in the 14th century. The 'Burgundian' political identity eventually crystallized around the Valois Duchy of Burgundy, which was distinct from but built on the heritage of the old kingdom.

The Avar Khaganate and Byzantium maintained a tributary relationship from the Avars' arrival on the Danube frontier (c. 558) until the failed joint Avar-Persian siege of Constantinople (626). Byzantium paid annual subsidies — gradually increasing — to keep the Avars from raiding the Balkans; the Avars used this money and the Slavic populations under their control to raid anyway. The siege of Thessalonica (586) and the siege of Constantinople (626) represented the peak of Avar-Slavic military pressure; the 626 failure broke the Avar coalition and began the Khaganate's decline, accelerated by the Frankish campaigns under Charlemagne (788–796) that destroyed it entirely.

The First Bulgarian Empire (founded 681 by Asparuh Khan) competed with Byzantium for dominance over the Balkans for 340 years. Major conflicts included: Avar-Bulgarian pressure on Constantinople (811–813), Khan Krum's destruction of the Byzantine army at Pliska (811, killing Emperor Nikephoros I in the only emperor killed in battle since 378), the conversion of Boris I (864), the Bulgarian-Byzantine war under Simeon I (who besieged Constantinople three times), and Basil II's systematic conquest culminating in Kleidion (1014). The rivalry defined the political character of the medieval Balkans.

The Second Bulgarian Empire (founded 1185 by the Asen brothers' revolt against Byzantine taxation) maintained a fierce rivalry with the restored Byzantine Empire, particularly after 1261. Bulgarian Tsar Kaloyan defeated and captured Latin Emperor Baldwin I at Adrianople (1205); Tsar Ivan Asen II achieved the Bulgarian Empire's maximum extent (1230), controlling most of the Balkans. The Second Bulgarian Empire collapsed into internal fragmentation after Ivan Asen II's death (1241), weakened by Mongol raids and internal dynastic disputes, leaving it unable to resist Ottoman absorption.

The Exarchate of Ravenna — the Byzantine administrative center in northern Italy established after Justinian's reconquest (540) — governed Byzantine Italy for over 200 years. Ravenna served as the western seat of imperial administration because its coastal position and surrounding marshes made it defensible against Lombard land power. The Exarchate's mosaics (San Vitale, Sant'Apollinare) represent the peak of Byzantine art in the West. The Lombard King Aistulf captured Ravenna (751), ending Byzantine administration in northern Italy; Pope Stephen II's subsequent appeal to Pippin III produced the Donation of Pippin and the Frankish-papal alliance.

Byzantine control of Italy was contested throughout the 6th–8th centuries: Justinian's reconquest (535–554) restored imperial rule, but the Gothic Wars' devastation left Italy economically prostrated. The Lombard invasion (568) fragmented imperial control to coastal enclaves (Ravenna, Rome, Naples, Sicily). The Exarchate of Ravenna — the Byzantine administrative center — was conquered by the Lombards (751), prompting the papacy to invite Frankish intervention. The Frankish-papal alliance effectively ended Byzantine political relevance in central and northern Italy, though Byzantine cultural influence persisted through the Norman period.

The Norman Kingdom of Sicily and the Byzantine Empire competed for control of the Adriatic and the Balkans throughout the 12th century. Roger II's fleet raided Byzantine ports (Corfu, Corinth, Athens) and captured Greek silk weavers in 1147–1148; William I's 'Bad' forces sacked Thessalonica (1185). Byzantine attempts to retake southern Italy failed; Manuel I Komnenos's alliance with Venice against Sicily (1171) and his Italian campaigns (1155–1158) achieved temporary gains quickly reversed. The Norman-Byzantine rivalry defined the geopolitics of the central Mediterranean until the Hohenstaufen inherited Sicily (1194).

The Byzantine-Ostrogothic conflict (535–554) — Justinian I's reconquest of Italy from the Ostrogothic Kingdom — was the most destructive war in Italian history. General Belisarius captured Sicily (535), Naples (536), and Rome (536) in a rapid advance, then General Narses completed the conquest after the Gothic King Totila's recovery and recapture of Rome (546, 550). The war lasted 20 years, killing or displacing perhaps a third of Italy's population, destroying the senatorial aristocracy, and collapsing urban life throughout the peninsula. The Lombard invasion followed 14 years after the war ended, exploiting Byzantine exhaustion.

Byzantine Sicily served as the empire's westernmost major province from Justinian's reconquest (535) until the Arab conquest (827–902). The island was administered by a strategos based at Syracuse and served as the empire's primary grain source and a base for naval operations in the central Mediterranean. The Arab siege of Syracuse (827–878) and the final conquest of Taormina (902) ended 367 years of Byzantine governance. Byzantine cultural influence in Sicily — Greek language, Orthodox Christianity, Byzantine art forms — persisted under Arab then Norman rule; the Norman kings deliberately preserved Greek administrative practices and multilingual court culture.

The Ottoman Empire's absorption of Byzantine territories occurred over a century-long process (1354–1453): Gallipoli fell (1354), Adrianople became the Ottoman capital (1365), Constantinople was surrounded on all sides after the 1390s, surviving through Timur's intervention (1402) and careful diplomacy. The final siege (1453) lasted 53 days; massive Hungarian-cast bombards breached the Theodosian Walls. Emperor Constantine XI died fighting on the walls. Mehmed II entered the city, prayed in Hagia Sophia, and proclaimed himself 'Caesar of Rome.' The fall shocked Western Christendom and ended 1,123 years of Roman imperial continuity.

The Byzantine Empire established a foothold in southern Iberia — the province of Spania — from 552 (when Emperor Justinian I exploited a Visigothic succession dispute) until 624 (when Visigothic King Suinthila expelled the last Byzantine garrison). Byzantine Spania controlled the coastal strip from Cartagena to the Strait of Gibraltar, including Malaga and Córdoba at its greatest extent. The Byzantine presence transmitted late Roman administrative culture, law, and artistic traditions to Iberia; the region's cities (Cartagena, Malaga) maintained their urban commercial character through the Byzantine period.

Carinthia was separated from Bavaria as an independent stem duchy in 976 by Emperor Otto II, who granted it to Henry of Carinthia (of the Luitpolding family). The duchy controlled the critical passes through the Karawanken Alps connecting Bavaria with northern Italy. Carinthia passed through several dynasties — Luitpoldings, Eppensteiners, Sponheims — before the Habsburgs acquired it in 1335, adding it to their growing Alpine domain. Combined with Austria (acquired 1282) and Styria (acquired 1282), Carinthia formed the nucleus of the 'Inner Austrian' lands that remained Habsburg until 1918.

Charlemagne's Avar Wars (788–796) eliminated the Avar Khaganate, which had dominated the Pannonian Plain (modern Hungary) for 200 years and had repeatedly devastated the Balkans and extorted tribute from Byzantium. The destruction of the Avar 'Ring' fortresses and the capture of the enormous Avar treasure (accumulated Byzantine tribute — reportedly nine wagonloads of gold) was the richest single windfall of the Carolingian era. The Avar population disappeared rapidly; their territory was organized as the Eastern March (Ostmark), precursor to Austria. Slavic populations moved into the Avar's former territory.
Charlemagne's imperial coronation (800) provoked Byzantine claim of sole Roman legitimacy; settled by Pax Nicephori (812).

East Francia emerged from the Treaty of Verdun (843) as Louis the German's share of the Carolingian Empire. It retained Carolingian administrative traditions — missi dominici, palace schools, the system of counties — but faced constant pressure from external enemies (Magyars, Vikings, Slavs) and internal fragmentation into great stem duchies (Bavaria, Saxony, Franconia, Swabia, Lorraine). The extinction of the East Frankish Carolingian line (911) led to the election of Conrad I (non-Carolingian) and then Henry I (Ottonian) — transforming East Francia into the Holy Roman Empire.

Middle Francia — the central strip of the Carolingian Empire granted to Emperor Lothair I at Verdun (843) — was an artificial construct with no ethnic, geographic, or linguistic coherence. It stretched from the North Sea to central Italy, encompassing Lorraine, Burgundy, Provence, and the Italian peninsula. After Lothair I's death (855), Middle Francia was partitioned among his three sons: Italy, Provence, and Lorraine (Francia Media). The instability of this middle zone — contested between France and Germany — created the perpetually disputed territories of Lorraine, Burgundy, the Low Countries, and northern Italy.

West Francia — Charles the Bald's share of the Carolingian Empire at Verdun (843) — was the core of the future French state. Charles the Bald maintained Carolingian institutional traditions but struggled against Viking raids (the siege of Paris, 885–886) and great nobles who used the crises to assert autonomy. The last West Frankish Carolingian, Louis V, died in 987; the nobles elected Hugh Capet (founder of the Capetian dynasty) rather than another Carolingian. The Capetian success in transforming West Francia into France — expanding royal demesne, building royal administration — took three centuries of patient work.

Castile and León were united and separated repeatedly through inheritance accidents and dynastic politics. Ferdinand I united them (1037–1065), then his will separated them; Fernando III united them permanently (1230). The union created the most powerful Iberian kingdom: Castile's military frontier culture combined with León's institutional depth and Roman Catholic tradition. The unified kingdom's resources enabled the conquest of Seville (1248), Murcia (1243), and Cádiz (1262), reducing the Muslim presence to the Kingdom of Granada — which survived as a tributary state until 1492.

The 'Crown of Castile' as a formal constitutional entity emerged from the permanent union of Castile and León under Fernando III (1230) and the subsequent integration of Murcia (1243), Seville (1248), and Cádiz (1262). The Crown's institutions — the Castilian Cortes, the chancillería, the royal council — developed throughout the 13th–14th centuries into a sophisticated royal administration. The Crown passed through the Castilian Trastámara dynasty (from 1369) before reaching Isabel I (1474), whose marriage to Ferdinand of Aragon (1469) created the personal union that became Spain.

The Champagne Fairs (held at Troyes, Provins, Lagny, and Bar-sur-Aube on a rotating annual calendar) were the premier commercial exchange in northern Europe from the late 11th to early 14th centuries. Italian merchants (especially Genoese and Venetian) brought Mediterranean luxury goods and letters of credit; Flemish and English merchants brought wool and cloth; northern European merchants brought furs and metalwork. The fairs' sophisticated financial instruments — bills of exchange, forward contracts, standardized units of account (the 'money of Champagne') — created the foundations of European commercial finance. Genoese-Venetian sea routes (from c. 1277) gradually bypassed the overland Champagne route.

The County of Champagne — one of the most commercially dynamic territories in medieval France, hosting the famous Champagne Fairs that served as the primary northern European commercial exchange — was absorbed into the French royal domain through marriage: Philip IV 'the Fair' of France married Joan I of Navarre and Champagne (1284), who was the heiress. The absorption of Champagne gave France control of the most important commercial fairs in northern Europe, shifting the commercial axis from independent county to royal domain. The Champagne Fairs declined thereafter as Genoese-Venetian sea routes (via Gibraltar, from c. 1277) bypassed the overland routes.

Connacht, the western Irish province, was closely associated with the High Kingship through the Uí Briúin and especially the Uí Conchobuir dynasties. Toirdelbach Ua Conchobair (Turlough O'Connor) and his son Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair (Rory O'Connor) were the last two Irish kings to make credible claims to the High Kingship before the Anglo-Norman invasion. Rory O'Connor (d. 1198) acknowledged English overlordship in the Treaty of Windsor (1175) after Henry II's Irish expedition; the subsequent fragmentation of Irish political power left Connacht as a reduced western rump kingdom under Rory's successors.

The Caliphate of Córdoba collapsed in the Fitna (civil war) of 1009–1031, fragmenting into approximately 23 Taifa kingdoms. The collapse followed a series of weak caliphs, the destruction of Medina Azahara by Berber mercenaries (1010), and the inability of any faction to maintain central authority. The Taifa kingdoms — often centered on individual cities — were militarily weak but culturally vibrant, producing the finest Arabic poetry and philosophy of the medieval period. Their weakness invited Christian military pressure (paying parias/tribute to Castile-León) and ultimately Almoravid intervention (1086).

The Ottoman Empire absorbed the Genoese colonies of the Crimean coast (Caffa, Soldaia) in 1475 and imposed Ottoman suzerainty over the Crimean Khanate — making the Giray dynasty (Chinggisid rulers of Crimea) vassals of the Ottoman Sultan rather than independent rulers. The Ottomans stationed garrisons at the major ports and used the Crimean Tatars as cavalry auxiliaries in their European campaigns. The arrangement created a mutually beneficial relationship: Crimean Tatars conducted slave raids against Poland-Lithuania and Russia, selling captives through the Ottoman slave markets at Caffa.
Pacta Conventa (1102) joined Croatia in personal union with Hungary; persisted through medieval period.

The Cumans (Kipchaks) maintained a complex relationship with Byzantium from the 11th century onward: sometimes raiding Byzantine Thrace, sometimes serving as Byzantine mercenaries, sometimes allied with Bulgarian enemies. Emperor Alexios I Komnenos allied with the Cumans against the Pechenegs at the Battle of Levounion (1091), using Cuman cavalry to destroy the Pecheneg threat. Subsequent Byzantine emperors employed Cuman mercenaries in their armies. The Bulgarian Asen dynasty used Cuman military support to establish the Second Bulgarian Empire (1185); Cuman marriage alliances with the Bulgarian tsars integrated them into Balkan elite culture.

The Principality of Galicia-Volhynia maintained a complex relationship with the Cumans (Kipchaks) of the adjacent steppe: sometimes fighting them (periodic raids), sometimes hiring them as mercenaries, and sometimes entering dynastic marriages. Prince Roman of Galicia used Cuman mercenaries in his campaigns. After the Mongol conquest (1237–1241), Galician princes navigated between Mongol suzerainty and western Christian alliances, sometimes using Cuman auxiliaries as a buffer. The Cumans' absorption into the Golden Horde eliminated them as a distinct political actor by the mid-13th century.

Kotyan Khan led approximately 40,000 Cuman families across the Carpathians into Hungary (1239) as refugees from the Mongol advance, accepting Hungarian suzerainty in exchange for settlement and military service. King Béla IV welcomed the Cumans as military manpower. When the Mongols invaded Hungary (1241), the Hungarian nobility accused the Cumans of treachery and massacred Kotyan Khan's encampment; the enraged Cumans withdrew to Bulgaria, leaving Hungary to face the Mongols alone. The Cumans later returned and settled permanently in the Hungarian Plain (the Kunság), where their descendants preserved their identity into the modern era.

The Second Bulgarian Empire (founded 1185) was established with Cuman (Kipchak) military support. The Asen brothers — Peter and Asen — who led the uprising against Byzantine taxation initially lacked sufficient military force; they recruited Cuman cavalry from across the Danube. The Cumans' mounted archer tactics were decisive against Byzantine armies. Kaloyan 'the Roman-Slayer' (r. 1197–1207) similarly used Cuman allies at Adrianople (1205) to defeat and capture Latin Emperor Baldwin I. The Asen dynasty's maternal Cuman connections (Queen Maria was reportedly of Cuman origin) integrated the Cumans into Bulgarian court culture.

The Kingdom of Cyprus was established by Guy of Lusignan (1192), who received it from Richard I after Richard had seized it en route to the Third Crusade. When Guy died without heirs, Cyprus passed to his brother Aimery (1194), who also became King of Jerusalem (1197) by marrying the heiress Isabella I. The Lusignan dynasty subsequently controlled both kingdoms simultaneously for decades. When Jerusalem fell to Saladin (1187) and was not recovered, Cyprus became the primary Crusader base in the eastern Mediterranean and the refuge for the Palestinian nobility.
Gaelic Dál Riata merged into broader Picto-Gaelic kingdom of Alba in ninth century; exact chronology debated.

The Gaelic Kingdom of Dál Riata (straddling the Irish Sea between Antrim and Argyll) and the Pictish kingdoms of northeastern Scotland coexisted, competed, and eventually merged into the Kingdom of Alba under Kenneth MacAlpin (c. 843). The mechanism of merger is debated: marriage alliance, conquest, or dynastic accident. Kenneth — who may have had both Pictish and Gaelic ancestry — united the two peoples; within generations the Pictish language had disappeared and Gaelic prevailed. The merger created the proto-Scottish kingdom that eventually became medieval Scotland through territorial expansion southward.

The Danelaw — the Norse-ruled territory of northern and eastern England established by the Great Heathen Army's settlement (865–878) — coexisted and competed with Wessex for nearly a century before the reconquest. The Danelaw was not a unified political entity but a patchwork of Danish-held towns (the Five Boroughs: Leicester, Nottingham, Derby, Stamford, Lincoln) and Norse-speaking rural areas. Alfred the Great's Treaty of Wedmore (878) established the boundary; his descendants — Edward the Elder (913–920) and Æthelflæd — reconquered it systematically, with the death of Eric Bloodaxe in 954 ending Norse Jorvik.

Deheubarth (southwest Wales) and Gwynedd (northwest Wales) competed and cooperated as the two most powerful Welsh kingdoms throughout the 10th–13th centuries. The most successful ruler of both — Llywelyn Fawr (Llywelyn the Great, 1195–1240) — united nearly all of Wales under Gwynedd's leadership, forcing English recognition in the Treaty of Worcester (1218). His grandson Llywelyn ap Gruffudd (Llywelyn the Last) achieved formal English recognition as Prince of Wales (1267), only to lose it after Edward I's conquest (1282–1283). The Deheubarth-Gwynedd rivalry was thus absorbed into the Welsh resistance to English conquest.

Dobruja (the territory between the Danube delta and the Black Sea, modern northeastern Bulgaria and eastern Romania) was a distinct sub-region of the Second Bulgarian Empire, sometimes ruled by semi-autonomous Dobrotiтsi (Dobrotitsa) princes. After the Bulgarian tsars' power declined in the early 14th century, Dobrotitsa (ruled c. 1347–1386) governed Dobruja effectively independently, allied with Genoa, issuing his own coinage and conducting foreign policy. His successor Ivanko submitted to Wallachia's Mircea the Elder before Ottoman conquest (1393–1396) absorbed the region.

Dobruja (the region between the Danube delta and the Black Sea coast, modern northeastern Bulgaria and eastern Romania) fell to the Ottomans after the Battle of Nicopolis (1396) and the subsequent Ottoman consolidation of Bulgaria. The region had been ruled by the Dobrotitsa (Dobruja principality) — a semi-autonomous Bulgarian successor state — until Mircea the Elder of Wallachia briefly controlled it. Ottoman control of Dobruja gave them dominance of the lower Danube's northern bank, controlling the approaches to the Danube delta and Black Sea.

The Norse Kingdom of Dublin — the most commercially important Norse settlement in Ireland — was captured by Strongbow (Richard de Clare, 2nd Earl of Pembroke) and Diarmait Mac Murchada's forces (1170), then taken under direct English royal control when Henry II arrived (1171). Dublin became the center of the English Lordship of Ireland, housing the English administration, the Anglo-Norman cathedral of Christ Church, and the merchant community that oriented Irish trade toward Bristol and the west of England. The shift from Norse to Anglo-Norman Dublin transformed the city's commercial and political character.

The Norse Kingdom of Dublin (established c. 841–853 as a longphort/fortified harbor) was the primary Scandinavian political entity in Ireland for 300 years. Dublin's kings — often ruling simultaneously in York, the Isle of Man, or the Hebrides — used the Irish Sea as a political and commercial zone. The Battle of Clontarf (1014) ended Norse political dominance, though Norse merchants remained dominant in Dublin's trade. The city was captured by the Anglo-Normans (1170) and the Norse community gradually assimilated. Dublin's street plan (Fishamble Street, Christchurch) and its commercial traditions were primarily Norse in origin.

East Anglia was settled by Danish Vikings of the Great Heathen Army after their defeat of King Edmund (killed 869) and the establishment of the Danelaw. The Danish settlement was dense — East Anglia has the highest concentration of Norse place names (Thorpe, Thwaite, -by endings) in England outside Yorkshire. The Danish ruling class quickly intermarried with the Anglo-Saxon population; the East Anglian Danelaw was among the first territories reconquered by Edward the Elder (913–920) using Alfred's burh system. The density of Scandinavian genetic heritage in modern East Anglian populations reflects this 50-year settlement.

East Anglia — conquered by the Vikings as part of the Danelaw in 869 (when they martyred King Edmund) — was recovered by Edward the Elder, Alfred the Great's son, during the reconquest campaigns of 913–920. Edward systematically built burhs (fortified towns) advancing into Danelaw territory, forcing Danish leaders to submit. East Anglia's recovery, along with Mercia and Essex, gave Edward control of England south of the Humber. The region became the economic core of medieval England, its Danelaw heritage visible in Norse place-names to this day.

The transformation of East Francia into the Holy Roman Empire occurred with Otto I's coronation as Emperor by Pope John XII (February 2, 962). Otto had already demonstrated imperial-scale authority by defeating the Magyars at Lechfeld (955) and was the undisputed dominant ruler of Latin Christendom. The imperial coronation linked his Frankish-German kingdom to the Roman imperial tradition and the papacy — creating a relationship that would generate centuries of conflict. The 'Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation' (the full title became standard in the 15th century) preserved Carolingian imperial ideology in a German institutional framework until 1806.

The County of Edessa (the northernmost Crusader state) and the Principality of Antioch maintained close cooperative relations throughout the 12th century, linked by geography, dynastic marriages, and shared threats from the Artukids and later the Zengids. When Zengi's forces besieged Edessa (1144), Antioch under Raymond of Poitiers failed to send relief — a failure partly explained by political tensions and partly by the swiftness of the siege. The fall of Edessa triggered the Second Crusade and permanently weakened the northern Crusader states.
Crusader states cooperated against Muslim neighbors; Baldwin of Boulogne moved from Edessa to Jerusalem.

England and Burgundy maintained a close alliance during the critical phase of the Hundred Years' War (1419–1435), following the Burgundian-English Treaty of Troyes (1420) that made Henry V heir to France. Philip the Good's alliance with England after the murder of his father John the Fearless (allegedly organized by the Dauphin, future Charles VII) at Montereau (1419) gave England the crucial French partnership that produced the Treaty of Troyes. The alliance held as long as Philip's personal grievance motivated it; the Congress of Arras (1435) reconciled Burgundy and France, decisively undermining the English position and beginning the final phase of French recovery.

The English Lordship of Ireland (1171–) was established when Henry II invaded to bring the Norman barons who had conquered Leinster (under Strongbow/Richard de Clare) under royal control. Pope Alexander III endorsed the invasion through the bull Laudabiliter (c. 1155, authenticity disputed). The subsequent English presence was limited: the 'Pale' around Dublin controlled by the crown; the 'Land of Peace' governed by Anglo-Norman lords who gradually 'went native'; and the 'Land of War' of Gaelic chiefs who accepted nominal English suzerainty. Ireland was never fully conquered in the medieval period.

English kings asserted overlordship over the Welsh kingdoms from the Norman Conquest onward, with Marcher Lords gradually pushing into Welsh territory. Llywelyn ap Gruffudd (Llywelyn the Last) achieved recognition as Prince of Wales by the Treaty of Montgomery (1267) but rebelled and was killed (1282). Edward I's Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) imposed English shires on Wales and built the most sophisticated castle-building program in Britain (Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech, Beaumaris). The native Welsh principality was extinguished but Welsh law, language, and culture survived under English administration.

The Despotate of Epirus and the Empire of Nicaea were the two main claimants to Byzantine imperial legitimacy after the Fourth Crusade (1204). Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epirus captured Thessalonica (1224) and proclaimed himself Emperor — directly challenging Nicaea's Theodore I Laskaris. The rivalry between the two 'Byzantine' claimants, sometimes violent, weakened both against the Latin Empire and later against the Bulgarians (Theodore was captured by Tsar Ivan Asen II at Klokotnitsa, 1230). Nicaea eventually prevailed, retaking Constantinople in 1261.

Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epirus captured the Latin Kingdom of Thessalonica (1224) — a Crusader state established for Boniface of Montferrat after 1204 — in a major westward expansion of Epirote power. The capture made Theodore the most powerful Greek ruler of the moment; he proclaimed himself Emperor of the Romans in 1224, the first claimant to challenge Nicaea's imperial monopoly. The capture of Thessalonica, however, led to overextension: Theodore's subsequent advance was halted by Bulgarian Tsar Ivan Asen II at the Battle of Klokotnitsa (1230), where Theodore was captured and blinded.

Seljuk Sunni expansion into Syria and Palestine directly challenged Fatimid Shia power; the Crusaders' arrival in 1099 was partly enabled by this Seljuk-Fatimid rivalry, as the two powers failed to coordinate a defense of Jerusalem.

The Este lords of Ferrara held the city as papal vicars, with the Este family recognized as hereditary vicars by Pope Nicholas III (1279). Ferrara's position at the Po delta made it strategically valuable for the Papal States; the Este maintained their position by balancing papal interests with imperial connections and by paying substantial annual fees to Rome. When the Este male line failed (1598), Pope Clement VIII claimed Ferrara as a papal fief by his interpretation of the vicariate's terms, absorbing the city into the Papal States despite protests from other Italian powers.

Ferrara and Venice maintained complex relations determined by Ferrara's position at the head of the Adriatic and controlling the Po delta — the commercial artery that fed Venice's hinterland trade. Ferrara's Este lords received Venetian commercial privileges in exchange for allowing Venetian merchants access to Po River trade routes. Periodic conflicts arose over transit rights and the salt trade (Ferrara competed with Venice in the Adriatic salt market). Venice's war of Ferrara (1482–1484) — an attempt to seize direct control of the Po delta — ended inconclusively when Pope Sixtus IV opposed Venetian expansion.

Florence, as the leading Guelf city of Tuscany, was a natural ally of the Lombard League against the Hohenstaufen emperors. Florence sent troops to support the League and benefited from Barbarossa's defeat at Legnano (1176) and Frederick II's struggles with the Italian communes. The Guelf-Ghibelline (papal-imperial) factional divisions that structured Florentine politics throughout the 13th–14th centuries originated in this alignment. The Guelf party's victory over the Ghibellines (expulsion of the Ghibellines after Benevento, 1266) transformed Florence into a Guelf city that subsequently defined itself in opposition to imperial power.

Florence and Milan maintained a perennial rivalry as the two dominant powers in central and northern Italy respectively. Their competition was partly territorial (control of Tuscany, access to the Ligurian coast) and partly ideological (Guelf Florence vs. Ghibelline Milan). The Visconti expansion toward Tuscany in the late 14th century — culminating in Gian Galeazzo Visconti's near-encirclement of Florence (1400–1402) — was broken only by his sudden death from plague. The Sforza-Medici alliance (1450s) transformed the relationship into cooperation, underpinning the Italian League (1455) that provided 40 years of relative peninsular stability.

The Duchy of Brittany maintained a semi-autonomous status within the French royal system, its dukes holding their territory as French vassals but effectively governing independently. Breton Celtic cultural distinctiveness — language, saints, legal customs — reinforced political separatism. The succession crisis following Duke Francis II's death (1488) allowed France to absorb Brittany through the marriage of his daughter Anne of Brittany to Charles VIII (1491) and then Louis XII (1499). The Edict of Union (1532) formally incorporated Brittany into France, though maintaining Breton legal privileges.

The relationship between France and England from the Norman Conquest (1066) through the Hundred Years' War (1337–1453) was defined by the English crown's possession of French fiefs — first the Duchy of Normandy, then the full Angevin Empire — creating a vassal-overlord relationship in which the King of England owed homage to the King of France for his French territories. French kings exploited English kings' position as vassals through the judicial mechanisms of the French court. The progressive elimination of English continental holdings — Normandy (1204), most of Aquitaine (by 1453) — drove both kingdoms' military and administrative development.

The counts of Flanders held their territory as French royal vassals, creating a persistent tension between Flemish autonomy and French overlordship. The relationship broke down under Philip IV 'the Fair' when he attempted direct royal administration of Flanders (1300). The Battle of Courtrai (1302) — Flemish weavers defeating the French cavalry — temporarily expelled French control. Philip recovered the county but never fully integrated it. Flanders's commercial ties with England (through the wool trade) repeatedly put it at odds with French royal interests during the Hundred Years' War.

The County of Toulouse — the dominant power in Languedoc — was drawn into the French orbit through the Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229). Count Raymond VI of Toulouse, suspected of harboring Cathars, was excommunicated and his lands attacked. The Treaty of Paris (1229) forced Count Raymond VII to surrender half his lands, to hunt heretics, and to marry his daughter Jeanne to Alphonse of Poitiers (Louis IX's brother). When Alphonse and Jeanne died without children (1271), Toulouse reverted to the French crown, completing the absorption of Languedoc and permanently eliminating the distinct Occitanian cultural sphere.

The Byzantine Empire formally recognized Charlemagne's imperial title in the Treaty of Aachen (812), negotiated with Emperor Michael I Rhangabe. Byzantium had initially rejected the coronation (800) as usurpation — the Empress Irene's regency created a constitutional argument that the Roman imperial throne was vacant, but Byzantium naturally rejected a western imperial rival. The 12-year negotiation ultimately produced recognition in exchange for Frankish relinquishment of Venetian and Dalmatian territorial claims. The recognition established the 'two emperor' system — East and West — that defined European political theory throughout the medieval period.

The Battle of Vouillé (507), in which Clovis I's Frankish forces defeated and killed the Visigothic King Alaric II, expelled the Visigoths from virtually all of Gaul — limiting them to the Iberian Peninsula and Septimania (the Mediterranean coastal strip now called Languedoc-Roussillon). The Frankish victory, supported by the Burgundians and celebrated by the papacy as a victory of Catholic Christianity over Arian heresy, made the Franks the unchallenged dominant power in Gaul. Clovis received the title of honorary consul from the Byzantine Emperor Anastasius, connecting the Frankish kingdom to the Roman imperial tradition.

The Kingdom of Galicia, created as a separate realm for García II when Ferdinand I of León-Castile divided his domains (1065), was rapidly reabsorbed into León after García's deposition by his brothers Alfonso VI and Sancho II (1071). The Galician territorial identity persisted, however — its separate legal customs, its pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela, and the Galician-Portuguese dialect that eventually became Portuguese. The County of Portugal, carved from Galicia in 1093 and granted to Henry of Burgundy, eventually broke away to become an independent kingdom (1139).

The Treaty of Nymphaion (March 1261), signed between Michael VIII Palaiologos of the Empire of Nicaea and Genoa, granted Genoa exclusive trading rights throughout the Byzantine Empire and the Black Sea in exchange for naval assistance against Venice and the Latin Empire. Genoese merchants replaced Venetians as the dominant commercial presence in Constantinople after Michael VIII's restoration. The Galata (Pera) quarter across the Golden Horn became effectively a Genoese city-state within Constantinople, with its own walls, government, and church. Genoese Black Sea colonies — Caffa in Crimea, Trebizond, Tana at the Don mouth — controlled the luxury trade routes.

Genoa's relationship with Byzantium was built on the Treaty of Nymphaion (1261), in which Michael VIII Palaiologos granted Genoa exclusive trading rights in the Black Sea and the Galata quarter of Constantinople in exchange for naval support against Venice and the Latin Empire. Genoese merchants replaced Venetians as the dominant commercial presence in Constantinople. Genoese colonies at Caffa (Crimea), Trebizond, and Pera (opposite Constantinople) controlled the Black Sea luxury trade routes. The relationship declined after the Ottoman conquest (1453), when Mehmed II revoked most Genoese privileges.

Genoa competed with Pisa for control of Sardinia throughout the 12th–13th centuries, exploiting the four indigenous Sardinian 'giudicati' (judgeships) through marriage alliances, commercial concessions, and military pressure. After the Battle of Meloria (1284) eliminated Pisan naval power, Genoa seemed positioned to absorb Sardinia — but the papacy intervened by granting Sardinia to the Crown of Aragon (1297), which conquered the island from the Genoese and the last indigenous giudicato (Arborea) in stages (1323–1420). Genoa retained only its colonies at Sassari and Bonifacio until Aragonese consolidation.

The rivalry between Genoa and Venice — the two dominant maritime republics of the medieval Mediterranean — was fought through four major wars (1253–1299, 1350–1355, 1373–1381, and through proxy conflicts). Genoese and Venetian trading posts throughout the Mediterranean brought them into constant competition. Venice's decisive victory at the Battle of Chioggia (1380–1381), where a Genoese fleet besieging Venice in its lagoon was destroyed, permanently broke Genoese naval power. Venice thereafter dominated the eastern Mediterranean trade routes until the Ottoman expansion.

The Kingdom of Georgia maintained a complex relationship with Byzantium from the 10th century onward — periodically allied (against the Seljuks), periodically in conflict (over Anatolia's border territories), and culturally deeply influenced by Byzantine art, theology, and court culture. The Georgian Golden Age under Queen Tamar (1184–1213) overlapped with the Fourth Crusade's dismemberment of Byzantium (1204); Georgian expansion into Trebizond helped create the Empire of Trebizond (1204) as a Byzantine successor state. The Mongol invasions (1220–1236) devastated Georgia and ended its role as a regional power.
Georgia under Mongol tribute through Ilkhanate (note: Ilkhanate not Golden Horde — using closest available).

The Empire of Trebizond was founded in 1204 by Alexios and David Komnenos — Byzantine princes who had been raised at the court of their great-aunt, Georgian Queen Tamar. When Constantinople fell to the Fourth Crusade, Tamar provided Georgian troops and financial support for the Komnenos brothers to establish themselves at Trebizond on the Black Sea coast. Georgia's military support made Trebizond's founding possible; the Komnenoi then established diplomatic connections with the Mongol Ilkhanate (marrying daughters to Mongol khans) that secured the principality's survival against Turkish pressure.

The Nasrid Emirate of Granada paid tribute (parias) to Castilian kings periodically throughout the 14th and 15th centuries, a tributary relationship that was interrupted by periods of conflict. Muhammad I, founder of the Nasrid dynasty (1232), had allied with Ferdinand III of Castile against the Almohads, accepting vassal status in exchange for survival. The tributary relationship allowed Granada to survive as a Muslim enclave for 260 years, providing Castile with revenue without the cost of outright conquest. The tribute payments ended when the Catholic Monarchs launched the Granada War (1482).

The Byzantine mission to Great Moravia (863) — led by the brothers Cyril and Methodius at Prince Rastislav's invitation — created the first Slavic alphabet (Glagolitic) and the first Slavic liturgy. Rastislav's motivation was political: he wanted a church independent of the Frankish bishops who were encroaching on Moravian autonomy. The brothers translated the Gospels, liturgy, and canon law into Slavic. Pope Hadrian II recognized the Slavic liturgy (868); after Cyril's death (869), Methodius continued as Archbishop of Moravia until his death (885). His disciples, expelled by Frankish bishops, carried the mission to Bulgaria, where it transformed Slavic literacy.

Great Moravia and the East Frankish kingdom maintained a complex relationship of conflict and dependence from Moravia's foundation (c. 830) through its destruction (906). Rastislav of Moravia sought independence from Frankish ecclesiastical domination by requesting Byzantine missionaries (862) — resulting in Cyril and Methodius's Slavic mission. His successor Sviatopluk negotiated a treaty with Louis the German (874) while maintaining autonomy. East Frankish princes allied with Magyar invaders who destroyed Moravia (906); the Franks subsequently failed to prevent Magyar raids westward.

Great Moravia sought papal recognition as an ecclesiastical independent entity — free from both Byzantine and Frankish ecclesiastical jurisdiction — and achieved this when Pope Hadrian II recognized the Slavic liturgy developed by Cyril and Methodius (868). Pope John VIII subsequently consecrated Methodius as Archbishop of Moravia (880), with jurisdiction over all Slavic-speaking peoples. After Methodius's death (885), Pope Stephen V reversed course, prohibiting the Slavic liturgy under Frankish pressure and expelling Methodius's disciples. The expulsion carried the Cyrillo-Methodian tradition to Bulgaria, where it ultimately survived and flourished.

The Great Schism of 1054, when papal legate Cardinal Humbert placed a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia (July 16, 1054) and Patriarch Michael Cerularius excommunicated the legates in return, formalized the split between the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches. The immediate issue was the filioque clause (whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son) plus papal primacy claims and liturgical differences (unleavened vs. leavened bread). The mutual excommunications were not lifted until 1964 (by Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras).

Norse Greenland (established c. 985 by Erik the Red) maintained commercial and administrative ties with Norway — the only source of timber, grain, and iron that the settlements required. Norway extracted tribute in the form of walrus ivory, white bears, and other Arctic luxury goods. The settlements accepted Norwegian royal sovereignty in 1261 (the same year as Iceland). The western settlement collapsed c. 1350 (likely from a combination of climate cooling and Inuit pressure); the eastern settlement persisted until c. 1408. The last certain record of the eastern settlement is a 1408 marriage recorded at the Hvalsey church.

Gwynedd (northwest Wales) was the most powerful Welsh kingdom, protected by the Snowdonian mountains from English military pressure. Its rulers — most importantly Llywelyn Fawr (the Great, 1195–1240) and Llywelyn ap Gruffudd (the Last, 1246–1282) — used Gwynedd's defensive advantages to unite Welsh resistance. Llywelyn Fawr's Treaty of Worcester (1218) achieved English recognition of his predominance; his grandson Llywelyn ap Gruffudd received formal English recognition as 'Prince of Wales' in the Treaty of Montgomery (1267). Edward I's conquest (1282–1283) ended the Welsh principality and built his ring of castles to prevent its recovery.

The Hanseatic League's relationship with Denmark was defined by control of the Sound (Øresund) — the narrow strait through which all Baltic trade passed and where Denmark collected tolls. The Hanse repeatedly clashed with Danish attempts to control or restrict Baltic trade: the War of 1361–1370 (after Valdemar IV seized Visby and Scania) ended with the Peace of Stralsund (1370), which gave the Hanse effective veto power over Danish royal succession. The relationship eventually shifted as Danish power recovered and the Hanse's member cities prioritized their individual interests over collective action.

The Hanseatic League maintained a major presence in England through the London Kontor known as the Steelyard (established 1320s on the Thames). Hanseatic merchants exported English wool and cloth, enjoying commercial privileges (low customs duties, legal extraterritoriality at the Steelyard) that English merchants resented. The relationship deteriorated in the 15th century as English merchants developed their own long-distance trading capacity and Parliament pressured successive kings to reduce Hanseatic privileges. Edward IV renewed the privileges in the Treaty of Utrecht (1473) in exchange for Hanseatic diplomatic support; the Steelyard was finally closed under Elizabeth I (1598).

Flanders was the western terminus of the Hanseatic trade network, with the Bruges Kontor (trading post) serving as the primary exchange point between Baltic goods (grain, timber, fur, amber, dried fish) and western luxury goods (English wool, Flemish cloth, spices from Genoa and Venice). Bruges's pre-eminence as a commercial center from the 12th through 14th centuries was built on this nexus. The Hanse's sanctions against Bruges (periodic 'kontorverlegungen' — transferring the Kontor to Dordrecht or elsewhere) demonstrated commercial leverage; Bruges's silting harbor and Antwerp's rise in the 15th century gradually shifted the Flemish commercial pole eastward.

The Hanseatic League's relationship with Norway was defined by the Bergen Kontor — one of the four main Hanseatic trading posts — established in Bergen's Bryggen (quay) district. German Hanseatic merchants virtually monopolized Norway's dried fish (stockfish) trade, exporting Norwegian cod to Catholic Europe's Friday markets while importing grain that Norway could not produce in sufficient quantities. The Hanse merchants in Bergen were notoriously exclusive, maintaining German language and customs and resisting Norwegian encroachment on their privileges. Bergen's Bryggen was effectively a German colonial quarter for over two centuries.

The Hanseatic League's Novgorod Kontor (established at the Church of St. Peter in Novgorod's German quarter) was the eastern anchor of the Hanseatic commercial system, providing access to the fur, wax, and honey of the Rus hinterland. German merchants traded cloth and salt for luxury goods that commanded premium prices in western Europe. The relationship was managed through strict protocols: German merchants were confined to their quarter, prohibited from Russian wives, and required to maintain fixed prices. Ivan III's closure of the Kontor (1494) — as punishment for Hanseatic failure to support Novgorod against Moscow — ended 250 years of direct commercial connection.

The Hanseatic League maintained extensive trading relationships with Sweden, operating through the key Baltic ports of Stockholm, Kalmar, and Visby (on Gotland). German Hanseatic merchants dominated Swedish trade in iron (from the Bergslagen region), copper, and timber — a dominance that Swedish kings periodically tried to limit through 'foreigners' exclusions. The Hanseatic capture of Stockholm (1389) and their support for the Kalmar Union (1397) represented Hanseatic political intervention; Erik of Pomerania's breach with the Hanse (1425) over Sound tolls led to war (1426–1435).

The Anglo-Saxon Heptarchy (the seven main kingdoms of early medieval England: Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex, and Wessex) was gradually consolidated into a single kingdom. Mercia dominated in the 8th century under Offa; the Viking invasions of the 9th century destroyed or subjugated all kingdoms except Wessex. Alfred the Great's survival of the Great Heathen Army's onslaught (871–878) and his subsequent reconquest made Wessex the foundation of English unification. His descendants — Edward the Elder, Æthelflæd, and Æthelstan — completed the consolidation by 927.

The County of Holland — originally a coastal county along the Meuse and Rhine delta — held imperial vassal status as part of the complex feudal hierarchy of the Low Countries. Holland's counts gradually expanded at the expense of the Duchy of Brabant and the Bishopric of Utrecht throughout the 13th–14th centuries. Burgundian acquisition of Holland (1428, through the Union of the House of Bavaria-Holland and then by purchase from Jacoba of Bavaria) integrated it into the emerging Burgundian state that eventually passed to the Habsburgs. Holland's exceptional commercial development (herring fishery, grain trade) made it the richest county per capita in the Empire.

The Golden Horde and the Anatolian Turkish beyliks competed for influence in the Black Sea and Pontic steppe region throughout the 14th century. The beyliks — including the Germiyanids, Sarukhanids, and Ramaids — operated within territories previously subject to Ilkhanid and then Golden Horde influence. The Ottoman beylik's rise complicated this relationship: as the Ottomans expanded into Thrace (1350s–1380s), they pushed the Golden Horde's southern influence northward. The Mongol-Ottoman confrontation culminated in Timur's defeat of Bayezid I at Ankara (1402), which temporarily reversed Ottoman gains.

The Principality of Galicia-Volhynia, after its 1241 Mongol devastation, became a tribute-paying vassal of the Golden Horde under Daniel of Galicia. Daniel alternated between accommodation (accepting the Horde's patent) and resistance (seeking crusade support from Pope Innocent IV, receiving a royal crown in 1253). The Horde used Galician troops in its western campaigns; Galician princes periodically made the journey to Sarai to renew their submission. After Daniel's line ended (1323), Galicia passed to Poland and Volhynia to Lithuania — both of which were rising powers outside the Horde's sphere, ending the tributary relationship.

Muscovite princes paid annual tribute (the 'Mongol yoke') to the Golden Horde from 1243 to 1480, when Ivan III formally ended tributary payments. The relationship was more complex than simple subjugation: Moscow's princes served as the Horde's primary tribute collectors for other Russian principalities, a role that enriched Moscow and gave it leverage over its neighbors. Ivan I 'Moneybag' (Kalita) used this role to accumulate territory. Ivan III's 'stand on the Ugra River' (1480) — when both sides backed down without fighting — marks the effective end of the tributary relationship.

Novgorod's relationship with the Golden Horde was indirect and episodic: the Mongols did not physically invade Novgorod (1237–1240) though they burned other cities, but they sent census-takers and tax collectors periodically. Alexander Nevsky — Prince of Novgorod and then Grand Prince of Vladimir — negotiated the tribute relationship with the Horde, accepting Mongol financial sovereignty while maintaining Novgorodian self-government. The 'anti-Mongol' riots in Novgorod (1257–1259), when census-takers arrived, were suppressed by Alexander Nevsky himself to preserve the tribute accommodation.

Pskov, as a junior partner and later dependency of Novgorod, shared in Novgorod's indirect relationship with the Golden Horde — paying tribute through Novgorod's collection mechanism rather than directly. Pskov's position on the western frontier (adjacent to the Teutonic/Livonian Order and Lithuania) meant its military concerns were primarily western, while the Mongol fiscal relationship was mediated through Novgorod. When Moscow absorbed Novgorod (1478), Pskov's Mongol-tributary relationship ended; Pskov was then absorbed by Vasili III (1510) through the same administrative consolidation that had ended Novgorodian independence.

The Crimean Khanate broke from the fragmented Golden Horde under Hacı I Giray (1441–1466), who established an independent Chinggisid dynasty controlling the Crimean Peninsula and the adjacent steppe. The Crimean Khanate quickly came under Ottoman suzerainty (1475–1478) after Mehmed II's Black Sea campaign captured the Genoese colonies. Under Ottoman protection, the Crimean Tatars became the most persistent raiding force against Poland-Lithuania and Muscovy, conducting slave raids that depopulated the Ukrainian steppe and provided the Ottoman Empire with enslaved workers. The Khanate persisted until Russian conquest (1783).

The Khanate of Kazan broke from the collapsing Golden Horde under Ulugh Muhammad (1438), who was expelled from the Horde's internal succession struggle and established himself at Kazan on the middle Volga. The Kazan Khanate controlled the key junction where the Volga and Kama rivers meet — the gateway to the Ural fur trade and the routes east toward Siberia. Kazan's mixed population (Tatar ruling class, Finno-Ugric Mari and Mordvin subjects) and strategic position made it Moscow's primary eastern adversary for a century, until Ivan IV's conquest (1552).

Tver was the most persistent rival to Moscow for leadership of northeastern Russia in the 14th century, its princes competing for the Golden Horde's patent (yarlyk) to collect tribute from other Russian principalities. The Horde often played Moscow against Tver: Prince Mikhail of Tver was executed in the Horde (1318) after a dispute with Moscow's Yuri Danilovich; Tver briefly recovered the Horde's favor but lost it again when Ivan I 'Moneybag' of Moscow outmaneuvered the Tver princes diplomatically. Tver's final attempt at independence — its 1327 anti-Mongol uprising — was suppressed by a joint Mongol-Muscovite punitive expedition.

Vladimir-Suzdal and the other northeastern Russian principalities fell to the Mongol invasion of 1237–1238, with Grand Prince Yuri II killed at the Battle of the Sit River (1238). The surviving princes — most prominently Alexander Nevsky — negotiated a tributary relationship with the Golden Horde, paying annual tribute in exchange for recognition of their rule and Mongol military protection against rivals. Alexander Nevsky's policy of accommodation (combined with military resistance to Swedes and Teutonic Knights) preserved the principality and established Moscow's Danilovich dynasty as the eventual heirs.

After the fall of Acre (1291), the Knights Hospitaller retreated to Cyprus, which they used as a base for another 20 years before conquering Rhodes (1309). Cyprus provided the order's headquarters, naval facilities, and recruitment grounds during the critical transition from a land-based military order to a maritime one. The order's presence in Cyprus also entangled it in the complex dynastic politics of the Lusignan kingdom — a relationship that both aided and complicated the order's development of its new Mediterranean naval role.

The Knights Hospitaller were founded in Jerusalem (c. 1099–1113) as a hospital order serving poor pilgrims, evolving into a military order by the mid-12th century. Their massive fortress of Krak des Chevaliers in Syria — built c. 1142–1170 — became the most formidable Crusader castle in the Levant. The Hospitallers held substantial fiefs throughout the Kingdom of Jerusalem and remained after the fall of Jerusalem (1187), based at Acre until 1291. Their military and organizational capacity — unlike the Templars — was redirected to naval warfare in the eastern Mediterranean after the fall of Acre.

Austria (the Ostarrichi/Ostmark) emerged as a separate march from Bavaria in 976 when Emperor Otto II granted it to Leopold of Babenberg. Elevated to a duchy (1156) by Frederick Barbarossa with the unique 'Privilegium Minus' (giving Austria exceptional rights including female succession), Austria became the primary Habsburg family domain when Rudolf of Habsburg was elected emperor (1273) and secured Austria by inheritance (1282). The Habsburgs used Austria as the base for their dynasty's continuous hold on the imperial title (1438–1806, with one brief interruption).

Bohemia was incorporated into the Holy Roman Empire as a stem duchy when the Přemyslid dynasty accepted imperial suzerainty (c. 950 under Boleslav I). As the Kingdom of Bohemia (elevated by Frederick Barbarossa in 1198), it became one of the seven electoral princes with special constitutional status: the King of Bohemia was the first among secular electors, presided over the electoral feast as royal cup-bearer (Mundschenk), and — uniquely among imperial territories — held his crown by hereditary right and was exempt from many imperial obligations. The Golden Bull of 1356 codified Bohemia's exceptional position.

The Kings of Bohemia held a unique dual position in the Holy Roman Empire: as kings, they held hereditary rule over the richest kingdom in the empire; as electoral princes, they were first among the secular electors with the right to choose the emperor. Charles IV (1346–1378) — simultaneously King of Bohemia and Holy Roman Emperor — made Bohemia the center of imperial politics, moving the imperial capital to Prague and issuing the Golden Bull (1356) that formalized electoral procedure with Bohemia in first place. Prague's University (founded 1348) was the first in central Europe.

The relationship between the Holy Roman Empire and the papacy was the defining tension of medieval European politics, oscillating between cooperation (the Ottonian-Gregorian partnership of the 10th century), conflict (the Investiture Controversy, 1076–1122), renewed cooperation (the Crusades), and catastrophic conflict (Frederick II vs. Innocent IV, 1239–1250). The fundamental question — who held ultimate authority in Christendom, the pope or the emperor — was never definitively resolved. The papacy's greatest victories (deposing Henry IV in 1076, deposing Frederick II in 1245) were matched by the empire's resilience and eventual institutional independence.

Bosnia maintained complex vassalage relations with Hungary, acknowledged as the nominal suzerain while Bosnian bans exercised effective independence. Hungarian interest in Bosnia was driven by Catholicism (Hungary used crusade ideology against the heterodox Bosnian Church) and strategic concern about the Adriatic coast. The Angevin kings of Hungary (from 1301) attempted to integrate Bosnia more firmly; King Tvrtko I of Bosnia (1353–1391) expanded Bosnian territory at Hungary's expense during the Angevin dynasty's weakness. The Ottoman conquest of Bosnia (1463) — which Hungary failed to prevent — opened the Adriatic flank to Ottoman raiding.

Hungary served as the primary barrier to Ottoman expansion into central Europe for 150 years. János Hunyadi (regent 1446–1453) won crucial victories at Belgrade (1456) and in the Long Campaign (1443–1444), but failed at Varna (1444) and Kosovo (1448). The Battle of Mohács (1526) — where King Louis II was killed and the Hungarian army annihilated — broke Hungary's defensive capacity. The country was subsequently partitioned among the Ottomans (central Hungary), the Habsburgs (western Hungary/Austria), and Transylvania (an Ottoman vassal). Hungary remained divided until 1699.

The dynastic connections that linked the Iberian crowns (Spain), the Holy Roman Empire, and the Low Countries were forged through a series of Habsburg marriages in the late 15th and early 16th centuries. Ferdinand and Isabella's daughter Juana ('the Mad') married Philip the Handsome, son of Emperor Maximilian I and Mary of Burgundy — connecting Castile to the Habsburg Netherlands and the imperial family. Their son Charles inherited Castile, Aragon, the Netherlands, and was elected Holy Roman Emperor (1519) as Charles V, creating the first empire 'on which the sun never set.'

The Icelandic Commonwealth (930–1262) maintained complex relations with the Norwegian crown: dependent on Norwegian timber and grain imports, subject to Norwegian pressure for conversion to Christianity (under Olaf Tryggvason, 999–1000), and eventually accepting Norwegian overlordship under the Old Covenant (Gamli sáttmáli, 1262–1264). The submission followed a decade of civil war among Icelandic chieftain clans (the Sturlungaöld) that left the commonwealth unable to maintain order. Iceland remained under the Norwegian and then Danish crown until 1944.

The Mamluks' victory at Ain Jalut (1260) halted the Mongol advance into Africa; intermittent warfare continued for decades, with the Ilkhanate repeatedly attempting to break through the Mamluk defensive line in Syria. The Ilkhans briefly allied with Crusaders and the Armenians against the Mamluks.

After the Battle of Köse Dağ (1243), the Sultanate of Rum becomes a vassal of the Ilkhanate. Seljuk sultans rule in name but require Mongol approval; the Ilkhanate extracts tribute and military service. This dependence accelerates the sultanate's fragmentation into rival Turkic beyliks.

The Kingdom of Jerusalem maintained diplomatic contact with Constantinople throughout its existence, reflecting both the shared Christian interest in the Holy Land and the Byzantine imperial claim to protect Eastern Christians. Byzantine emperors provided financial subsidies and occasionally military aid to Jerusalem (notably Manuel I Komnenos's coordination with the Crusaders). The marriage alliance between Emperor John II Komnenos and the Latin kingdom was discussed but never completed. Byzantine hostility toward the Crusader states (especially Antioch) complicated cooperation with Jerusalem.

The Viking Kingdom of Jorvik (York) — established by the Danish Great Heathen Army in 866 — was the center of Norse power in northern England. A series of Norse and Norwegian kings ruled Jorvik in an unstable succession. The Wessex king Eadred finally expelled and killed Erik Bloodaxe (the last King of Jorvik) in 954, ending the kingdom. Jorvik's recovery brought all of England north of the Humber under Wessex/English control for the first time, completing the political unification of England that Æthelstan had begun at Brunanburh (937).

The Viking Kingdom of Jorvik was created within the former Kingdom of Northumbria when Halfdan Ragnarsson settled his forces there (876) after the Great Heathen Army's conquest. Jorvik controlled the southern portion of Northumbria (roughly Yorkshire), while the northern portion (Bernicia, modern Northumberland) was governed by a native English aristocracy under Danish suzerainty. The two parts of Northumbria had different experiences: Jorvik became the most Scandinavian-influenced urban center in England; Bernicia's Anglo-Saxon aristocracy maintained more of their culture. When Eadred expelled Eric Bloodaxe (954), the reunited Northumbria was reintegrated into the English kingdom.

Medieval Sardinia was divided into four indigenous 'giudicati' (judgeships) — Cagliari, Arborea, Torres (Logudoro), and Gallura — autonomous states that developed after the breakdown of Byzantine control (9th–10th centuries). The giudicati maintained their independence through shifting alliances with Genoa, Pisa, and the papacy while resisting outside absorption. The Church played a crucial role through the 'regnum Sardiniae et Corsicae' papal grant (1297 to Aragon); the Giudicato of Arborea — the last native Sardinian state — resisted Aragonese conquest until 1420, led by the remarkable Eleonora d'Arborea, who codified Sardinian law in the Carta de Logu (c. 1395).
