The Duchy of Holstein — a German-speaking territory held by the Danish crown as a fief of the Holy Roman Empire (since 1460 united with the Duchy of Schleswig under the Treaty of Ripen) — created a persistent constitutional entanglement between Denmark and the Empire. Danish kings ruled Holstein as German princes and Schleswig as Danish dukes, simultaneously holding membership in both the Danish crown and the imperial Diet. The Holstein connection brought German commercial interests and culture into the Danish crown, facilitating Hanseatic trade but also creating a German-Danish cultural borderland that persisted until the Second World War.

The Kalmar Union (1397–1523), established by Queen Margaret I of Denmark (regent for her grandnephew Eric of Pomerania), united Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under a single crown while preserving each kingdom's laws and institutions. Margaret I effectively governed all three until her death (1412). The union was plagued by Swedish resistance to Danish dominance; Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson's revolt (1434) began the cycle of Swedish separatism that culminated in the Stockholm Bloodbath (1520) and the definitive Swedish exit under Gustav Vasa (1523).

Egbert of Wessex — who had spent time in exile at Charlemagne's court — conquered Kent from the Mercian sphere of influence (825) after his decisive victory over Mercia at Ellendun. Kent's absorption gave Wessex control of Canterbury (the ecclesiastical capital of England), the key port of Sandwich, and the richest agricultural land in southeast England. Essex, Sussex, and Surrey submitted simultaneously. The absorption of Kent and the southeast transformed Wessex from a regional power into the dominant English kingdom.
Khazar-Arab Wars (note: against caliphal Damascus, not Iberian Umayyads — relationship reflects broader Umayyad pressure).

The Byzantine Empire and the Khazar Khaganate maintained a consistent alliance against their shared enemies: the Islamic Umayyad and Abbasid Caliphates and, later, the Bulgars. Byzantine emperors cemented the alliance through dynastic marriages: Constantine V married a Khazar princess (Tzitzak, baptized Eirene), making his son Leo IV 'the Khazar.' The Khazars' conversion to Judaism (traditionally dated c. 740) did not disrupt the alliance; Byzantium valued the Khazars as a buffer on the northern Black Sea steppe. The Khazars' eventual destruction by Sviatoslav I of Kiev (965) removed the Byzantine steppe buffer and directly contributed to the Pecheneg pressure on Byzantium.

The Khazar Khaganate controlled the Pontic steppe (modern Ukraine and southern Russia) from the 7th to 10th centuries, serving as a buffer state between Byzantine Christendom and the Islamic caliphates. The Khazar ruling elite famously converted to Judaism in the 8th century. They controlled the key trade routes between the Baltic and the Caspian, collecting tolls from Varangian (Viking) merchants trading the river routes to Constantinople. Sviatoslav I of Kiev destroyed the Khazar state in 965, opening the steppe to successive nomadic groups — Pechenegs, then Cumans, then Mongols.

Following the Mongol destruction of Kiev (1240), Russian principalities become tributaries of the Golden Horde. Princes must travel to Sarai to receive their yarlik (patent) from the khan. This arrangement lasts until Moscow's Ivan III refuses tribute payment in 1480.

The Principality of Galicia-Volhynia emerged as the southwestern successor state of Kievan Rus after the Mongol invasions (1241). Under Roman the Great (d. 1205) and his son Daniel of Galicia (1201–1264), it was the most powerful post-Kievan polity, seeking recognition from both the papacy (Daniel received a papal crown in 1253) and the Mongol Horde. The principality occupied a crucial position between Poland, Lithuania, Hungary, and the Horde, conducting a sophisticated multi-directional diplomacy. After Daniel's line died out (1323), Galicia was absorbed by Poland and Volhynia by Lithuania.

Moscow emerged as a major principality only in the 13th century, its rise enabled by cooperation with the Mongol Golden Horde and geographic advantages (forests, rivers, central position). The Metropolitanate of Russia transferred to Moscow (1325), giving it ecclesiastical primacy. Ivan I 'Moneybag' (1325–1341) collected Mongol tribute for neighboring principalities and used his privileged position to accumulate territory. Ivan III (1462–1505) ended tribute, annexed Novgorod and Tver, and established Moscow as the 'Third Rome' following Constantinople's fall.

Novgorod maintained a distinct political trajectory from Kiev and later Moscow, governed by a boyar oligarchy through a veche (popular assembly) with elected posadniki (mayors) and invited military princes with strictly limited powers. Novgorod's commercial empire extended to the Arctic and connected with the Hanseatic League's eastern trade network. It survived the Mongol invasions (1237–1240) undamaged. Ivan III's absorption of Novgorod (1478) — accompanied by the deportation of the boyar families and the abolition of the veche — eliminated the most democratic polity in medieval Russia.

Vladimir-Suzdal emerged as the dominant northeastern Russian principality under Andrei Bogolyubsky (1157–1174), who moved the grand princely seat from Kiev to Vladimir and sacked Kiev itself (1169) — a shocking desacralization of the traditional center. The transfer of power from Kiev to Vladimir reflects the demographic shift of Russian population northward (away from the steppe frontier) that had been underway since the 11th century. Vladimir became the ecclesiastical and political center of Russia until the rise of Moscow in the 14th century.

Galicia (northwestern Iberia, modern Galicia/Spain and northern Portugal) was briefly a separate kingdom under García II, son of Ferdinand I of León-Castile, who divided his realm among his sons at death (1065). García received Galicia; he was deposed by his brothers Sancho II and Alfonso VI (1071) and imprisoned until his death (1090). Galicia's distinct Celtic cultural heritage — Galician-Portuguese language, different legal customs — gave it a persistent regional identity even after reabsorption into León. The County of Portugal, carved from Galicia in 1093, eventually became an independent kingdom (1139).

The Duchy of Athens was created after the Fourth Crusade (1204) when the Crusader division of Byzantine territory granted Attica and Boeotia to Othon de la Roche, a Burgundian lord who took the title 'Megaskyr' (Great Lord) rather than duke. Athens became an important secondary Crusader state, held by the de la Roche family until 1308, then by the Brienne family (1308–1311). The Catalan Company — mercenaries who had fought for Byzantium — seized Athens (1311) after defeating the French knights at the Battle of the Kephissos; the Catalans held Athens until 1388, when it passed to the Florentine Acciaiuoli.

The Principality of Achaea (the Morea, comprising the Peloponnese) was the most successful and most stable of the Crusader states created after the Fourth Crusade (1204). Geoffrey I of Villehardouin and his successors built a functioning feudal state on Byzantine foundations, maintaining Byzantine administrative structures while imposing French feudal customs on top. The Assizes of Romania (the law code of the Latin states in Greece) was developed in Achaea. At its height, Achaea was the model 'Western' state in the Mediterranean, admired even by Byzantine observers for its efficient governance.

The Latin Empire of Constantinople (1204–1261) maintained formal sovereignty over a vast Latin feudal empire in Greece and Anatolia, but the Empire of Nicaea — the primary Byzantine successor state — contested this claim through continuous military pressure and diplomatic competition. The Nicaean emperors (Theodore I Laskaris, John III Vatatzes, Theodore II Laskaris) systematically reconquered Byzantine territories from the Latin Empire, leaving Constantinople as an isolated city by the 1250s. The Latin emperors appealed constantly for Western aid that never materialized in sufficient force, and John de Brienne's desperate defense ultimately gave way when Michael VIII Palaiologos retook Constantinople (1261).

The Kingdom of Thessalonica was created after the Fourth Crusade's division of Byzantine territory, with Boniface of Montferrat receiving Thessalonica and Macedonia. Boniface had expected to receive Constantinople itself; his disappointment at Baldwin of Flanders's election as Latin Emperor led to immediate tensions. The Kingdom of Thessalonica was the second Latin state in Greece after the Latin Empire of Constantinople, but it was peripheral and militarily exposed. Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epirus captured it in 1224, ending 20 years of Latin rule.

Leinster, the southeastern Irish province, was the kingdom that initiated the Anglo-Norman conquest by inviting Strongbow's intervention. King Diarmait Mac Murchada, expelled by High King Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair and his Uí Néill allies, recruited Anglo-Norman barons from Wales (led by Richard de Clare 'Strongbow') and returned to reconquer his kingdom (1169–1170). Strongbow married Diarmait's daughter Aoife and inherited Leinster on Diarmait's death (1171). Henry II then arrived to bring the Anglo-Norman barons under royal control, effectively beginning the English Lordship of Ireland.

León and Castile were periodically united through dynastic inheritance: Ferdinand I (1037–1065) first united them by inheriting Castile and conquering León; they were re-split among his sons and reunited under Alfonso VII (1126–1157), split again, and finally permanently united under Fernando III (1230). Each union was driven by inheritance accidents rather than administrative planning; each split by the tradition of equal inheritance among sons. Fernando III's permanent union was facilitated by the simultaneous failure of the Leonese male line and his mother Berenguela of Castile's political skill in managing the succession.

Ferdinand I of León-Castile, following Iberian tradition, divided his kingdom among his sons at death (1065): Sancho II received Castile, Alfonso VI received León, and García II received Galicia. The division was immediately unstable — Sancho II forced his brothers to cede their shares (1071–1072), only to be assassinated at the siege of Zamora. Alfonso VI then reunited all three kingdoms. Fernando III permanently reunited Castile and León (1230), ending the periodic separations. The division practice, imported from Frankish custom, repeatedly destabilized Iberian kingdoms.

Lithuania and the Golden Horde competed for control of the western Eurasian steppe and the Orthodox Ruthenian principalities from the 1340s onward. Lithuanian expansion under Algirdas (1345–1377) pushed into Horde-controlled territory; the Battle of Blue Waters (1362) broke Horde military power in the western steppe, enabling Lithuania to extend to the Black Sea coast. Lithuania's rise was partly enabled by the Horde's internal civil wars ('the Great Troubles,' 1359–1380s). The Horde's power continued to decline after Kulikovo (1380) and Timur's campaigns (1395–1396), ceding western steppe dominance to Lithuania and eventually to Poland-Lithuania.

The Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Grand Principality of Moscow competed for control of the Orthodox Ruthenian principalities — the former lands of Kievan Rus — throughout the 14th and 15th centuries. Lithuania under Algirdas expanded aggressively eastward, defeating the Golden Horde at Blue Waters (1362) and pushing Lithuanian control to within 50 miles of Moscow. Moscow under Ivan III reversed this, annexing Novgorod (1478) and Tver (1485) and scoring a diplomatic victory at the Battle of the Vedrosha (1500). The competition shaped which Slavic peoples would align with Latin (Polish-Lithuanian) versus Orthodox (Muscovite) civilization.

The Union of Krewo (1385) and the subsequent Jagiellonian dynasty created the political entity that dominated central-eastern Europe for 200 years. Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania married Polish Queen Jadwiga, was baptized as Władysław II Jagiełło, and was crowned King of Poland (1386). Lithuania — the last major pagan state in Europe — converted to Catholic Christianity. The combined Polish-Lithuanian state defeated the Teutonic Order at Grunwald (1410), expanded into Ukraine and Ruthenia, and became the largest state in Europe under the mature Jagiellonian dynasty. The Union of Lublin (1569) transformed the personal union into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

The Lombard Kingdom's periodic campaigns to capture Ravenna — the Byzantine Exarchate's capital and the last major imperial center in northern Italy — define the political history of Italy from 568 to 751. King Aistulf finally captured Ravenna in 751, eliminating Byzantine administration in northern Italy and forcing the papacy to seek Frankish protection. The 183-year Lombard-Byzantine conflict over northern Italy created the political fragmentation that would persist: Byzantine enclaves (Rome, Naples, Venice, Sicily) vs. Lombard-controlled hinterlands, with the papacy caught between them.

The Lombard Kingdom's expansion in Italy periodically threatened the papacy's independence and territorial holdings. The Lombard capture of the Exarchate of Ravenna (751) — eliminating the last Byzantine administrative center in northern Italy — left the papacy without its traditional protector. Pope Stephen II's appeal to Pippin III of the Franks (754) for military protection, secured by the Donation of Pippin (756), created the Franco-papal alliance that replaced Byzantine protection. The Lombard threat thus inadvertently produced the Carolingian Empire — Charlemagne conquered the Lombard Kingdom entirely (774) at papal request.

Lorraine — the western portion of the old Middle Francia between France and Germany — became a persistent constitutional problem of the Holy Roman Empire. Divided into Upper and Lower Lorraine (959), it was repeatedly contested between France and Germany. The French crown encroached gradually on the western portions; the War of the Breton Succession and later Burgundian Wars saw French influence extend. The imperial side was defended by the German prince-bishops of Metz, Toul, and Verdun. The Three Bishoprics were eventually absorbed by France (Henry II, 1552) though the empire did not formally recognize this until the Peace of Westphalia (1648).

The Luxembourg dynasty acquired the Bohemian crown through John of Luxembourg's marriage to Eliška Přemyslovna (1310) and used it as the springboard for imperial power. John's son Charles IV (1346–1378) became simultaneously King of Bohemia, Holy Roman Emperor, and the most powerful ruler in 14th-century Europe. Charles IV made Prague the imperial capital, founded the University of Prague (1348), built the Charles Bridge, and issued the Golden Bull (1356) that gave Bohemia electoral primacy. The Luxembourg connection transformed Bohemia from a Přemyslid into a Bohemian-German-Luxembourg hybrid court.

Magyar cavalry raids devastated East Francia repeatedly from 899 to 955, penetrating as far as Burgundy, Lorraine, Saxony, and Italy. The raids — lightning fast, burning crops and towns, returning before resistance could organize — exposed the inadequacy of Carolingian defense. The Saxon kings Henry I 'the Fowler' organized systematic counter-measures: building burgs (fortified towns), training heavy cavalry, and negotiating a 9-year truce (926–934) that bought time. His son Otto I finally crushed the Magyars at the Battle of Lechfeld (955), ending the raids and demonstrating German military superiority that enabled Otto's imperial coronation (962).

The Magyar migration into Pannonia (895–896) brought the Hungarian tribes into direct conflict with the First Bulgarian Empire, whose Khan Simeon I had been raiding Byzantine territory. A Byzantine-Magyar alliance attacked Bulgaria from the north while Byzantine forces pressed from the south (894–896). Simeon defeated the Magyars in the counterattack, killing their prince Liutold; he then made peace with Byzantium. The Magyar-Bulgarian conflict shaped the early history of both peoples: it contributed to the Magyar migration further west into the Carpathian Basin and gave Simeon the free hand to pursue his Byzantine-focused imperial ambitions.

Magyar nomadic cavalry raids from the Pannonian Plain destroyed Great Moravia (906), eliminating the most sophisticated Slavic state of the early medieval period. The Magyars had been invited as allies by East Frankish princes against Moravia; they proved impossible to control and subsequently raided deep into Germany, France, and Italy for half a century until their decisive defeat at Lechfeld (955). The destruction of Great Moravia permanently eliminated the Slavic Cyrillo-Methodian tradition from the Danube basin, driving it eastward to Bulgaria.

Mamluk sultans Baybars and Qalawun systematically dismantled the remaining Crusader states; Caesarea (1265), Jaffa (1268), Krak des Chevaliers (1271), and Acre (1291) fell in a methodical campaign that ended the Crusader presence in the Holy Land.

The Kingdom of the Isles (comprising the Hebrides and the Isle of Man) was an insular Norse kingdom that had existed under Norwegian suzerainty since Viking settlement (9th century). Its kings — most notably Godred Crovan (d. 1095), who united Man and the Hebrides — maintained a semi-independent status while nominally acknowledging Norwegian overlordship. King Haakon IV of Norway's expedition to the Hebrides (1263) to reassert Norwegian authority ended with the indecisive Battle of Largs; Haakon died returning to Norway. The Treaty of Perth (1266) transferred all islands to Scotland for 4,000 marks silver.

The Treaty of Perth (1266) transferred the Kingdom of the Isles (including the Isle of Man and the Hebrides) from Norway to Scotland following the Battle of Largs (1263), where a Norwegian fleet under King Haakon IV Haakonsson was repulsed. The transfer was secured for 4,000 marks and an annual payment of 100 marks. The Lordship of the Isles, created from the former kingdom, maintained a semi-autonomous Gaelic culture within the Scottish framework, with MacDonald lords operating almost independently of the Scottish crown until the title was forfeited in 1493.

The Kingdom of Meath occupied a unique position in Irish political geography as the seat of the High Kingship at Tara — the symbolic center of Irish kingship. Meath's kings were often nominal subordinates of the High King rather than independent rulers. In the 12th century, Meath was divided between Leinster (under Strongbow) and the Anglo-Norman barons after the English intervention (1169–1171), effectively ending Meath's distinct political existence as an Irish kingdom. The 'Lord of Meath' became an Anglo-Norman title under Walter de Lacy.

Mercia and Wessex contested hegemony over England south of the Humber from the 7th century through the Viking Age. Mercia dominated under Æthelbald (716–757) and Offa (757–796) — the latter building Offa's Dyke as a Welsh border and receiving papal recognition as a near-king. Wessex reasserted itself under Ecgberht (802–839). The Viking Great Army destroyed Mercia as an independent kingdom (877); Mercia was thereafter governed jointly by Alfred's son-in-law Æthelred and, after Æthelred's death, by Alfred's daughter Æthelflæd 'Lady of the Mercians,' who completed the Danelaw reconquest before her death (918).

The Merovingian Franks and the Lombard Kingdom of Italy maintained generally hostile but occasionally cooperative relations throughout the 6th–8th centuries. The Merovingians periodically attempted to assert overlordship over the Lombards and intervened in Italian politics; Lombard expansion southward into central Italy was checked by Frankish-papal pressure. The Lombard-Merovingian relationship was complicated by Arian-Catholic religious differences (the Lombards were initially Arian); the conversion of the Lombard queen Theodolinda to Catholicism (c. 589) and the gradual Lombard conversion shifted the dynamic. The Lombard kingdom was ultimately conquered by Charlemagne (774) at papal request.

The Carolingian family (Major-domos/Mayors of the Palace) gradually displaced the Merovingian dynasty from effective power, beginning with Pepin II's victory at the Battle of Tertry (687). Charles Martel governed as the real power under nominal Merovingian kings, famously refusing to have himself crowned king. His son Pippin III (751) deposed the last Merovingian king Childeric III with papal approval, had himself anointed king by the papacy, and founded the Carolingian dynasty. The transition was careful to maintain legitimacy: Pippin obtained papal sanction, and Childeric was merely tonsured and sent to a monastery rather than executed.

Milan evolved from a self-governing commune (from the late 11th century) to a Signoria under the Visconti family (from 1277), then to a formal duchy when Emperor Wenceslaus granted Gian Galeazzo Visconti the ducal title (1395). The commune's institutions — consuls, the podestà system — were gradually replaced by Visconti autocracy. After Filippo Maria Visconti's death (1447), a brief Ambrosian Republic (1447–1450) tried to restore communal government; Francesco Sforza's conquest (1450) created the Sforza duchy that dominated Lombardy until 1499.

Moldavia became an Ottoman tributary after Stephen the Great's reign (ruled 1457–1504), despite his earlier resistance — he defeated Ottoman armies at Vaslui (1475) and Racova (1476), receiving the title 'Athlete of Christ' from Pope Sixtus IV. After Stephen's death, Moldavia accepted Ottoman suzerainty while maintaining internal self-governance. Moldavian princes paid annual tribute (haraç) and provided military contingents but retained their Orthodox Church, their legal system, and the right to elect (subject to Ottoman approval) their own rulers. This 'autonomous tributary' model preserved Moldavian culture through 300+ years of Ottoman suzerainty.

Moldavia acknowledged Polish suzerainty periodically from the mid-14th century onward, with Moldavian princes sometimes paying homage to Polish kings. Stephen the Great (1457–1504) maintained the most complex multi-directional diplomacy: fighting the Ottomans (Vaslui, 1475), acknowledging Polish suzerainty (Treaty of Kolomea, 1485), and seeking Western crusade support simultaneously. Poland's protection was unreliable — it failed to prevent Ottoman tributary imposition — but Moldavian princes used the Polish connection as diplomatic leverage and occasionally as a source of military support against internal rivals.

Hulagu Khan sacks Baghdad (February 1258), executing the last Abbasid Caliph al-Musta'sim; the 500-year Abbasid Caliphate ends. The event is considered one of the most devastating in Islamic history; the House of Wisdom is destroyed and the irrigation systems of Mesopotamia irreparably damaged.

The Mongol invasion of Hungary (1241) under Batu Khan and Subutai destroyed approximately 20–50% of Hungary's population through battle, massacre, and famine. King Béla IV fled to a Dalmatian island; the Mongols occupied the Hungarian plain. Only news of Ögedei Khan's death (1241) caused the Mongol withdrawal in spring 1242. Béla IV spent the remainder of his reign rebuilding Hungary: granting noble privileges, building stone castles, settling Cumans and other nomadic peoples as military colonists. The rebuilt Hungary successfully resisted a second Mongol invasion (1285).

The Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus (1237–1240) under Batu Khan and Subutai was the most destructive event in Russian medieval history. Ryazan fell in December 1237, Vladimir in February 1238, Kiev in December 1240. Estimates suggest 50–80% of urban populations were killed; the archaeological record shows destruction layers in virtually every Rus city. The Mongol 'yoke' that followed (1240–1480) imposed annual tribute, census-taking, and the use of Mongol administrative systems (the decimal military unit structure). The invasion permanently shifted the demographic center of Russian civilization northward.

Two major Mongol invasions devastated Poland (1241, 1259–1260) but failed to produce permanent occupation. The first invasion destroyed Kraków and Wrocław, killing Duke Henry II of Silesia at the Battle of Legnica; the second looted large areas of Lesser Poland. Unlike Russia, Poland experienced the invasions as devastating raids rather than permanent conquest and tribute extraction. Duke Bolesław V 'the Chaste' rebuilt Kraków with a formal municipal charter (1257) immediately after the first invasion. The invasions fragmented Poland into competing principalities for another century, delaying Piast reunification until Władysław I (1320).

The Despotate of the Morea was established by Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos after the Byzantine restoration (1261) as a province governed by imperial princes (often sons of the emperor). From its initial base at Mystras, the Despotate gradually expanded to reclaim the Peloponnese from the Crusader Principality of Achaea. The Despotate became the most culturally vibrant part of the late Byzantine Empire: the Mystras court under the Palaiologos family hosted humanist scholars (Gemistos Plethon, George Scholarios) whose ideas influenced the Italian Renaissance. The Ottomans conquered it in 1460.

The Khanate of Kazan — founded when Ulugh Muhammad broke from the Golden Horde (1438) and established himself at Kazan on the middle Volga — became Moscow's most persistent eastern opponent in the 15th century. Moscow and Kazan fought repeatedly over control of the Volga trade route and the loyalty of the Mari, Chuvash, and Mordvin peoples of the middle Volga. Moscow suffered serious defeats (Ivan III's defeat at the Oka, 1469; the 1521 Kazan raid that reached Moscow). Kazan was finally conquered by Ivan IV 'the Terrible' in 1552 — the first major Russian expansion east of the Volga.

Vasili III of Moscow annexed the Republic of Pskov (1510) by summoning its posadniki (mayors) to Moscow, arresting them, and abolishing the veche (popular assembly). Pskov — which had maintained republican self-government like Novgorod, though less wealthy — had been a loyal ally of Moscow against Novgorod and the Teutonic Order. Its annexation completed Moscow's control of northwestern Russia. Three hundred Pskovian noble families were deported and replaced with Muscovite settlers, following the same pattern used in Novgorod (1478).

Tver — Moscow's chief rival for supremacy over northeastern Russia throughout the 14th and early 15th centuries — was finally annexed by Ivan III in 1485 after a military expedition supported by the defection of Tver's own boyars. The last Tver prince, Michael Borisovich, fled to Lithuania. With Novgorod (1478) and Tver (1485) both absorbed, Moscow controlled virtually all of northeastern Russia. Ivan III's title shifted to 'Sovereign of All Russia' — a claim that defined Russian territorial ambitions for the next century.

Moscow and Tver competed for dominance over northeastern Russia for nearly a century (1304–1408), with both claiming the title of Grand Prince of Vladimir and the Golden Horde's patent (yarlyk) to collect tribute. The rivalry involved alternating alliances with the Horde: when Moscow's prince held the patent, he used it to accumulate territory; when Tver's prince held it, he did likewise. Dmitry Donskoy's victory at Kulikovo (1380) and Moscow's collaboration in suppressing Tver's anti-Mongol revolt (1327) finally broke Tver's capacity for competition; Ivan III's conquest of Tver (1485) ended the rivalry definitively.

Munster (southern Ireland) was the province from which Brian Boru rose to challenge the Uí Néill monopoly on the High Kingship. Brian Boru of the Dál Cais clan within Munster became King of Munster, then High King of Ireland after forcing Mael Sechnaill II's submission (1002). His death at Clontarf (1014) — the battle he won — prevented the consolidation of a hereditary Irish monarchy. After Brian, Munster split into Thomond and Desmond, with the high kingship contested between Leinster (Diarmait Mac Murchada) and Connacht (Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair) before the Anglo-Norman conquest ended effective native Irish high kingship.

The Kingdom of Naples (the Angevin mainland kingdom of Sicily) and Florence maintained generally cooperative relations based on Florentine banking finance for Angevin military operations and Florence's dependence on Neapolitan grain. The Bardi and Peruzzi banking companies' massive loans to King Robert of Naples (1309–1343) — and their subsequent default when Robert's successor could not repay them — caused the greatest banking collapse in medieval Europe (1342–1343), temporarily destroying Florence's financial system. The later Aragonese Kingdom of Naples (from 1442) and the Medicis reached pragmatic accommodation within the Italian League (1455).

Navarre and Aragon were united under Sancho III 'the Great' of Pamplona (1004–1035), who also controlled Castile and León temporarily — the closest medieval Iberia came to a single Christian kingdom before Ferdinand and Isabella. His death produced the familiar disaster: partition among sons. Aragon (under Ramiro I) and Navarre (under García III) became separate kingdoms that only reunited briefly under Alfonso I 'the Battler' (ruled both 1104–1134). Alfonso I's death without heirs permanently separated them: Aragon passed to Ramon Berenguer IV through marriage; Navarre elected García Ramírez.

Navarre and Castile competed along the upper Ebro/Rioja frontier from the 10th through 13th centuries, with control of the Rioja wine-producing region and the Basque provinces (Álava, Guipúzcoa, Vizcaya) periodically contested. Navarrese kings of the Jiménez dynasty (including Sancho III 'the Great,' 1004–1035, who briefly united most of Christian Iberia) gave way to Castilian dominance after Navarrese-Castilian wars in the 1060s–70s. Navarre lost the Rioja to Alfonso VI of Castile (1076) and subsequently oriented northward toward France; Navarre's French dynastic connections from 1234 onward aligned it with France rather than Castile.

The Empire of Nicaea and the splinter Kingdom of Thessalonica (established by Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epirus after his capture of the city in 1224) were competing Byzantine successor states. John III Vatatzes of Nicaea invaded Thessalonica, captured Theodore's nephew Manuel (1242), and forced the Thessalonican court to accept Nicaean imperial precedence (renouncing their imperial title for the lesser title of 'despot'). Nicaea subsequently absorbed Thessalonica (1246) under John III, eliminating the last separate Epirote/Thessalonican claim to Byzantine imperial succession.

The Norman Conquest (1066) created an inseparable link between the Duchy of Normandy and the Kingdom of England: William I and his heirs ruled both simultaneously. The relationship created the 'English problem' in French feudal law — the King of England was simultaneously a vassal of the French crown for Normandy. This dual status generated permanent tension: English kings built military resources in England to defend or recover their French possessions; the French crown treated English kings' French fiefs as a permanent source of legal leverage. The dynamic drove Anglo-French relations for 150 years until Philip II Augustus conquered Normandy (1204).

Normandy — held by English kings as a French fief since the Norman Conquest (1066) — was lost by King John after Philip II Augustus declared his fiefs forfeit (1202) and besieged Château Gaillard (1203–1204). The fall of Rouen (June 1204) completed the conquest. Normandy's absorption doubled the French royal domain and gave Philip II access to the Channel coast. The Duchy was granted to the King's sons periodically but returned to the crown in 1468 when Louis XI confiscated it from his brother Charles. Normandy's cultural and administrative traditions — including common law elements — continued to influence French governance.

The Kingdom of Dál Riata (a Gaelic kingdom straddling the Irish Sea between northeastern Ireland and western Scotland) competed and occasionally cooperated with Northumbria, the dominant Anglo-Saxon kingdom of northern Britain. The pivotal moment was the Battle of Mag Roth (637, Ireland) and the subsequent Battle of Strathcarron (642), which effectively divided Dál Riata's Irish and Scottish parts. Northumbrian expansion under Oswald and Oswiu brought Anglian political influence to the Firth of Forth; the Synod of Whitby (664) resolved the Celtic-Roman Christian tension that had defined the Northumbrian-Dál Riatan cultural intersection.

The Viking Kingdom of Jorvik (York) emerged within the former Kingdom of Northumbria when the Great Heathen Army captured York (866) and established a Norse kingdom there. Northumbria's native English aristocracy was largely killed or displaced; subsequent Jorvik kings alternated between Norse (Halfdan Ragnarsson, Sigurd, Eric Bloodaxe) and Anglo-Danish rulers. The kingdom's instability — six kings in 20 years during the 940s-950s — reflected the competition between Viking factions and the Wessex reconquest campaign. Eric Bloodaxe's death (954) ended Jorvik and merged Northumbria into the English kingdom.

Cnut the Great (ruled 1016–1035) assembled the North Sea Empire — England, Denmark, Norway, and nominally parts of Sweden — the largest empire in Northern Europe since the Romans. Cnut's empire linked the Viking and Anglo-Saxon worlds: he governed England with Anglo-Saxon institutions while maintaining Scandinavian kingship networks. The empire dissolved on his death (1035) through inheritance disputes among his sons. Harold Harefoot (England) and Sweyn (Norway) died young; Harthacnut's death (1042) ended the Danish line and restored the Wessex dynasty under Edward the Confessor.

Novgorod and Sweden competed for control of Finland and the eastern Baltic coastline throughout the 12th–14th centuries. Swedish expansion into Finland (the Swedish crusades, 1157–1293) and their fortress at Vyborg (1293) brought them into direct conflict with Novgorod's fur-trade tributary zone. Alexander Nevsky's victory over Swedish forces at the Battle of the Neva (1240) — which earned him his epithet 'Nevsky' (of the Neva) — temporarily halted Swedish expansion. The border between Swedish Finland and Novgorodian Karelia was formalized in the Peace of Nöteborg (1323), which divided Karelia between the two powers.

The Orkney Islands were settled by Norse Vikings in the late 9th century and governed as a Norwegian earldom. The Earls of Orkney — notably Sigurd the Stout (d. 1014, killed at Clontarf) and later the canonized Magnus Erlendsson — maintained a culturally rich Norse society that produced the Orkneyinga Saga. Norwegian royal authority over Orkney was periodically asserted but practically limited. The islands were pawned to Scotland in 1468–1469 when King Christian I was unable to pay his daughter's dowry, ending 600 years of Norse sovereignty.

The Orkney and Shetland Islands — Norwegian possessions since Viking settlement in the 9th century — were pawned to Scotland in 1468–1469 by King Christian I of Denmark-Norway as security for his daughter Margaret's dowry (for her marriage to King James III of Scotland). The pledge was never redeemed; Scotland absorbed the islands permanently. The transfer completed Scotland's territorial consolidation of the northern isles and ended Norwegian dominion over the Hebrides-Orkney region that the Treaty of Perth (1266) had begun. Shetland and Orkney retained Norse customary law (Udal law) for centuries.

The Principality of Achaea (the Morea/Peloponnese) was a Latin crusader state established after the Fourth Crusade (1204). The Byzantine Despotate of the Morea gradually recovered much of the Peloponnese from the Latins throughout the 14th–15th centuries. When Mehmed II's Ottoman forces invaded in 1460, the Despotate — already weakened by internal conflicts between the brothers Demetrios and Thomas Palaiologos — offered minimal resistance. The Peloponnese was absorbed into the Ottoman Empire; the remaining Latin principality (Venetian Nauplion and Modon) held out longer.

The Florentine Acciaiuoli family had ruled Athens as a duchy since 1388. Mehmed II's army besieged Athens in 1456; the Acropolis fell in June 1458. Athens became an Ottoman provincial town; the Parthenon was converted to a mosque. The last Latin duke of Athens, Franco Acciaiuoli, was executed. Mehmed II visited Athens and reportedly admired its ancient monuments. The city's population had dwindled to a few thousand by this point, a shadow of its ancient and Byzantine greatness.

Bosnia was conquered by Mehmed II in 1463 in a rapid 8-day campaign. King Stephen Tomašević — who had just refused to pay tribute — was captured and beheaded. The speed of the conquest shocked European observers; Bosnia had briefly appealed for Western help that never arrived. Many Bosnian nobility converted to Islam to retain their estates — creating the Bosnian Muslim community that persists to the present day. Herzegovina (under Stjepan Vukčić Kosača) held out until 1482.

The Second Bulgarian Empire fell to the Ottomans in stages: Tarnovo (the capital) fell in 1393, and the last Bulgarian tsardom — centered at Vidin under Ivan Sratsimir — was conquered after the Battle of Nicopolis (1396). Bulgaria remained under direct Ottoman administration for nearly 500 years (until 1878), the longest period of any Balkan nation under Ottoman rule. The Bulgarian church (the Patriarchate of Tarnovo) was suppressed and subordinated to the Greek Patriarchate of Constantinople.

The Byzantine Despotate of the Morea (the Peloponnese) — ruled by the brothers Demetrios and Thomas Palaiologos — fell to Mehmed II's invasion in 1460. The brothers had been fighting each other rather than organizing a defense; Demetrios surrendered and was given a pension; Thomas fled to Rome. The Peloponnese became an Ottoman province. Thomas Palaiologos carried the relic of St. Andrew's head and the claim of Byzantine imperial title to Rome, where his descendants maintained the nominal title of Byzantine emperors.

The Serbian Despotate — successor to the Serbian Empire after the fragmentation following Emperor Stefan Dušan's death (1355) — became an Ottoman vassal after Kosovo (1389) and the Ottomans gradually absorbed it over the following decades. The Battle of Kosovo (1448) sealed Serbian subjugation. The Despotate's capital Smederevo fell in 1459, seven years after Constantinople. With Serbian independence gone, the Ottomans controlled the entire western Balkans from the Danube to the Adriatic.

The Empire of Trebizond — the last surviving Byzantine successor state, ruled by the Komnenos dynasty since 1204 — was conquered by Mehmed II in August 1461, eight years after Constantinople. Mehmed blockaded the harbor while his army advanced through the Pontic Alps. Emperor David Komnenos surrendered after a month; he was later executed despite promises of safety. Mehmed II claimed the title 'Caesar of Rome' after both conquests, completing the elimination of all Greek Christian imperial states.

The relationship between the papacy and the Holy Roman Empire oscillated between the cooperative model (Ottonian era: the emperor protects the papacy, the papacy legitimizes the emperor), the catastrophic conflict of the Investiture Controversy (1076–1122), a renewed but unstable cooperation (Crusades), and the existential pope-emperor conflict under Frederick II (1239–1250). The fundamental tension — who holds ultimate authority in Latin Christendom — was never resolved: the papacy's greatest victories (Walk to Canossa 1077, deposition of Frederick II 1245) were matched by imperial resilience; the empire's greatest victories (Synod of Worms 1076, antipopes) were checked by papal ingenuity.

Pope Urban II's call at Clermont (1095) and the subsequent success of the First Crusade created the Kingdom of Jerusalem as a papal project, with successive popes claiming overlordship. Jerusalem's kings held their crown as vassals of the Pope, a claim the papacy consistently maintained even when the crusader kings ignored it. Pope Innocent III's insistence on controlling the Fourth Crusade (which he failed to do) and the Fifth Crusade (which he tried to micromanage) demonstrates the papacy's sense of proprietary interest in the crusader enterprise. The papacy recognized Jerusalem's succession rules and intervened in disputed elections.

Pope Nicholas II's recognition of Robert Guiscard as the papacy's vassal for his Italian conquests (1059) established the fundamental constitutional framework for the Norman relationship with Rome. The papacy received military protection against imperial and local enemies; the Normans received papal legitimacy for their conquests and a free hand to organize the church in Norman-controlled territories. This arrangement worked spectacularly well for the Investiture Controversy era — the Normans rescued Gregory VII from Henry IV's siege (1084). When the Hohenstaufen inherited the Norman kingdom (1194), this useful military alliance became the papacy's worst nightmare.

Afonso Henriques, Count of Portugal (from 1128), sought papal recognition of Portuguese royal dignity to legitimize his independence from León. After defeating the Moors at the Battle of Ourique (1139) and proclaiming himself king, he placed Portugal under papal protection, paying an annual tribute (the 'denarius Sancti Petri'). Pope Alexander III formally recognized Portugal as a kingdom (1179) in the bull Manifestis Probatum. The papal recognition was Portugal's international legitimization and protection against Leonese absorption — a model similar to the earlier Polish appeal to the papacy for protection from German crusading.

Pope Nicholas II recognized Robert Guiscard and his Norman brothers as vassals of the papacy for their Italian and Sicilian conquests (1059), transforming the Normans from opportunistic warlords into papal champions. The arrangement was mutually beneficial: the Normans gained legitimacy for their conquests; the papacy gained a powerful military ally against the Holy Roman Empire. Roger I's conquest of Muslim Sicily (1061–1091) was conducted under papal blessing. The Papal-Norman alliance fundamentally altered Italian politics — the Normans protected Rome from imperial pressure during the Investiture Controversy.

Pope Stephen II's anointing of Pippin III and his sons as 'Kings of the Franks and Patricians of the Romans' (754) — repeated by Pope Hadrian I at Charlemagne's coronation (781) and culminating in Leo III's imperial coronation (800) — established the principle that papal anointing legitimized royal and imperial authority. The Carolingians reciprocated with the Donation of Pippin (756) and military protection of Rome. This exchange created the political theology of medieval Europe: royal/imperial authority derives from God through the Church, making the pope the gatekeeper of legitimate secular power. The Investiture Controversy was the inevitable consequence.

The Ottonian emperors (Otto I, II, III, Henry II) and the papacy developed a cooperative model in which the emperor protected and reformed the papacy while the pope consecrated the emperor and supported imperial ecclesiastical policy. Otto I deposed corrupt popes (John XII, Leo VIII) and appointed replacements; Pope Sylvester II (Gerbert of Aurillac, elected with Otto III's support) was the most intellectually distinguished pope of the 10th century. The system worked because both sides benefited from cooperation; it broke down under the reforming popes of the mid-11th century who rejected imperial control of papal appointments.

The Pechenegs — Turkic nomads occupying the Pontic steppe after destroying the Khazar Khaganate (965) — became one of Byzantium's most dangerous neighbors in the 10th–11th centuries. They served as Byzantine mercenaries and intermediaries with Rus, but also raided Byzantine Thrace repeatedly. Emperor Basil II's policy of buying Pecheneg neutrality through tribute and diplomatic manipulation became increasingly expensive. Emperor Isaac I Komnenos fought them (1059); Emperor Romanos IV lost at Manzikert (1071) while distracted by simultaneous Pecheneg pressure in Europe. Emperor Alexios I finally crushed the Pechenegs at the Battle of Levounion (1091) with Cuman allies.

The Pechenegs — Turkic nomads who occupied the Pontic steppe after the Khazar Khaganate's collapse — were Kiev's most dangerous steppe neighbors in the late 10th century. They besieged Kiev in 968 (forcing Sviatoslav I to return from his Balkan campaigns); they killed Sviatoslav himself at the Dnieper rapids (972) during his return from Bulgaria. Prince Vladimir I (980–1015) built a defensive line of fortresses along the Steppe border. His son Yaroslav 'the Wise' decisively defeated the Pechenegs in 1036, after which they largely dissolved as a political force, replaced by the Cumans.
Union of Pictish and Dál Riatan realms under Kenneth MacAlpin narrative; boundaries disputed in scholarship.

The Pictish kingdoms of northeastern Scotland (Fortriu, Ce, Fidach, and others) suffered devastating Viking raids beginning in the late 8th century — the monasteries of Iona (raided 795, 802, 806) were the most famous targets but Pictish coastal settlements were also hit. The pressures from Norse settlement in Orkney and Shetland (from c. 800) and Norse-Irish raids on the western coast squeezed Pictish territories. Norse settlement in the northern isles fundamentally altered Pictish culture in those regions; the Norse place-name layer in Orkney and Shetland (nearly 100% Norse) reflects the completeness of the displacement.

Pisa and Genoa competed as rival maritime cities in the western Mediterranean, particularly for control of Corsica and Sardinia. The defining conflict was the Battle of Meloria (1284), in which a Genoese fleet decisively defeated the Pisan fleet; thousands of Pisan sailors were taken prisoner (they were kept in Genoa for years — the Genoese saying was 'to see Pisa, go to Genoa'). Meloria ended Pisa's status as a major naval power; Genoa took control of Corsica, and Pisa subsequently came under Florentine influence. Pisa's distinctive architectural achievements (Leaning Tower, baptistery) reflect the commercial wealth of its 11th–12th century prime.

Pisa developed commercial and political interests in Sardinia beginning in the 11th century, competing with Genoa for influence over the four indigenous giudicati. Pisa's influence was strongest in Cagliari and Gallura (southeastern Sardinia) through dynastic marriages with the giudici families. The commercial concessions Pisa extracted — reduced port duties, trading posts — gave Pisan merchants privileged access to Sardinian silver and agricultural exports. After the Battle of Meloria (1284) broke Pisan naval power, Pisan influence in Sardinia waned rapidly; Genoese pressure and eventual Aragonese conquest (1323) ended Pisan commercial presence.

After the decisive Jagiellonian victory at Grunwald (1410), the Teutonic Order's military power was permanently broken. The subsequent Thirteen Years' War (1454–1466) — fought with Polish-Lithuanian support for the Prussian Confederation of cities that revolted against the Order — ended with the Second Peace of Thorn (1466): the Order ceded Royal Prussia to Poland (including Danzig/Gdańsk and the Vistula corridor) and became a Polish vassal for the remaining Ducal Prussia. The Order's last Prussian grand master, Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach, converted to Lutheranism (1525) and secularized the remaining territory as the Duchy of Prussia.

The Piast Polish kings competed with the Teutonic Order for control of Pomerania and later Samogitia (Lithuanian territory claimed by the Order) throughout the 13th–14th centuries. Władysław I 'the Short' unified fragmented Poland (1320) and immediately challenged the Order, winning the famous lawsuit at the papal court of Avignon (1320–1321) that granted Poland reparations — never collected. The Piast conflict with the Order established the territorial claims that the Jagiellonians later enforced militarily. The loss of Danzig/Gdańsk to the Order (1308) was the grievance that drove Polish policy toward the Order for 150 years.

Portugal and Castile were in periodic conflict throughout the medieval period over the Tagus-Douro borderlands, the direction of the Reconquista, and dynastic succession claims. Portugal (independent from 1139 under Afonso Henriques) pressed its Reconquista southward independently, completing it in 1249 (Afonso III's capture of the Algarve) — decades before Castile finished. Successive succession crises (1383–1385, 1580) brought the two crowns into conflict and eventually union: Philip II of Spain inherited Portugal (1580) through his mother, uniting the Iberian crowns until the Portuguese Restoration (1640).

Ragusa (Dubrovnik) existed within the Byzantine sphere of influence as a duchy under the Theme of Dalmatia until the 12th century. Byzantine cultural influence is visible in Ragusa's Orthodox community and its Greek-influenced legal practices. When Venice gained Ragusa under the Treaty of Zadar (1204, confirmed 1205), Byzantine influence waned. The city's sophisticated diplomatic tradition — maintaining simultaneous relations with multiple great powers — developed partly from its Byzantine administrative heritage and its position as a crossroads between Latin and Orthodox worlds.

Ragusa (Dubrovnik) transferred from Venetian to Hungarian overlordship under the Treaty of Zadar (1358), paying an annual tribute to the Hungarian crown in exchange for protection and commercial privileges in Hungarian-controlled Adriatic ports. Hungarian overlordship was far lighter than Venetian — the Hungarians had no commercial fleet to compete with Ragusan merchants — giving Ragusa effective independence while maintaining nominal vassalage. This arrangement lasted until the Ottoman threat and Venice's power made renewed accommodation with Venice more practical (1420, temporarily) and with the Ottomans thereafter.

Ragusa (Dubrovnik) began paying annual tribute to the Ottoman Empire (initially 1,500 ducats, rising to 12,500 ducats by the 16th century) in exchange for trading privileges throughout Ottoman-controlled territories. This arrangement — tribute in exchange for commercial access — was Ragusa's defining diplomatic achievement: paying Ottoman tribute while maintaining Christian sovereignty, Venetian and Papal recognition, and commercial networks that extended from Alexandria to London. The Republic maintained this position until French conquest (1808) by playing overlords against each other with extraordinary skill.

Venice acquired Ragusa under the Treaty of Zadar (1205) following the Fourth Crusade, maintaining overlordship until 1358 when the Treaty of Zadar (1358) transferred Ragusa to the Kingdom of Hungary-Croatia. Venetian rule gave Ragusa its commercial infrastructure (the Fondaco system, standardized weights and measures) but also subjected it to unfavorable trade restrictions. Ragusa's eventual break from Venice — achieved through Hungarian overlordship — gave it the greater commercial freedom that enabled its 15th-century golden age.

The Sultanate of Rum occupied territory that Byzantium considered its heartland; the two states competed for Anatolia for two centuries. Byzantine attempts to reconquer the Anatolian plateau failed at Myriokephalon (1176). The Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople (1204) temporarily reduced Byzantine pressure on Rum.

The Counts, then Dukes, of Savoy held their Alpine territories as imperial vassals, controlling the vital Alpine passes (Mont Cenis, Great St. Bernard) that were the primary routes between France, Germany, and Italy. This strategic position made Savoy indispensable to imperial policy: emperors crossing the Alps to Italy needed Savoyard cooperation. Savoy's count was elevated to Duke by Emperor Sigismund (1416). The duchy's position between France and the Empire gave it permanent diplomatic significance — playing French and imperial ambitions against each other — that belied its small size.

Saxony was the most powerful of the five German stem duchies, its territory extending from the Rhineland to the Elbe, with the Saxon dukes directing the Christian mission into Slavic lands to the east. The Ottonian dynasty (Henry I, Otto I, Otto II, Otto III, Henry II) was Saxon, making Saxony the origin of the medieval German kingdom and the Holy Roman Empire. Henry the Lion's downfall (1180) — stripped of both Saxony and Bavaria by Frederick Barbarossa — split the duchy; the eastern half became the new Duchy of Saxony (Wittenberg branch); the western half remained with local counts. The Wettin dynasty eventually acquired the eastern Saxon title.

Anglo-Scottish relations from the Norman Conquest (1066) through the medieval period were defined by English attempts at dominance and Scottish resistance. The Wars of Scottish Independence (1296–1357) — triggered by Edward I's attempt to make Scotland an English vassal — produced William Wallace, Robert Bruce, and the Declaration of Arbroath (1320). The 1328 Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton recognized Scottish independence. The 'Auld Alliance' with France defined Scottish policy throughout the Hundred Years' War. Periodic warfare continued until the Union of Crowns (1603).

The Auld Alliance (the 'Old Alliance' between Scotland and France, traditionally dated to 1295) was the defining axis of Scottish foreign policy for over 200 years. Formally renewed multiple times, the Alliance provided Scotland with French diplomatic support and occasional military assistance against English pressure; France received Scottish military manpower for service in the French army (the Scots Guard, established 1418, protected French kings personally until 1830). The Alliance peaked when Scots fought at Baugé (1421) and the Hundred Years' War; it faded after the Scottish Reformation (1560) aligned Scotland with Protestant England.

Seljuk expansion into Armenia and Anatolia brought the sultanate into sustained conflict with Byzantium. Manzikert (1071) was the decisive moment: the capture of Emperor Romanos IV opened Anatolia to Turkic settlement. Byzantine Emperor Manuel I's defeat at Myriokephalon (1176) ended any prospect of reconquest.

The Sultanate of Rum emerges from the Great Seljuk Empire as an autonomous branch ruling Anatolia ('Rum' = Roman, i.e., Byzantine lands); grows fully independent after the fragmentation of the Great Seljuk Empire following Malik Shah's death (1092).

Bosnia maintained a complex tributary relationship with the Serbian Kingdom and later Empire for much of the 12th–14th centuries. Serbian kings claimed suzerainty over Bosnian bans; Bosnia operated with considerable autonomy in practice, its Christian identity distinct from both Catholic and Orthodox norms (the 'Bosnian Church,' whose exact nature is debated). Stefan Dušan's expansion (1340s) incorporated Bosnia into the Serbian imperial sphere, but after his death (1355) Bosnia regained independence and expanded under Ban Tvrtko I, who crowned himself King of Bosnia and Serbia (1377), claiming Serbian royal heritage.

Stefan Dušan's Serbian Empire (1346–1355) disintegrated rapidly after his death, fragmenting into regional lords — the most important being the Mrnjavčević brothers (controlling Macedonia), the Dejanović family, and eventually the Lazarević family's Serbian Despotate centered on Belgrade. Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović reassembled much of Serbia into a functioning state, only to die at Kosovo (1389). His son Stefan Lazarević became a Serbian Despot (1402) under Byzantine suzerainty — also serving as an Ottoman vassal. The Despotate's capital Smederevo fell in 1459, ending Serbian statehood for 360 years.

Stefan Dušan — the most powerful Serbian ruler — transformed the Serbian Kingdom into an empire through rapid military conquests of Byzantine Macedonia, Albania, and Epirus (1334–1345). He crowned himself 'Emperor and Autocrat of the Serbs and Greeks' at Skopje on Easter 1346, establishing a Serbian patriarchate (previously subordinate to Constantinople) at the same ceremony. Dušan's law code (Zakonik, 1349) codified Serbian customary law on Byzantine models. His empire — the largest state in the Balkans — collapsed within a decade of his death (1355) as regional magnates asserted independence against his weaker successors.

The Serbian Nemanjić dynasty and the Bulgarian tsardom competed for Balkan hegemony and Byzantine succession throughout the 13th–14th centuries. Stefan Nemanja allied with the Bulgarians against Byzantium; his successors alternately competed and cooperated with Bulgaria. Stefan Dušan's conquest of much of Bulgaria's western Macedonian territories (1330s) as part of his Balkan empire-building directly weakened Bulgaria before the Ottoman advance. The Bulgarian-Serbian competition prevented Balkan Christian unity and created the fragmented political landscape that the Ottomans exploited.

Serbia and Bulgaria competed as rival Orthodox Christian empires in the Balkans throughout the 12th–14th centuries, both claiming succession to Byzantine imperial prestige. The competition was partly military (Bulgarian Tsar Kaloyan captured a Latin emperor; Serbian Tsar Stefan Dušan proclaimed himself 'Tsar of the Serbs and Greeks') and partly cultural (competing patriarchates, competing styles of Byzantine court culture). Stefan Dušan's rapid conquest of Bulgaria's western territories (1330s) and his claim to the imperial title (1346) represented Serbia's peak; Bulgaria's simultaneous fragmentation into rival tsardoms left neither state able to resist the Ottomans.

The Kingdom of Sicily passed from the Norman Hauteville dynasty to the Hohenstaufen (Staufen) when Constance — the posthumous daughter of Roger II of Sicily and heiress of the Norman kingdom — married Henry VI of Germany (1186). Henry VI conquered Sicily (1194) despite resistance; their son Frederick II was raised in Sicily and became Emperor Frederick II — simultaneously Holy Roman Emperor and King of Sicily/Naples. The union of imperial and Sicilian power was the papacy's greatest nightmare: encirclement of the Papal States. It drove the catastrophic pope-emperor conflict (1239–1250).

Siena and Florence were rival Tuscan city-states with competing banking families, trade routes, and political allegiances — Florence was Guelf, Siena predominantly Ghibelline. Siena won the most famous battle between them at Montaperti (1260), where the Florentines were catastrophically defeated (the Arbia river 'ran red,' in Dante's words). Siena never followed up its military advantage; Florence recovered, and the Guelf victory throughout Italy (after Benevento, 1266) marginalized Siena's Ghibelline alignment. The Black Death (1348) hit Siena disproportionately hard, killing perhaps half the population and preventing the completion of its cathedral expansion.

The Duchy of Spoleto — a Lombard duchy in central Italy that survived the Carolingian conquest of the main Lombard kingdom (774) — maintained a complex, often hostile relationship with the papacy and a gradually evolving one with the Carolingian/imperial overlords. Situated between Rome and northern Italy, Spoleto periodically threatened the papacy, served as a buffer against other Lombard principalities, and was granted to various imperial supporters. Pope Innocent III incorporated Spoleto into the Papal States (1198) through a combination of political maneuvering and imperial weakness during the Staufen succession crisis.

Pope Innocent III, exploiting the Staufen succession crisis (1197–1209) during which the rival claimants Philip of Swabia and Otto IV were both seeking papal recognition, reasserted papal control over the duchy of Spoleto and other territories of the 'Patrimony of Peter.' By 1198–1200, Innocent III had incorporated Spoleto into the Papal States, citing the Donation of Charlemagne and the prior claims of the papacy. The incorporation was part of Innocent III's broader assertion of papal temporal sovereignty that made him the most powerful pope in medieval history.

The Angevin conquest of the Kingdom of Sicily (Naples and Sicily) from the Hohenstaufen followed papal invitation and French military support. Charles of Anjou defeated and killed Manfred (Battle of Benevento, 1266) and then Conradin (Battle of Tagliacozzo, 1268). The Angevin Kingdom of Naples (as the mainland part came to be known after the Sicilian Vespers separated the island) was the wealthiest state in the Italian peninsula. Charles I of Anjou's aggressive Mediterranean ambitions — attempting to recreate an Angevin empire from Naples to Constantinople — provoked the Vespers reaction (1282) that permanently split the kingdom.

The Kingdom of Strathclyde (Brythonic/Welsh-speaking kingdom of the Clyde Valley, centered on Dumbarton Rock) maintained a gradually subordinate relationship to the Kingdom of Alba (the emerging Gaelic-Pictish Scottish kingdom) throughout the 9th–10th centuries. After the Viking destruction of Dumbarton (870), Strathclyde came under increasing Alba influence. The kingdom passed to Constantine II of Alba's grandson (c. 890) and was effectively an appanage of the Scottish crown by the early 10th century, finally absorbed under Malcolm II (1018). Its absorption gave Scotland control of the Clyde Valley and the border with Northumbrian England.
Brythonic Strathclyde absorbed into expanding Scottish realm over eleventh century; dates approximate.

Styria (the Steiermark) emerged as a separate imperial march from Carinthia in the late 10th century, elevated to a duchy in 1180 (by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa). Duke Ottokar IV of Styria, dying without heirs, bequeathed Styria to Duke Leopold V of Austria in the Georgenberg Pact (1186). Habsburgs definitively acquired Styria in 1282 when Rudolf I partitioned the Austrian territories among his sons. Combined with Austria and Carinthia, Styria formed the 'Inner Austrian' core of the Habsburg domain, providing the dynasty with iron deposits from the Erzberg — the richest iron mine in medieval Europe.

The Suebian Kingdom of Galicia (northwestern Iberia), established by the Suebi (Sueves) after the 409 crossing of the Rhine, was absorbed by the Visigothic Kingdom under Leovigild's conquest (585). The Suebi had converted to Catholic Christianity under Bishop Martin of Braga (c. 550–580) — one of the earliest Germanic Catholic conversions — before their conquest by the Arian Visigoths. Their territory (roughly modern Galicia and northern Portugal) was incorporated as a province, but the Galician provincial identity persisted through the Visigothic period and the subsequent Arab conquest.

Swabia was one of the five original stem duchies of the East Frankish/German kingdom, its dukes holding key strategic territory in the southwest — the upper Rhine, Lake Constance, and the Alpine passes. The Hohenstaufen family gained Swabia in 1079 (through Frederick I's marriage to Agnes, daughter of Emperor Henry IV) and used it as the base for their imperial dynasty. After the Hohenstaufen extinction (Conradin, 1268), the duchy fragmented: no new duke was appointed, and Swabia's territory was gradually absorbed by the Habsburgs, the Swiss Confederation, and various lesser princes.

Charles the Bold of Burgundy's attempt to build a coherent territorial state between France and the Empire brought him into conflict with the Swiss Confederation, which saw Burgundian expansion as an existential threat. The Wars of Burgundy (1474–1477) produced three decisive battles — Grandson, Murten, and Nancy — in which Swiss pike formations annihilated Burgundian cavalry and artillery. Charles the Bold was killed at Nancy (January 5, 1477), his body found frozen in a ditch. Louis XI of France seized the Duchy of Burgundy; Charles's daughter Mary married Maximilian of Habsburg, giving the Habsburgs the Low Countries.
Swiss Confederation gradually freed itself from Habsburg/Imperial control; effective independence by Swabian War (1499).

The Swiss Confederation's expansion into the Vaud (acquired 1536) and Valais brought it into repeated conflict with the Duchy of Savoy, whose territories surrounded the Swiss cantons to the south and west. The Swiss defeated Savoy at the Battle of Laupen (1339) and in subsequent campaigns in the late 14th century. The conflict was partly about control of Alpine passes and partly about the liberation of Vaud's cities (Lausanne, Geneva) from Savoyard feudal control. The Swiss acquisition of Vaud (1536) made the Confederation the dominant power in the western Alps.

The Nasrid Emirate of Granada emerged from the third Taifa period following the Almohad collapse. Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Nasr established himself at Granada (1232), quickly absorbing Almería and Málaga to create the largest surviving Muslim state in Iberia. Granada's survival required accepting Castilian suzerainty and paying tribute (parias) — first paid to Fernando III of Castile, who used Nasrid troops against Seville (1248). The Nasrid dynasty ruled for 260 years through a combination of mountain geography, tribute diplomacy, maritime connections with Morocco, and skillful exploitation of Castilian-Aragonese competition.

The Knights Templar were founded in Jerusalem c. 1119 by Hugh de Payns and Godfrey de Saint-Omer to protect pilgrims on the dangerous roads to Jerusalem. St. Bernard of Clairvaux wrote their rule and championed their recognition at the Council of Troyes (1129). The Templars became the most powerful military order in the Crusader states — holding massive castles like Château Pèlerin — and simultaneously developed the first European banking system, allowing pilgrims to deposit money in Europe and withdraw it in the Holy Land. The Order's enormous wealth and privileges made it politically dangerous after the fall of Acre (1291).

The Livonian Order (the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, founded 1202, absorbed into the Teutonic Order 1237) controlled Livonia and Estonia — the northeastern Baltic crusading territory — as a nominally subordinate branch of the Teutonic Order. In practice, the Livonian master operated with considerable independence, as the geographic separation from Prussia made direct control difficult. The Livonian Order suffered a catastrophic defeat at the Battle of the Ice (Lake Peipus, 1242) against Alexander Nevsky's Novgorodian forces, permanently halting expansion eastward. The Order dissolved with the Livonian Confederation's collapse (1561).

The Second Peace of Thorn (October 1466) ended the Thirteen Years' War (1454–1466) by requiring the Teutonic Order to cede Royal Prussia (including Danzig/Gdańsk and the Vistula corridor) to Poland-Lithuania and to render feudal homage to the Polish king for the remaining 'Ducal Prussia.' The Order's Grand Master was obligated to swear loyalty to the Polish crown and provide military service. The provision was deeply humiliating to the Order's traditional claim of direct papal/imperial sovereignty; it was never fully accepted by the Order, which sought imperial support for its revision.

The Teutonic Order's Baltic state transformed from a crusading military order-state into a secular duchy when Grand Master Albert of Hohenzollern-Ansbach (1511–1525) converted to Lutheranism on Martin Luther's advice (1525) and secularized the remaining Ducal Prussia as a hereditary Hohenzollern duchy under Polish suzerainty. The transformation was theologically radical — the first major application of Lutheranism to state reorganization — and politically significant: the Hohenzollern Duchy of Prussia became the nucleus of the future Kingdom of Prussia that eventually unified Germany.

The Empire of Trebizond was founded by Alexios and David Komnenos in 1204 — the same year as Constantinople's fall to the Fourth Crusade — with Georgian Queen Tamar's military support. The Komnenoi claimed the Byzantine imperial title before settling on 'Emperor of the East' after Michael VIII Palaiologos's restoration of Constantinople (1261). Trebizond controlled the Black Sea port at the terminus of the Persian/Silk Road trade routes, making it commercially vital. Its survival depended on playing Mongol, Turkish, and Byzantine powers against each other through diplomacy and dynastic marriages — until the Ottomans ended it (1461).

The County of Tripoli — founded by Raymond IV of Toulouse (1105) after he failed to conquer Tripoli outright — and the Kingdom of Jerusalem maintained a close but occasionally contentious relationship throughout the 12th century. Tripoli served as the land bridge between Antioch and Jerusalem and provided critical military manpower. Raymond III of Tripoli served as regent of Jerusalem (1174–1177, 1185–1186) and his faction's quarrel with the Lusignan party contributed to the Frankish defeat at Hattin (1187). Tripoli survived the fall of Jerusalem; it was the last Crusader territory on the Syrian mainland, falling in 1289.

Tuscany was nominally an imperial march (the Margraviate of Tuscany), with the margraves appointed by the emperor to administer the territory. Countess Matilda of Tuscany (1046–1115) — the last and greatest of the margraves — allied firmly with the papacy against the empire, sheltering Pope Gregory VII and witnessing the Walk to Canossa (1077). Her donation of her lands to the papacy (1102) was contested by the emperor. After Matilda's death, Tuscany's communes gradually asserted autonomy; Frederick Barbarossa attempted to reimpose imperial control in the 1160s–1180s but ultimately failed. The Tuscan cities achieved de facto independence confirmed by the Peace of Constance (1183).

Countess Matilda of Tuscany, who had sheltered Pope Gregory VII during Henry IV's humiliation at Canossa (1077) and was the papacy's most powerful Italian ally, donated all her lands to the papacy in her will (1102, renewed 1115). The 'Matildine Lands' — central Tuscany including Lucca, Modena, Reggio, and Mantua — were disputed between the papacy and the empire for over a century after her death (1115). Emperor Frederick II's settlement (1213) ceded them to the papacy in exchange for imperial support, though enforcement was never complete. The donation contributed to the Papal States' territorial claims in Tuscany.

Ulster, as one of the five traditional provinces of Ireland (along with Munster, Leinster, Connacht, and Meath), contributed warriors and tribute to the High King system but frequently asserted regional autonomy. The Uí Néill dynasty — which dominated Ulster and also monopolized the High Kingship of Ireland — split into Northern and Southern branches. Brian Boru's challenge to Uí Néill dominance of the high kingship culminated in the Battle of Clontarf (1014). The Anglo-Norman conquest fragmented Ulster among native Irish chiefs and incoming Anglo-Norman lords.

The Abbasid Revolution (747–750) overthrows the Umayyad Caliphate; the last Umayyad caliph Marwan II is defeated at the Battle of the Zab and killed in Egypt. The Abbasids move the capital from Damascus to the newly founded Baghdad (762).
Mediterranean naval and territorial competition; Umayyad Iberia distinct from caliphal Damascus but participated in broader Mediterranean conflict.
Umayyad raids into Frankish territory checked at Tours (732); ended with Pepin's recovery of Septimania.

Abd al-Rahman III of the Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba proclaimed himself Caliph in 929 — a direct challenge to the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad and the Fatimid Caliphate in Tunisia. The proclamation was a response to Fatimid pressure on Spain's North African trade and represented the peak of Umayyad power in al-Andalus. The Caliphate of Córdoba (929–1031) coincided with the apex of Moorish learning and art (the Great Mosque expansion, the palace-city of Medina Azahara). The caliphate collapsed in the chaos of the Fitna (1009–1031), fragmenting into the Taifa kingdoms.

The Umayyad conquest of Visigothic Hispania (711–718) was among the fastest and most complete conquests in medieval history. Tariq ibn Ziyad's victory at Guadalete (711) killed King Roderic and eliminated the Visigothic army; Musa ibn Nusayr's subsequent campaigns reduced the remaining cities through a combination of military force and accommodation (many Visigothic noble families converted to Islam and retained their estates). Toledo surrendered without a siege; only the northern mountains (Asturias, Basque Country, Pyrenean valleys) retained Christian organization. The conquest established al-Andalus as a Umayyad province directly governed from Damascus/Córdoba.

Venice's relationship with Byzantium was structured through a series of golden bulls (imperial rescripts) that granted progressively more extensive commercial privileges. Alexios I's golden bull (1082) granted Venice duty-free trade throughout the empire in exchange for naval assistance against the Normans — a more favorable position than Byzantine citizens. Subsequent agreements modified these terms. The 1171 arrest of Venetian merchants throughout the empire (by Manuel I, who favored Genoese competition) temporarily collapsed the relationship; the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople (1204) was partly Venetian revenge for this humiliation. The Latin Empire then granted Venice a permanent quarter and extensive Aegean territories.

Venice held a privileged trading position within the Byzantine Empire from 1082 (Alexios I's Golden Bull granting trading rights) onward, paying no customs duties and operating with greater freedom than Byzantine citizens. The relationship was exploitative: Venetian commercial dominance of Byzantine ports damaged the empire's own merchant class and finances. Byzantine resentment culminated in the 'Massacre of the Latins' (1182), when the mob killed thousands of Venetians and other Latins in Constantinople. The Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople (1204) — largely shaped by Venetian interests — was the violent culmination of a century of tension.

Venice acquired Cyprus (1489) when Queen Catherine Cornaro — a Venetian noblewoman who had married the last Lusignan king James II — abdicated under Venetian pressure after her husband and infant son died. Venice's acquisition of Cyprus gave it the most strategically located island in the eastern Mediterranean, directly on the sea routes from Alexandria to Venice. Cyprus served as Venice's main eastern naval base and commercial entrepôt for over 80 years until Selim II's Ottoman invasion (1570–1571) — the campaign that preceded the Battle of Lepanto.

The Duchy of Naxos (or Duchy of the Archipelago) was a Venetian-backed crusader state in the Cyclades Islands, created by Marco Sanudo (1207) after the Fourth Crusade. Sanudo, a Venetian nobleman, conquered the Cyclades and established a Latin duchy that would persist for over 350 years until Ottoman conquest (1579). The duchy was formally a fief of the Latin Empire of Constantinople; after 1261 it maintained autonomy by accepting Ottoman suzerainty while retaining Catholic Latin governance. The duchy's extraordinary longevity demonstrates Venetian skill in establishing durable island outposts.

The Treaty of Verdun (843) — signed after three years of Carolingian civil war following Louis the Pious's death — permanently divided the Carolingian Empire among his three surviving sons: Louis the German (East Francia/Germany), Charles the Bald (West Francia/France), and Lothair (Middle Francia + the imperial title). The partition created the political geography of Western Europe: France and Germany as separate states, with the contested 'middle strip' (Lorraine, Burgundy, Italy) as the perpetual battleground between them for the next 1,100 years.

The Sicilian Vespers (1282) permanently split the Kingdom of Sicily into two distinct states: the island of Sicily under Aragonese rule (Peter III of Aragon, 1282–1285) and the mainland kingdom (Naples) remaining under the Angevins. The split was formalized in the Peace of Caltabellotta (1302), which recognized Frederick III of Sicily as king of the island and Charles II of Naples as king of the mainland. The divided kingdom persisted for over 150 years, with periodic wars (the Wars of the Sicilian Vespers, 1282–1302; the later Angevin-Aragonese conflicts) until the Aragonese-ruled dynasty also acquired Naples (1442).

The Viking Age in England (793–954) transformed the political map of the British Isles. Beginning with the Lindisfarne raid (793), Scandinavian raids intensified until the Great Heathen Army's invasion (865–878) conquered all Anglo-Saxon kingdoms except Wessex. Alfred the Great's survival and eventual treaty with Guthrum (878) established the Danelaw; his descendants reconquered it by 954. The second Viking Age brought Cnut the Great (1016–1035) as King of England and creator of the North Sea Empire. The Norman Conquest (1066) — conducted by Norsemen who had assimilated into French culture — was the Vikings' final and most enduring impact on England.
Viking raids on West Francia, including Paris (845, 885), led to Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte and Normandy.

The Umayyad conquest of Hispania (711–718) destroyed the Visigothic Kingdom in a remarkably short campaign. Tariq ibn Ziyad's initial crossing (711) and the victory at Guadalete (where Roderic was killed) was followed by Musa ibn Nusayr's systematic reduction of the remaining Visigothic cities. Toledo, the Visigothic capital, surrendered without a siege; many Visigothic noble families converted to Islam and retained their estates as clients (mawali) of the new rulers. Only the northern mountain regions (Asturias, the Basque Country) resisted; these became the seed of the Reconquista.
