The Volga Bulgaria — a Turkic Muslim state on the middle Volga — maintained commercial relations with Kievan Rus through the river trade routes. Rus merchants traveled up the Volga to trade at Bulgar (the Volga Bulgarian capital), exchanging slaves, furs, and forest products for silver dirhams from the Islamic world and luxury goods. The relationship was also politically competitive: Sviatoslav I of Kiev campaigned against the Volga Bulgars (965) as part of his eastern campaigns that also destroyed the Khazar Khaganate. The subsequent relationship was commercially productive but periodically disrupted by Rus-Bulgarian border conflicts.

The Volga Bulgaria — a Turkic Muslim trading state controlling the middle Volga fur trade route between the Baltic and the Caspian — was destroyed by the Mongols during the western campaign (1236–1237), several months before the assault on Kievan Rus. Batu Khan's forces sacked the Volga Bulgarian capital (Bulgar/Bilyar) in 1236; the population was massacred or enslaved. The destruction eliminated Islam's most northerly advanced state and the primary intermediary in the Baltic-Caspian fur trade, reshaping the economic geography of the Eurasian steppe.

Wallachia maintained a complex relationship with the Kingdom of Hungary as a nominal vassal that frequently asserted effective independence. Hungarian kings claimed suzerainty over Wallachia as a buffer against Tatar and later Ottoman pressure; Wallachian voivodes paid tribute and provided military service intermittently. The Battle of Posada (1330) — in which Wallachian Prince Basarab I defeated Charles I of Hungary's invasion force in a mountain ambush — established Wallachian de facto independence. Mircea the Elder maintained a more cooperative relationship with Hungary as a counterbalance to Ottoman pressure, but never accepted permanent Hungarian control.

Wallachia and Moldavia — the two Danubian principalities that constitute modern Romania — shared Vlach/Romanian language and culture but developed as separate principalities. Wallachia (founded c. 1310) and Moldavia (c. 1359) both navigated between Ottoman suzerainty (both became Ottoman tributaries, Wallachia from 1396, Moldavia from 1456) and Hungarian/Polish protection. The two principalities occasionally coordinated — Mircea the Elder of Wallachia and Alexander the Good of Moldavia both at times resisted Ottoman pressure — but were never permanently united in the medieval period.

Wallachia became an Ottoman tributary in stages following the Battle of Nicopolis (1396), though Mircea the Elder had already acknowledged Ottoman suzerainty earlier (1393). The arrangement — paying haraç (tribute) and providing military contingents while maintaining internal self-governance — was periodically disrupted by resistance. Vlad III 'the Impaler' (Dracula) famously broke from Ottoman suzerainty and impaled Ottoman envoys (1459), triggering a massive Ottoman invasion. Wallachia's mountain passes and forest terrain, combined with diplomatic maneuver between the Ottomans and Hungary, allowed it to maintain autonomy through the tribute system.

The Capetian dynasty transformed West Francia into the Kingdom of France through three centuries of patient royal domain expansion, administrative development, and dynastic continuity. Hugh Capet (elected 987) ruled only the Île-de-France directly; his great-granddaughter would have recognized little 'France' beyond Paris. Philip II Augustus (1180–1223) doubled the royal domain by conquering Normandy and Anjou. Louis IX (1226–1270) institutionalized royal justice. Philip IV 'the Fair' (1285–1314) built the royal bureaucracy. By 1300, France was the most powerful and administratively sophisticated monarchy in Europe.

Zeta (modern Montenegro) maintained resistance to Ottoman conquest after the fall of Serbia (1459) under the Crnojević lords, who used the mountainous terrain and Venetian coastal support to hold out until 1499. Lord Ivan Crnojević established the first printing press in the South Slavic world (1494) at Cetinje, producing liturgical books in Cyrillic. After the Crnojević submission (1499), Zeta's mountains provided natural fortress conditions that prevented effective Ottoman administration; the region maintained effective autonomy under the Prince-Bishops of Montenegro through the Ottoman period.

Zeta (the coastal principality corresponding to modern Montenegro) was a constituent territory of the Serbian state under the Nemanjić dynasty, ruled by cadet branches of the dynasty as appanages. After the Battle of Kosovo (1389) and the fragmentation of the Serbian Empire, Zeta gained increasing autonomy under the Balšić and then Crnojević dynasties. The Zeta nobility fought ongoing resistance to Ottoman expansion while the Serbian Despotate's main territories fell; the Crnojevići maintained Zeta (Montenegro) as the last bastion of Serbian Christian statehood until 1499.

Zeta (Montenegro) maintained a complex relationship with the Serbian Despotate (1402–1459) under the Lazarević and Branković dynasties. The Zeta lords (Balšić, then Crnojević) periodically acknowledged Serbian Despotat suzerainty while maintaining effective independence. After the fall of the Despotate (Smederevo, 1459), Zeta under the Crnojević family became the last organized Serbian Christian resistance to Ottoman conquest — a role it maintained through its mountain geography, Venetian coastal support, and distance from the main Ottoman axes of advance.
The Peace of Zadar in 1358 transferred Dalmatia from Venice to Hungary.
The Peace of Zadar in 1358 allowed Ragusa to negotiate full independence.
Ragusa became a major Adriatic trading power maintaining independence between Venice, Hungary, and the Ottoman Empire.
In 1468 Ragusa negotiated a tribute agreement with the Ottoman Empire, paying an annual sum in exchange for trading privileges.
The Ottoman tribute arrangement allowed Ragusa to operate as a commercial intermediary between the Christian and Muslim worlds.
The Commune of Siena established self-governance in 1147 as a merchant-dominated republic.
Siena became one of the major banking centres of medieval Europe, with families financing popes and kings.
At the Battle of Montaperti in 1260 Siena routed the Florentine Guelfs.
The 1260 victory at Montaperti temporarily made Siena the dominant city in Tuscany.
The Black Death of 1348 killed approximately half of Siena's population within months.
Siena's cathedral, under construction to become the largest in Christendom, was left unfinished after the 1348 plague.
Richard I of England departed on the Third Crusade with Philip II of France around 1190.
Richard I of England conquered Cyprus from its Byzantine ruler during the Third Crusade.
Richard I retook Acre after a two-year siege and won the Battle of Arsuf in 1191.
The Treaty of Jaffa in 1192 allowed Christian pilgrims access to Jerusalem without political control of the city.
Otto IV of Brunswick, a Welf, was elected Holy Roman Emperor in 1198 with the support of Pope Innocent III.
Otto IV was crowned emperor in Rome in 1209.
After Otto IV invaded papal territories in Italy, Innocent III excommunicated him and backed the Hohenstaufen candidate Frederick II.
Otto IV's defeat at the Battle of Bouvines in 1214 destroyed his power base, leaving Frederick II as undisputed emperor.
Robert Bruce killed his rival John Comyn in a Dumfries church in February 1306.
Robert Bruce was crowned King of Scotland at Scone in 1306.
Robert Bruce won the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314.
English recognition of Scottish independence came with the Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton in 1328.
The English Franciscan Roger Bacon finished the Opus Majus in 1267 at the request of Pope Clement IV.
The Opus Majus surveyed mathematics, optics, astronomy, alchemy, and moral philosophy and advocated an experimental method.
Roger Bacon was a Franciscan friar active at Oxford and Paris who advocated systematic empirical observation, mathematics, and experimentation.
Roger Bacon wrote his Opus Majus in 1267 for Pope Clement IV, arguing for educational reform.
Roger Bacon proposed a calendar reform later reflected in the Gregorian calendar adopted about 300 years afterward.
Roger II of Sicily was crowned king on 25 December 1130 by Antipope Anacletus II.
Roger II consolidated Sicily, southern Italy, and parts of North Africa into the Kingdom of Sicily.
Roger II's royal chancery at Palermo operated in Greek, Arabic, and Latin.
Roger II codified the Assizes of Ariano, establishing royal law superseding feudal custom.
Benedict of Nursia founded the monastery of Monte Cassino around 529.
Benedict of Nursia wrote the Rule of Saint Benedict, a code regulating monastic life through prayer, work, and study.
The Rule of Saint Benedict became the dominant framework for western monasticism.
Grand Prince Vladimir of Kiev formally adopted Byzantine Christianity in 988.
In 988 Vladimir of Kiev ordered the mass baptism of the Rus population in the Dnieper at Kiev.
Vladimir's adoption of Byzantine Christianity aligned Rus with Constantinople rather than the Latin West.
Prince Vladimir I of Kievan Rus accepted Byzantine Christianity and was baptized at Chersonesus in Crimea around 988.
Vladimir I married the Byzantine princess Anna, the first dynastic marriage between Rus and Byzantium.
Vladimir ordered the mass baptism of the Kievan population in the Dnieper River following his conversion.
Hulagu Khan's Mongol army sacked Baghdad over thirteen days in February 1258.
The last Abbasid Caliph al-Musta'sim was executed following the Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258.
The Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258 destroyed the House of Wisdom library.
Batu Khan's western Mongol army, guided by Subutai, stormed Kiev after a brief siege in December 1240.
Contemporary accounts describe Kiev reduced to rubble after the Mongol storming of 1240.
After the 1240 sack the Kievan political confederation of Rus principalities ceased to exist as an independent entity.
Alaric I's Visigoths sacked Rome over three days in August 410.
The sack of 410 was the first time Rome had fallen to foreign enemies in 800 years.
The sack of Rome in 410 prompted Augustine to write The City of God in part as a response.
King Louis IX of France led the Seventh Crusade against Egypt.
Louis IX's crusader army captured Damietta in 1249.
The French crusader army was defeated by Mamluk forces at the Battle of Al Mansurah and Louis IX was captured in April 1250.
Louis IX was ransomed for 800,000 gold bezants.
Saladin, a Kurdish general in the service of the Zengid sultan Nur ad-Din, became vizier of the Fatimid Caliphate in Cairo in 1169.
Saladin ended the Fatimid dynasty on the death of the last Fatimid caliph in 1171.
On Nur ad-Din's death in 1174 Saladin seized Damascus, unifying Egypt and Syria under his control.
Saladin died in Damascus on 4 March 1193.
After Saladin's death in 1193 his empire was partitioned among his sons and his brother al-Adil.
Saladin's Ayyubid state ruled Egypt, Syria, and parts of the Hejaz.
Saladin annihilated the Kingdom of Jerusalem's army at the Horns of Hattin on 4 July 1187.
Jerusalem surrendered to Saladin on 2 October 1187 after a two-week siege.
Under Saladin's surrender terms Jerusalem's citizens were ransomed rather than massacred.
News of Jerusalem's fall prompted Pope Gregory VIII to issue the bull Audita tremendi calling the Third Crusade.
At the Horns of Hattin on 4 July 1187 Saladin captured King Guy of Lusignan and destroyed the Crusader army.
Balian of Ibelin negotiated the surrender of Jerusalem to Saladin on 2 October 1187.
Saladin allowed Jerusalem's Christian population to ransom themselves and depart in peace after the 1187 surrender.
The 1187 fall of Jerusalem to Saladin triggered the Third Crusade.
Sassanid Persian forces under Khosrow II captured Jerusalem in 614 after a 21-day siege.
The True Cross was carried off from Jerusalem to Ctesiphon after the Sassanid capture of 614.
Emperor Heraclius's counter-offensive eventually recovered the True Cross in 628.
The Dominican friar Girolamo Savonarola rose to prominence in Florence in 1494 after the expulsion of the Medici.
Savonarola organized 'Bonfires of the Vanities' in Florence that burned cosmetics, mirrors, secular books, and artworks.
Savonarola was excommunicated by Pope Alexander VI in 1497.
Savonarola was arrested, hanged, and burned in the Piazza della Signoria on 23 May 1498.
Charlemagne began the Saxon Wars in 772, the longest campaign of his reign, lasting until 804.
Charlemagne destroyed the Irminsul, a sacred Saxon pillar, in 772.
At the Massacre of Verden in 782 Charlemagne reportedly executed 4,500 Saxon prisoners in a single day.
The Capitulary of Saxony in 785 imposed Christianity on the Saxons on pain of death.
In 1054, Cardinal Humbert and Patriarch Michael Cerularius exchanged excommunications in the Hagia Sophia, formalizing the split between the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.
The 1054 schism was driven by disputes over ecclesiastical authority and theological differences including the filioque controversy and clerical celibacy.
The East-West schism hardened with the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople in 1204.
Edward I of England invaded Scotland in 1296 and removed the Stone of Destiny, triggering the Wars of Scottish Independence.
William Wallace won a victory at Stirling Bridge in 1297.
Around 843 CE, Kenneth MacAlpin unified the Pictish and Scottish kingdoms, establishing Alba, the precursor of Scotland.
Gaelic language and culture gradually supplanted Pictish traditions in the kingdom of Alba.
In 1320, the Scottish nobility wrote the Declaration of Arbroath to Pope John XXII, arguing for Scottish independence and recognition of Robert Bruce as king.
The Declaration of Arbroath stated that if Bruce agreed to English rule, the Scots would choose another king to defend their freedom.
Bernard of Clairvaux preached the Second Crusade beginning in 1147 in response to Zengi's capture of Edessa in 1144.
Louis VII of France and Conrad III of Germany led the Second Crusade, the largest Crusade to that date.
The Second Crusade's siege of Damascus in 1148 ended in retreat, marking the first major Crusade to fail completely.
Pope Innocent II convened the Second Lateran ecumenical council at the Lateran in April 1139, following the death of Antipope Anacletus II.
The Second Lateran Council of 1139 annulled the acts of Antipope Anacletus II and condemned contemporary heresies.
The Second Lateran Council of 1139 enacted the prohibition on clerical marriage as a matter of canon law.
In 1055, the Seljuk Turkish leader Tughril Beg entered Baghdad and received the title of Sultan from the Abbasid Caliph, ending Buyid Shia domination of the caliphate.
The Seljuks, recent converts to Sunni Islam, became its military champions after entering Baghdad in 1055.
Tughril Beg's successors Alp Arslan and Malik Shah built a Seljuk empire stretching from Central Asia to the Mediterranean.
Francesco Sforza, a condottiere who had married the illegitimate daughter of the last Visconti duke, seized Milan in 1450 after three years of the failed Ambrosian Republic.
Under Francesco Sforza, Milan became one of Italy's most stable and prosperous states and commissioned the Ospedale Maggiore.
Francesco Sforza helped balance the Italian powers through the Italian League.
On the evening of 30 March 1282, a riot began near the Church of the Holy Spirit outside Palermo after a French soldier assaulted a Sicilian woman.
Within a month of 30 March 1282, approximately 8,000 French soldiers and officials were massacred across Sicily.
King Peter III of Aragon invaded Sicily within weeks of the 1282 uprising with a Hohenstaufen inheritance claim.
The Sicilian Vespers of 1282 permanently separated Sicily from the mainland Angevin kingdom.
The Sicilian Vespers uprising began at the Church of the Holy Spirit outside Palermo on 30 March 1282, at the bell call for evening prayer.
Within six weeks of the 1282 uprising, the entire island of Sicily had expelled or killed the French Angevin garrison.
Peter III of Aragon arrived in Sicily in August 1282 and was accepted as king of Sicily by the rebels.
Between June and August 626, a combined Avar-Slav-Persian force besieged Constantinople while Emperor Heraclius campaigned in Persia.
During the 626 siege, the Byzantine navy prevented the Avars from ferrying Persian troops across the Bosphorus and destroyed Slav boats attempting the crossing.
The Avars raised the siege of Constantinople in August 626 after a final assault failed.
The Umayyad Caliphate launched its first major assault on Constantinople from 674 to 678, establishing a naval base at Cyzicus and launching annual summer attacks on the city's sea walls.
Byzantine Greek fire, projected by ships' siphons, destroyed the Arab fleet during the 674-678 siege of Constantinople.
The failure of the 674-678 siege forced the Umayyad Caliph Muawiyah to sue for peace and pay annual tribute to Byzantium.
On 15 July 1099, the First Crusade assaulted and captured Jerusalem in a single day's fighting.
The 1099 capture of Jerusalem was followed by a massacre of the city's Muslim and Jewish population.
After the 1099 capture, Godfrey of Bouillon became the first ruler of Jerusalem, taking the title 'Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre' rather than 'king'.
The 1099 capture of Jerusalem fulfilled Pope Urban II's call at Clermont in 1095 and created the Kingdom of Jerusalem.
From May to June 1097, a combined Byzantine-Crusader force besieged Nicaea, the capital of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum.
During the 1097 siege of Nicaea, Emperor Alexios I arranged for the city to surrender directly to the Byzantines rather than the Crusaders, preventing a sack.
After the 1097 surrender of Nicaea, the Crusaders were paid compensation by Alexios I for being denied plunder.
The First Crusade's eight-month siege of Antioch succeeded in 1098 when a Frankish traitor opened a gate.
After taking Antioch in 1098, the crusaders were immediately besieged by a Muslim relief army.
Inspired by the discovery of the Holy Lance, the starving crusaders sallied out from Antioch in 1098 and routed the Muslim forces.
In 626, a combined Avar-Sassanid-Slav force besieged Constantinople while Emperor Heraclius campaigned deep inside Persia.
The Theodosian Walls of Constantinople, defended by Patriarch Sergius and a small garrison, repelled the 626 assault.
The failure of the 626 siege contributed to the Avar confederation's decline and enabled Heraclius's decisive victory over Persia in 627.
A Viking fleet besieged Paris from November 885 to October 886, attempting to sail past it to raid Burgundy.
Count Odo of Paris and Bishop Gozlin organized an 11-month defense of the two bridges across the Seine, preventing the Vikings from passing.
King Charles the Fat arrived with an army during the siege of Paris but paid the Vikings tribute and allowed them to pass through.
Odo's defense of Paris made him popular enough to be elected King of West Francia in 888.
A Viking fleet besieged Paris from November 885 through October 886.
Count Odo of Paris organized a defense that held the two stone bridges, blocking the Viking advance up the Seine.
Emperor Charles the Fat arrived with an army but paid the Vikings tribute and allowed them to raid Burgundy rather than attacking.
Odo's heroism and Charles the Fat's humiliation at the siege of Paris led to Odo's election as king of West Francia in 888.
The counterweight trebuchet, developed in the 12th century, was capable of hurling 100-300 kg projectiles and transformed medieval siege warfare.
The Crusader states responded to the trebuchet threat with concentric castle defenses, round towers, and complex approaches at fortifications such as Krak des Chevaliers and Margat.
Rich silver veins discovered in Bohemia's Kutná Hora district made it the largest silver source in Europe by 1300, producing an estimated 5-6 tonnes annually at peak.
King Wenceslas II's 1300 mining ordinance, the Ius regale montanorum, codified royal control and stable coinage in the new Prague groschen.
At the Battle of Sluys on 24 June 1340, an English fleet under Edward III encountered a French fleet of approximately 200 ships in the harbor of Sluys.
The French chained their ships together in defensive lines at Sluys, and English archers devastated the French crews before men-at-arms boarded and captured the ships.
The French fleet was annihilated at Sluys in 1340, and Edward III won uncontested control of the English Channel for years.
The bull Ad conditorem canonum of 1322 and Cum inter nonnullos of 1323 rejected the absolute-poverty doctrine of the Spiritual Franciscans, holding that Christ and the apostles owned property.
Several Spiritual Franciscans, including Michael of Cesena and William of Ockham, fled to Bavaria under Louis IV's protection after the condemnation.
Edward I of England summoned the 'Model Parliament' in November 1295, the first assembly to include magnates, bishops, knights from each shire, burgesses from each borough, and lower clergy.
The purpose of the 1295 Model Parliament was to grant taxes for simultaneous wars against Scotland, France, and Wales.
The Model Parliament of 1295 established the pattern of two knights per shire and two burgesses per borough as standard for subsequent parliaments.
Edward I issued the Statute of Acton Burnell in October 1283, creating a registry of merchant debts before the mayors of London, York, and Bristol.
Under the 1283 Statute of Acton Burnell, defaulting debtors could be imprisoned and their lands and chattels seized by certified writ.
The Statute of Acton Burnell was superseded by the broader Statute of Merchants in 1285.
Edward III's parliament enacted the Statute of Labourers in 1351, capping wages at pre-Black-Death levels and compelling labourers to accept work at customary rates.
The 1351 Statute of Labourers aimed to neutralise the post-plague labour shortage that had pushed wages up by a factor of two to three.
Edward I issued the Statute of Mortmain in November 1279, forbidding the alienation of land to ecclesiastical corporations without royal licence.
The crown's concern behind the Statute of Mortmain was that land granted to perpetual religious bodies drained the king's tenurial and fiscal base.
Subsequent statutes through 1290 tightened the licensing regime established by the Statute of Mortmain.
A North Sea storm surge on the night of 14 December 1287 breached the coastal defences of the Frisian coast, killing an estimated 50,000-80,000 people.
The 1287 flood enlarged the Zuiderzee, drowned the Lauwers, and reshaped the coastline of what becomes the Netherlands.
A North Sea storm surge on 16 January 1219 inundated the Frisian and Holstein coasts, killing an estimated 36,000 people.
The 1219 storm surge permanently reshaped the coastline of what is now the German Bight, obliterating several villages and forming new tidal bays.
The Suebi crossed the Pyrenees into Iberia in 409 CE as Roman frontier control collapsed.
The Suebi settled in northwestern Iberia and established one of the earliest Germanic kingdoms in the post-Roman world.
The Suebi converted to Catholic Christianity by the 560s CE.
The Visigothic king Leovigild conquered and absorbed the Suebi kingdom in 585 CE, ending it after nearly 175 years of existence.
The absorption of the Suebi kingdom in 585 CE completed the Visigothic unification of the Iberian Peninsula.
Around 851, an Arab merchant known as Sulaymān al-Tājir wrote the earliest surviving Arabic eyewitness account of voyaging from Siraf and Basra to Khānfū (Guangzhou).
The account, the Akhbār al-Ṣīn wa-l-Hind ('Reports of China and India'), was expanded by Abu Zayd al-Sirafi around 916.
The Akhbār al-Ṣīn wa-l-Hind is a foundational text of the medieval Arabic-language geography of the Indian Ocean and the Tang treaty-port system.
Prince Sviatoslav I of Kiev campaigned against the Khazar Khaganate, destroying its fortresses along the Don and Volga rivers.
In 965 Sviatoslav I sacked the Khazar capital Sarkel.
By 969 Sviatoslav I destroyed Itil, the main Khazar city on the Volga delta.
The collapse of the Khazar state allowed the Pechenegs and later the Cumans to fill the steppe vacuum.
The Swabian War, fought from January to September 1499, was the final conflict between the Swiss Confederation and the Holy Roman Empire over Swiss autonomy.
Emperor Maximilian I attempted to impose imperial taxation and court jurisdiction on the Swiss cantons, which the Swiss refused.
Swiss forces defeated imperial and Swabian League forces at the battles of Hard, Bruderholz, and Dornach.
The Peace of Basel of September 22, 1499 granted the Swiss Confederation de facto independence from imperial jurisdiction.
A rapidly fatal disease causing high fever, profuse sweat, and death within 24 hours appeared in England in late summer 1485, weeks after Henry VII's victory at Bosworth.
London was hit hardest by the 1485 sweating sickness, with two lord mayors dying in succession.
Recurrent outbreaks of the sweating sickness occurred in 1508, 1517, 1528, and 1551 before the disease vanished after 1551.
Around 1252 Birger Jarl founded Stockholm as a fortified town controlling trade between Lake Mälaren and the Baltic Sea.
Stockholm grew into the dominant Swedish city and commercial centre through Hanseatic League connections.
Around 1008 Olof Skötkonung became the first Swedish king to be baptised, marking the formal beginning of Swedish Christianisation.
Pagan resistance to Christianisation continued at Uppsala until the late 11th century.
In 1434 Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson led a popular uprising of Swedish miners and peasants against Danish exploitation under the Kalmar Union.
The Engelbrekt rebellion established Sweden's first Riksdag (parliament) in 1435.
In 1291 the Forest Cantons of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden signed the Federal Charter pledging mutual defense.
The Swiss Confederation won victories at Morgarten in 1315 and Sempach in 1386.
The Swiss won the Battle of Morgarten in November 1315.
Following Morgarten, the three forest cantons of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden renewed their Eternal League in 1315.
Additional cantons joined the Swiss Confederation: Lucerne in 1332, Zürich in 1351, and Bern in 1353.
The Synod of Pavia of February 1160 was convened by Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa to settle the disputed papal election of 1159 between Alexander III and Victor IV.
The Synod of Pavia declared Victor IV the legitimate pope.
Alexander III excommunicated both Victor IV and Barbarossa.
The resulting schism lasted 18 years from 1159 to 1177 and ended at the Peace of Venice in 1177 when Barbarossa submitted to Alexander III after his defeat at Legnano in 1176.
In 664 King Oswiu of Northumbria convened a synod at Whitby Abbey to resolve the conflict between the Celtic Church and the Roman Church over the method of calculating the date of Easter.
Oswiu decided in favor of the Roman tradition over the Celtic tradition of St. Columba.
The Synod of Whitby's decision integrated England into the universal Roman Church and marginalized the Celtic monastic tradition.
King Oswiu of Northumbria convened the Synod of Whitby in 664 to resolve the conflict between Celtic Christianity and Roman Christianity over the dating of Easter and tonsure styles.
Oswiu ruled in favor of Rome, citing Peter's authority over the keys of heaven.
The decision aligned England with Rome and ended the distinctive Celtic church tradition in Northumbria.
At the Battle of Tagliacozzo on August 23, 1268, Charles of Anjou, with papal and French backing, defeated Conradin, the last Hohenstaufen claimant to the kingdom of Sicily.
Charles's general Erard de Valéry feigned retreat to break the Staufen advance, then counterattacked with a concealed reserve force.
Conradin was captured fleeing and publicly beheaded in Naples, ending the Hohenstaufen dynasty's struggle for Sicily.
Timur (Tamerlane), a Turco-Mongol ruler from Samarkand, conducted large-scale conquests in the late 14th century.
Timur destroyed the Golden Horde in 1395-1396, sacked Delhi in 1398, defeated the Mamluks in Syria in 1400-1401, and destroyed the Ottoman army at Ankara in 1402.
Timur's empire collapsed on his death in 1405.
In 1402 Timur (Tamerlane) defeated and captured Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I at the Battle of Ankara.
After the Battle of Ankara, Timur restored independent Anatolian principalities and returned to Central Asia, dying in 1405.
The Ottoman Interregnum of 1402-1413 temporarily halted Ottoman expansion and gave Byzantine Constantinople a 50-year reprieve.
German crusaders from Lübeck and Bremen founded a field hospital at the Siege of Acre around 1190 that became the Teutonic Order in 1198.
The Teutonic Knights were invited to defend Hungary's southeastern frontier, then redirected to the Baltic in 1226.
The Teutonic Knights conquered and Christianized Prussia and Latvia, creating a military state that ruled until 1525.
On July 15, 1410, the combined Polish-Lithuanian army under King Władysław II Jagiełło and Grand Duke Vytautas defeated the Teutonic Order at Grunwald (Tannenberg).
Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen and most of the Teutonic Order's leadership were killed at Grunwald.
Under the Peace of Thorn of 1411, the Teutonic Order paid reparations but retained Prussia.
In 1309 the Teutonic Order moved its Grand Master's seat from Venice to Marienburg (Malbork) in Prussia.
Marienburg castle, expanded through the 14th century, became the largest Gothic brick castle in the world.
The Teutonic Order governed Prussia by building roads, founding cities, and organizing agricultural colonization.
In 1226 Duke Conrad I of Masovia invited the Teutonic Knights to help subdue the pagan Prussian tribes raiding his territories.
The Golden Bull of Rimini of 1226, granted by Frederick II, gave the Teutonic Order autonomous governance of Prussia as an imperial fief.
Beginning in 1230, the Teutonic Order waged a systematic crusade of conquest and colonization in Prussia lasting 50 years, replacing the Baltic Prussian people with German settlers.
The Third Council of Toledo of 589, convened by King Reccared I of the Visigoths, formalized the conversion of the Visigothic ruling class from Arianism to Catholic Christianity.
Reccared publicly abjured Arianism, followed by his bishops and nobles.
The council issued canons unifying the Visigothic church on Roman lines and prohibiting mixed marriages between Catholics and heretics.
The Third Crusade, fought from 1189 to 1192 and led by Philip II of France, Frederick Barbarossa, and Richard I of England, responded to Saladin's capture of Jerusalem in 1187.
Frederick Barbarossa drowned in Cilicia in 1190 and his German army dissolved.
Richard I reconquered the coastal cities and defeated Saladin at Arsuf and Jaffa.
The Treaty of Jaffa of 1192 gave Christians access to Jerusalem without sovereignty, leaving the Kingdom of Jerusalem surviving on the coast.
In 680 Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad, refused to pledge loyalty to Umayyad Caliph Yazid I and marched toward Kufa with 72 followers to lead a revolt.
Husayn ibn Ali was intercepted at Karbala and massacred with his companions on the 10th of Muharram in 680.
Husayn's death created the foundational trauma of Shia Islam, observed as Ashura, and established the Sunni-Shia schism.
Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican friar at the University of Paris, wrote the Summa Theologiae between 1265 and 1274.
The Summa Theologiae was an unfinished synthesis of Aristotelian philosophy and Christian theology using the Scholastic method of objection, counter-argument, and resolution.
Aquinas's natural law theory held that reason can discern moral principles independently of revelation, becoming a foundation of Catholic social and political thought.
In 1370 Timur (Tamerlane) established his empire from Samarkand, beginning conquests that would stretch from Delhi to Ankara.
Timur was a lavish patron of art and architecture, and Samarkand under him became one of the finest cities in the world.
In 1402 Timur defeated Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I at the Battle of Ankara.
Bayezid I was captured at Ankara and reportedly died in captivity.
Timur's defeat of Bayezid I nearly destroyed the Ottoman Empire and gave Constantinople another half-century of existence.
Sultan-Husayn Bayqara ruled from Herat from 1469 to 1506, representing the cultural zenith of the Timurid dynasty.
Bayqara's court attracted the poet Jami and the artist Bihzad, whose miniature paintings defined Persian visual art for centuries.
The Timurid architectural legacy shaped later Mughal and Safavid art.
In July 1402 Timur (Tamerlane) invaded Anatolia and defeated the Ottoman army at the Battle of Ankara.
Sultan Bayezid I was captured at Ankara, the first Ottoman sultan taken prisoner in battle, and died in Timurid captivity.
Timur dismembered the Ottoman Empire, restoring Anatolian beyliks and returning Anatolia to its pre-Ottoman fragmentation.
An Ottoman interregnum from 1402 to 1413 followed as Bayezid's sons fought over the throne.
On May 25, 1085, Alfonso VI of León-Castile captured Toledo, the ancient Visigothic capital, from the Taifa of Toledo.
Toledo fell after negotiation rather than assault, and Alfonso offered religious toleration to its Muslim and Jewish populations.

The conquest of Toledo gave Alfonso access to Toledo's library of Arabic scholarly manuscripts, feeding the translation movement that transmitted Arabic and Greek science and philosophy to Western Europe.
The Treaty of Alcáçovas of September 4, 1479 ended the War of Castilian Succession of 1475-1479 between Portugal and the Catholic Monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella.

Portugal recognized Isabella as rightful Queen of Castile, and Spain recognized Portuguese sovereignty over the Azores, Madeira, the Cape Verde Islands, and trade along the African coast south of the Canaries.
Spain received the Canary Islands under the Treaty of Alcáçovas, the first formal division of Atlantic colonial spheres and predecessor to the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494.
After the English victory at Poitiers in 1356 and the capture of French King John II, France agreed to the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360.
Under the Treaty of Brétigny, England gained full sovereignty over Aquitaine, Calais, and other territories amounting to roughly a third of France.
John II's ransom was set at three million gold écus, and Edward III renounced his claim to the French throne.
Within a decade Charles V of France recovered most of the territories ceded at Brétigny through diplomatic and guerrilla warfare.
The Treaty of Brétigny was concluded in May 1360, temporarily ending the first phase of the Hundred Years' War.
Under the Treaty of Brétigny (1360), England received full sovereignty over Aquitaine, Calais, Ponthieu, and other territories amounting to nearly a third of France.
The 1360 settlement set the ransom of the captured King John II of France at 3 million gold écus.
Under the Treaty of Brétigny (1360), Edward III renounced his claim to the French throne.
The Treaty of Devol was imposed by Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos on the Norman prince Bohemund I in September 1108, following Bohemund's failed invasion of the Byzantine Balkans (1107–1108).
The Treaty of Devol (1108) required Bohemund I to become a Byzantine vassal for the Principality of Antioch, to return all territories taken from Byzantium, and to accept a Byzantine duke in Antioch.
The Treaty of Devol was never enforced, because Bohemund I died in 1111 and his nephew Tancred, who had refused to sign, held Antioch as regent.
The Treaty of Devol (1108) established Byzantine sovereignty claims over Antioch that persisted for decades.
In the Treaty of Arras (1435), Duke Philip the Good of Burgundy abandoned the English alliance and recognised Charles VII as legitimate king of France.
By the Treaty of Arras (1435), Charles VII granted Philip the Good the towns of the Somme and exemption from feudal homage during Philip's lifetime.
On the death of Lothair II without legitimate heirs in 870, his uncles Louis the German and Charles the Bald divided his Middle-Frankish realm (Lotharingia) between them.
The 870 partition of Lotharingia ran from the North Sea down the Meuse to the Saône, establishing a Romance/Germanic linguistic boundary in the Low Countries.

Charles the Bald and Louis the German partitioned the inheritance of their nephew Lothair II at Meerssen on 8 August 870, dividing the Middle Francia of the Treaty of Verdun (843) along the rivers Meuse, Saône, and Rhône.
By the Treaty of Meerssen (870), East Francia gained Frisia, the lower Rhineland, Alsace, and most of Burgundy.
Philip IV of France signed the Treaty of Paris with Count Robert III of Flanders in 1303, partially resolving the conflict that began with the Battle of the Golden Spurs (1302).
The Treaty of Paris (1303) had Flanders acknowledge French suzerainty while recognising Flemish urban liberties and reducing French direct control.
The subsequent Treaty of Athis-sur-Orge (1305) imposed heavy financial penalties on Flanders but failed to incorporate it fully into France.
The Treaty of Verdun (843) was signed by the three surviving sons of Louis the Pious after three years of civil war following his death, permanently dividing the Carolingian Empire.

By the Treaty of Verdun (843), Louis the German received East Francia, Charles the Bald received West Francia, and Lothair I received the middle strip (Lorraine, Burgundy, Italy) plus the imperial title.
The Treaty of Verdun (843) created the 'Middle Francia' corridor between East and West Francia.
Henry III of England and Louis IX of France signed the Treaty of Paris in 1259.
In the Treaty of Paris (1259), Henry III formally renounced English claims to Normandy, Anjou, Maine, Touraine, and Poitou, which had been lost by King John in 1204.
In the Treaty of Paris (1259), Louis IX recognised English lordship over Gascony and compensated Henry III with revenues from several French dioceses.
Under the Treaty of Paris (1259), Henry III had to perform liege homage to Louis IX as feudal lord for his remaining continental territories.
In the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte (911), King Charles the Simple of West Francia granted the lower Seine estuary to the Viking chieftain Rollo.
Under the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte (911), Rollo and his followers accepted baptism, became French vassals, and undertook to defend the Seine from further Viking raids.
The Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte (911) created the Duchy of Normandy, named for the 'Northmen'.

The Treaty of Tordesillas was signed on 7 June 1494, mediated by Pope Alexander VI, dividing the non-European world between Spain and Portugal along a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands.
Under the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494), land east of the meridian line was assigned to Portugal and land west to Spain.
The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) was a revision of the papal bull Inter Caetera (1493), negotiated after Columbus's first voyage revealed Spanish claims in the Atlantic.
The Tordesillas line gave Portugal Brazil, which the navigator Cabral reached in 1500.
The Treaty of Troyes, signed 21 May 1420, made Henry V of England heir to the French throne through his marriage to Catherine of Valois, daughter of Charles VI.
Under the Treaty of Troyes (1420), Charles VI disinherited his son the future Charles VII and recognised Henry V as regent and heir to France.
The Treaty of Troyes (1420) provided that England and France would be united under a single crown on Charles VI's death.
Henry V died in August 1422 and Charles VI died in October 1422, leaving the infant Henry VI as nominal king of both England and France.
The Treaty of Troyes, signed 21 May 1420, made Henry V of England heir to the French crown and regent of France during the lifetime of Charles VI.
Under the Treaty of Troyes (1420), Henry V married Charles VI's daughter Catherine of Valois and the Dauphin Charles (future Charles VII) was declared illegitimate.
Following the deaths of Henry V and Charles VI in 1422, the nine-month-old Henry VI became nominal king of both England and France.
Following Alfred the Great's victory at the Battle of Edington in May 878, the Danish Great Heathen Army under Guthrum sued for peace.
The Treaty of Wedmore (878) required Guthrum and 30 of his leading men to accept Christian baptism, with Alfred as godfather, and Guthrum took the Christian name Æthelstan.
After the Treaty of Wedmore (878), Guthrum withdrew his forces to East Anglia, and the division of England between Wessex and the Danelaw followed in subsequent agreements.
In 843, Empress regent Theodora restored the veneration of icons at a synod presided over by Patriarch Methodius.
The 'Triumph of Orthodoxy' (843) was thereafter commemorated annually on the first Sunday of Great Lent.
The troubadour movement originated around 1100 in Occitan-speaking southern France with Duke William IX of Aquitaine, creating Europe's first major vernacular literary culture.
Troubadours composed lyric poetry in Occitan celebrating fin'amors, a code of idealized courtly love and service to a lady.
The troubadour tradition spread to northern France (trouvères), Germany (Minnesingers), and Iberia.
The Council of Elne (1027) and the Council of Toulouges (1041) extended the Peace of God by prohibiting warfare on certain days of the week and during Lent and Advent (the Treuga Dei).
The Truce of God became general canon law through 11th-century papal endorsement.
In 750, Abbasid armies defeated and executed the last Umayyad caliph Marwan II, who had fled to Egypt where he was caught and killed.
The Abbasids massacred members of the Umayyad family at a banquet in 750.
The Umayyad prince Abd al-Rahman escaped through North Africa to Spain, founding the Emirate of Córdoba and maintaining Umayyad rule there until 1031.
Umayyad general Qutayba ibn Muslim conquered Transoxiana, capturing Bukhara (706), Samarkand (711), and Ferghana (713).
Muhammad ibn Qasim conquered Sind (modern Pakistan) for the Umayyads in 711–715.
The early 8th-century Umayyad campaigns brought major Silk Road cities and the western gateway of the Indian subcontinent into the Islamic world.
The Berber Muslim general Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from North Africa to Iberia with 7,000 troops in April 711, landing at Gibraltar (Jabal Tariq).
At the Battle of Guadalete in July 711, the Visigothic King Roderic was killed and his army destroyed.
Within five years of 711, Arab and Berber forces conquered most of the Iberian Peninsula, with only the Asturian mountains in the far northwest resisting.
Pope Boniface VIII's bull Unam Sanctam (1302) asserted that submission to the Roman pontiff is necessary for salvation.
Unam Sanctam (1302) articulated the doctrine of papal plenitude of power against Philip IV of France.
Queen Margaret I of Denmark architected the personal union of Denmark, Sweden, and Norway at Kalmar in June 1397, with her great-nephew Eric of Pomerania crowned king of all three.
The Kalmar Union (1397) was proposed as a response to the growing power of the Hanseatic League and the Holstein nobility.
The Kalmar Union controlled the Baltic sea lanes and the Sound tolls, representing the largest territorial entity in northern Europe.

Ruprecht I of the Palatinate founded the University of Heidelberg under Pope Urban VI's bull of 23 October 1385, the first continuously surviving university on German territory of the Holy Roman Empire.
The University of Heidelberg opened on 18 October 1386 with Marsilius of Inghen as its first rector.
Cardinal Conrad of Urach issued statutes for the medical school at Montpellier in 1220, formalising a community of physicians teaching there since the late 12th century.
Pope Honorius III granted Montpellier Studium Generale recognition in 1289.
Emperor Frederick II issued the Generalis lictera at Syracuse in 1224, founding a state university at Naples to train administrators and jurists for his Sicilian-imperial bureaucracy.
The University of Naples (1224) was the first European university created by direct state act.
A secession of masters and students from Bologna founded the Studium Generale at Padua in 1222, in protest at infringements on Bolognese scholarly privilege.
Padua developed particular strength in law and, from the 14th century, in medicine and natural philosophy.
Around 1170, the masters teaching in the schools attached to the cathedral of Notre-Dame in Paris organised themselves into a self-governing universitas.
Royal protection in 1200 and the statutes of Robert of Courson in 1215 formalised the University of Paris corporation.
Charles IV's foundation charter of 7 April 1348 established the University of Prague, the first university east of the Rhine and north of the Alps.
Pope Clement VI's bull of 26 January 1347 had granted prior papal approval for the University of Prague.
Alfonso IX of León established a Studium Generale at Salamanca by royal charter in 1218, the earliest such royal foundation in the Latin West.
Alfonso X of Castile-León confirmed and expanded the Salamanca statutes in 1254, and Alexander IV granted the ius ubique docendi in 1255.
The Treaty of Paris of 12 April 1229 ended the Albigensian Crusade and obliged Raymond VII of Toulouse to found and endow a university.
The University of Toulouse (1229) was endowed with chairs in theology, canon law, and the liberal arts, explicitly to combat Cathar heresy through orthodox scholastic teaching.
Duke Rudolf IV's foundation charter of 12 March 1365 established the Studium Generale at Vienna in competition with Charles IV's Prague.
Pope Urban V's confirmation of the University of Vienna followed in 1384.
In 988, Vladimir I of Kiev sent approximately 6,000 Norse Varangian warriors to the Byzantine emperor Basil II.
The dispatch of Varangian warriors in 988 was part of a marriage alliance in which Vladimir I received Basil II's sister Anna.
These Varangian warriors formed the Varangian Guard, an elite mercenary regiment serving Byzantine emperors for centuries.
According to the Primary Chronicle, Slavic and Finnish tribes invited the Varangian leader Rurik to rule Novgorod in 862.
The year 862 is traditionally marked as the founding of the Rus state.
Rurik's successors extended their rule down the Dnieper River trade route and founded Kyiv as their capital.
The dynasty founded by Rurik ruled Russia until 1598.
According to the Primary Chronicle, the Slavic and Finnic tribes of Novgorod invited the Varangian chieftain Rurik to rule them in 862.
Rurik's accession established the Rurikid dynasty.
The Battle of Varna was fought on November 10, 1444, between a crusading force under Wladyslaw III of Poland-Hungary and the Ottoman army of Sultan Murad II.
Wladyslaw III broke the 1444 Peace of Szeged after papal pressure and advanced to Varna on the Black Sea.
King Wladyslaw III was killed during the Battle of Varna.
The Ottoman victory at Varna ended the last serious attempt to drive the Ottomans from Europe.
Vasco da Gama's fleet arrived at Calicut, India, in 1498, completing the first European sea voyage to Asia.
The sea route around the Cape of Good Hope bypassed the Ottoman-controlled eastern Mediterranean and undermined the Venetian and Mamluk spice trade monopoly.
Portuguese control of Indian Ocean sea lanes transformed global commerce within decades of 1498.
Venice's Arsenal employed around 2,000 workers operating an assembly-line production system.
At peak production in the early 16th century, the Venetian Arsenal could produce a galley per day.
The Venetian Arsenal used standardized parts, sequential assembly, specialized workers, and state management of production.
Venice consolidated ship construction at a single state-run complex on the eastern lagoon.
By 1450 the Venetian Arsenal employed approximately 16,000 workers.
By 1450 the Venetian Arsenal could produce a fully-rigged galley in 24 hours using interchangeable parts and assembly-line construction.
Venice organized the mude system of state-organized merchant galley convoys to the Levant, Flanders, and the Black Sea.
Departure and return dates for the mude convoys were fixed by the Venetian Senate.
The mude galleys were state-owned and leased to merchants.
The mude system carried high-value goods including spices, silk, and luxury cloth.
In 1268, Venice faced a severe grain shortage requiring imports from Egypt and Byzantium.
Venice imported grain despite papal prohibitions on trade with Muslims.
Venice repeatedly traded with the Mamluks throughout the Crusader period.
In 1516, the Venetian Senate ordered Jews to live on the Ghetto Nuovo, a former foundry island.
Jews in the Venetian ghetto were locked in at night, required to wear distinctive badges, and barred from owning property outside the ghetto.
Jews in the Venetian ghetto were permitted to practice their faith, maintain synagogues, and engage in commerce.
The Venetian ghetto model spread to other Italian and European cities.
In 1489, Queen Catherine Cornaro ceded Cyprus to the Republic of Venice.
Venice's control of Cyprus from 1489 gave it a crucial eastern Mediterranean island.
The Ottomans took Cyprus from Venice in 1571.
According to later tradition, the lagoon communities of the Veneto elected Paoluccio Anafesto as the first Doge of Venice in 697.
By the late 8th century Venice functioned as a self-governing community under nominal Byzantine suzerainty.
Charlemagne's treaty with Byzantium in 810 confirmed Venetian independence from Frankish authority.
In 1284, the Venetian Great Council authorized the minting of the gold ducat.
The Venetian gold ducat contained 3.5 grams of pure gold, matched in weight to the Florentine florin.
The Venetian ducat circulated unchanged in weight and fineness for five centuries.
In 1202, the Fourth Crusade contracted with Venice for transport to Egypt, agreeing to pay 85,000 silver marks.
When the crusaders could not pay, Doge Enrico Dandolo proposed attacking Zara as partial payment.
After sacking Zara, the Fourth Crusade was redirected to Constantinople.
The crusaders sacked Constantinople in April 1204.
Doge Enrico Dandolo redirected the Fourth Crusade to sack Constantinople in 1204.
Venice gained a quarter of the Byzantine Empire, including Crete, Euboea, and key Aegean ports, after the 1204 sack of Constantinople.
In 1261, Michael VIII Palaiologos recaptured Constantinople with Genoese support, expelling Venice.
The 1261 expulsion began a prolonged Venetian-Genoese rivalry that culminated in the War of Chioggia (1378-1381).
Venice ultimately emerged dominant from the War of Chioggia.
In 1082, Emperor Alexios I Komnenos granted Venice extraordinary commercial privileges in the Golden Bull.
The 1082 Golden Bull was granted in exchange for Venetian naval assistance against Robert Guiscard's Norman invasion of the Balkans.
The Golden Bull gave Venice the right to trade throughout the Byzantine Empire without paying customs duties.
The Golden Bull granted Venetian merchants their own quarter in Constantinople, Durazzo, and other major cities.
The Sicilian Vespers uprising began on the evening of March 30, 1282, near the Church of the Holy Spirit outside Palermo.
The Sicilian Vespers uprising killed approximately 8,000 French officials and soldiers across Sicily.
Peter III of Aragon, whose wife Constance held a Hohenstaufen claim to Sicily, invaded within weeks of the Vespers.
The Sicilian Vespers triggered the Wars of the Sicilian Vespers (1282-1302) and permanently separated Sicily from the mainland Angevin kingdom.
In 1365, Ottoman forces under Sultan Murad I took Adrianople (Edirne) and made it the new Ottoman capital in Europe.
The Ottomans used Adrianople as the base for the conquest of Thrace and Bulgaria in the 1370s.
Adrianople remained the Ottoman capital until Mehmed II moved it to Constantinople after 1453.
In 845, a Norse fleet of 120 ships sailed up the Seine and reached Paris.
Charles the Bald paid 7,000 pounds of silver to make the Vikings leave Paris, the first major Danegeld.
The Norse settled in Normandy in 911 under Rollo.
In 845, a Norse fleet of 120 ships sailed up the Seine and sacked Paris on Easter Sunday.
Charles the Bald paid a ransom of 7,000 pounds of silver to persuade the Vikings to leave Paris in 845.
The 845 ransom was the first of many Danegeld payments by the West Frankish crown.
In 862, Rurik, a Varangian leader from Sweden, was invited by Slavic tribes to rule Novgorod.
Rurik's arrival in 862 marks the foundation of the Rurikid dynasty.
The Rurikid dynasty ruled Russia until 1598.
Around the year 1000, Leif Erikson sailed from Greenland and established a brief Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows on northern Newfoundland.
Later expeditions by Thorfinn Karlsefni encountered indigenous peoples whom the Norse called Skraelings.
The Norse colony in Newfoundland was abandoned within a generation.
In 589, King Reccared I of the Visigoths converted from Arianism to Nicene Christianity at the Third Council of Toledo.
Reccared's conversion brought the Visigothic nation into the Catholic fold and enabled the fusion of Visigothic nobility with the Hispano-Roman church hierarchy.
Norse Varangian merchants developed the Volga trade route running from Scandinavia through Ladoga and Novgorod down the Volga River to the Caspian Sea and Islamic Abbasid markets.
The Volga trade brought large quantities of Arabic silver dirhams to Scandinavia.
Along the Volga route the Norse sold furs, amber, honey, wax, and enslaved peoples.
In 1267, Henry III of England recognized Llywelyn ap Gruffudd as Prince of Wales under the Treaty of Montgomery.
The Treaty of Montgomery was the only time England officially acknowledged a native Welsh prince with the title Prince of Wales.
Edward I's conquest of Wales (1277-1283) extinguished independent Welsh princeship.
In 1077, the excommunicated Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV performed penitential submission at Canossa castle before Pope Gregory VII.
Pope Gregory VII absolved Henry IV after his penance at Canossa.
Henry IV later regained power and drove Gregory VII into exile.
The Wars of the Roses began with the First Battle of St Albans in May 1455.
The Wars of the Roses were fought between the Houses of York and Lancaster, both descended from Edward III.
Over roughly 30 years of the Wars of the Roses, the English throne changed hands six times.
The Wars of the Roses ended with Henry Tudor's victory at Bosworth Field in 1485 and the founding of the Tudor dynasty.
The Peasants' Revolt of June 1381 was the most widespread popular uprising in English medieval history.
The Peasants' Revolt was triggered by an unpopular poll tax and post-Black Death economic grievances.
Rebels under Wat Tyler and John Ball breached London, murdered Archbishop Sudbury, and burned John of Gaunt's Savoy Palace.
Wat Tyler was killed by the Lord Mayor of London in the presence of Richard II at Smithfield.

Edward I of England completes the conquest of native Wales with the defeat and death of Llywelyn ap Gruffudd (killed November 1282) and the capture and execution of his brother Dafydd (1283).

Llywelyn had been the first and last native prince recognized by the English crown (Treaty of Montgomery, 1267); his alliance with Simon de Montfort and his marriage plans (Llywelyn's fiancée Eleanor de Montfort had died in childbirth) created the rift with Edward I.
The Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) divides Wales into shires and imposes English law.
Edward I's program of castle building (Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech, Beaumaris) creates the most sophisticated medieval fortification program in Britain.
On Christmas Day 1066, ten weeks after Hastings, William is crowned king of England at Westminster Abbey by Archbishop Ealdred of York.
Norman troops outside, hearing shouts of acclamation inside, mistake them for an attack and burn surrounding buildings, the ceremony completes amid smoke.

William of Ockham, English Franciscan philosopher, develops Nominalism (only individual things are real; 'universals' are just names) against the Realist-Scholastic tradition, and writes political tracts attacking Pope John XXII's authority over secular rulers.
Living at Munich under Louis IV's protection after fleeing Avignon, he articulates arguments for the limitation of papal temporal power and the priority of imperial authority in secular matters.
Franciscan friar William of Rubruck, sent by Louis IX of France from Acre in May 1253, travels via Constantinople, Sudak, and the Volga to the Mongol court at Karakorum (December 1253).
At the court of Möngke Khan he participates in the famous May 1254 inter-religious debate with Nestorian Christians, Muslims, and Buddhists.
Manuscripts of an early complete Middle English translation of the Latin Vulgate, associated with John Wycliffe and his Oxford circle, circulate from c.
A revised version attributed to John Purvey follows c.
The translation is later banned by Arundel's Constitutions (1409).

An English synod at Blackfriars in London condemns twenty-four propositions drawn from the writings of John Wycliffe, including his rejection of transubstantiation and the temporal endowment of the Church.
Wycliffe retires to Lutterworth, where he completes the translation of the Vulgate into Middle English.
John Wycliffe, Oxford theologian, advocates translating the Bible into English so ordinary people can read it directly, and attacks clerical wealth and papal supremacy.
His followers (Lollards) produce English Bible translations.
Wycliffe's ideas directly inspire Jan Hus in Bohemia and, through Hus, Martin Luther, making him a crucial Protestant precursor.
After sixteen years in Central Asia and India, including extended study at Nalanda monastery, Xuanzang returns with 657 Sanskrit manuscripts and Buddha relics.
Tang Taizong establishes a translation bureau at the Da Cien temple; over the next two decades Xuanzang and his team translate 76 sutras (~1,300 fascicles) into Chinese.
Buddhist monk Xuanzang leaves the Tang capital in defiance of an imperial travel ban to seek authentic Sanskrit sources of Mahayana doctrine.
Travels via the northern Silk Road through Turfan, Kucha, Samarkand, and Bactria, then crosses the Hindu Kush into Gandhara and the Ganges plain.
Tang Buddhist monk Yijing (635–713) completes a 24-year journey to India by the southern sea route via Srivijaya (Sumatra), in contrast to Xuanzang's overland route.
Spends a decade at Nalanda; returns with 400 Sanskrit texts via Srivijaya, where he writes his record of Mahayana monastic discipline in the Indian Ocean world.
On his fourth treasure-fleet voyage (1413–1415) under the Yongle Emperor's commission, Zheng He's detached squadrons reach Hormuz, Aden, and Mogadishu.
A Mogadishu envoy returns with the fleet to Nanjing, bringing the giraffe that became famous in early-Ming court iconography as the qilin.
